Viracocha.title: Viracocha
Viracocha.blind: The creator deity had human appearance and a beard, and ordered the building of a great city, traveling sometimes with companions also called by his name. He rose from a great lake during a time of darkness to bring forth light, making the sun, moon, and stars. He formed humankind by breathing into stones, but his first creation was a race of brainless giants who displeased him; he destroyed them with a flood and made better humans from smaller stones, scattering them across the world. He then disappeared across a great sea, walking upon the water, never to return. He wandered the earth disguised as a beggar, teaching his creations the foundations of civilization and performing miracles, though many refused his teachings and fell into warfare, causing him to weep. It was believed he would return in times of trouble. He was described as a man of medium height, white-skinned, wearing a white robe, carrying a staff and a book. In one telling he had a son and two daughters, all minor deities. He destroyed the people around the great lake with a flood lasting sixty days and nights, sparing two beings, a son of the sun deity and a woman representing fertility, who carried a golden staff and founded a civilization. In another version he fathered the first eight humans, and had a wife associated with the sea. In yet another legend, he had two sons whom he sent to visit distant tribes to test their obedience, naming plants and teaching which were edible, medicinal, or poisonous. The three eventually reached a city and the seacoast, where they walked across the water and vanished.

Quetzalcoatl.title: Quetzalcōātl
Quetzalcoatl.blind: The deity, a feathered serpent, had several conflicting birth stories: in one, a virgin woman was visited in a dream by a supreme god and bore him; in another she conceived by swallowing a precious stone; in a third she was struck in the womb by an arrow shot by a hunter god and gave birth nine months later; in a fourth he was born from an earth goddess, who already had four hundred children forming a band of stars in the sky. Another account made him one of four sons of a creator couple, each ruling a cardinal direction as one of four gods: the deity over the West as god of light, justice, mercy and wind; a war god over the South; a farming god over the East as god of gold and farming; and a fourth god over the North as god of night and sorcery. The deity was linked to the morning star while his twin was the evening star, both aspects of a planet. He invented books and the calendar and gave a grain crop to mankind. He journeyed to the underworld, and with the help of another deity created the current race of mankind from the bones of earlier destroyed races, giving them life with blood drawn from his own ears, calves, tongue, and penis. Later, tricked by the night god into drinking a fermented drink, he slept with his celibate priestess sister. Ashamed, he had himself sealed in a stone chest and burned; his ashes rose and his heart became the morning star. He also brought a cacao plant from a sacred mountain to a people and taught the women to make chocolate.
Quetzalcoatl.story: Quetzalcoatl, a feathered-serpent deity, had several conflicting birth stories: in one, a virgin named Chimalman was visited in a dream by the god Ometeotl and bore him; in another she conceived by swallowing an emerald; in a third she was struck in the womb by an arrow shot by the god Mixcoatl and gave birth nine months later; in a fourth he was born from the goddess Coatlicue, who already had four hundred children forming the Milky Way. Another account made him one of four sons of the creator couple Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl, each ruling a cardinal direction as a Tezcatlipoca: Quetzalcoatl over the West as god of light, justice, mercy and wind; Huitzilopochtli over the South as god of war; Xipe Totec over the East as god of gold and farming; and Tezcatlipoca over the North as god of night and sorcery. Quetzalcoatl was linked to the morning star while his twin Xolotl was the evening star, both aspects of Venus. He invented books and the calendar and gave maize to mankind. He journeyed to the underworld, Mictlan, and with the help of Cihuacoatl created the current race of mankind from the bones of earlier destroyed races, giving them life with blood drawn from his own ears, calves, tongue, and penis. Later, tricked by Tezcatlipoca into drinking pulque, he slept with his celibate priestess sister Quetzalpetlatl. Ashamed, he had himself sealed in a stone chest and burned; his ashes rose and his heart became the morning star. He also brought the cacao plant from a sacred mountain to the Toltec people and taught the women to make chocolate.

Kukulkan.title: Kukulkan
Kukulkan.blind: The main figure is a serpent deity told about in several tales. In one, the figure is a boy born as a snake. As he grows, it becomes clear he is the plumed serpent, and his sister cares for him in a cave. He grows so large that she can no longer feed him, so he flies out of the cave into the sea, causing an earthquake. To let his sister know he is still alive, the figure causes earth tremors every year in a certain month. In another tale, the figure is a winged serpent who flies to the sun and tries to speak with it, but the sun, in its pride, burns his tongue. The same telling says the figure always travels ahead of a rain deity, helping to predict the rains, his tail moving the winds and sweeping the earth clean. Among another people, the figure is portrayed as an evil, monstrous snake, the pet of the sun deity. She destroys much of the world, then tries to kill herself during a long journey between life and death. During this journey she meets a boy who shares food with her; he follows her back to the human world, and she constructs her own country there.

Votan.title: Votan
Votan.blind: The hero was present at a great building constructed by order of his uncle, intended to reach up to a heavenly realm. When the building failed, every people was given its own language, and the hero was charged by a sky deity to divide the lands of a certain region among them. The hero belonged to a royal lineage and established a kingdom named after a serpent symbol on a river, which eventually extended across a wider region to a coastal area. He also led seven families from a distant place to this continent and assigned them lands. Some accounts say the hero defeated a hostile people, built a great city, and established an empire that covered much land. The hero made four trips back to a distant homeland. He was also known by a title referring to a wooden drum and as a jaguar deity of darkness, and his name was one of twenty day names in a local calendar. Descendants of the hero were said to live in a village, forming a family bearing his name. Ritual objects associated with the hero were kept in a sanctuary until they were removed and burned in a public square by a religious official.
Votan.story: Votan was present at a great building constructed by order of his uncle, intended to reach up to heaven. When the building failed, every people was given its own language, and Votan was charged by God to divide the lands of a region called Anahuac among them. Votan belonged to a royal lineage and established a kingdom called "Snake House" on a river, which eventually extended across a wider region to the Pacific coast. He also led seven families from a distant place to this continent and assigned them lands. Some accounts say Votan defeated a people called the Quiname, built a great city, and established an empire that covered much land. Votan made four trips back to a distant homeland. He was also known as "Lord of the Horizontal Wooden Drum" and as a jaguar god of darkness, and his name was one of twenty day names in a local calendar. Descendants of Votan were said to live in a village, forming a family bearing his name. Ritual objects associated with Votan were kept in a sanctuary until they were removed and burned in a public square by a bishop.

Bochica.title: Bochica
Bochica.blind: A mythical figure was remembered in different ways by different witnesses: some described him as a building that had been destroyed by foreign conquerors; others said he was the father of a great cat (perhaps a wild predator) that had been attacking travelers on local roads; others called him an idol; and when asked who he was, one witness replied that he was a wind, dwelling at the site of the destroyed building. In a later, more developed account, he became a civilizing hero who descended to earth to found a religion. He appeared first in one town, and later in another town, where the people welcomed him with hospitality. He then retreated into a cave, where many local chiefs came to visit him seeking wisdom. Chiefs from several nearby towns came to consult him. After the supreme being of the people sent them to a particular city, that city became a sacred place, where a great temple dedicated to the sun was built, and religious festivals were organized to commemorate the hero's arrival.

Adapa.title: Adapa
Adapa.blind: After a great flood, humanity was left without guidance, which led to the rise of the hero, a mortal man and sage or priest of the temple of the wise god in a certain city. The wise god, sometimes considered his father, had given the hero great wisdom but not eternal life. While carrying out his duties, the hero was fishing on a great river when the sea became rough from a strong wind and his boat capsized. Angered, the hero broke the wings of the south wind, preventing it from blowing for seven days. The sky god called the hero to account for this action, but the wise god instructed the hero to gain the sympathy of two gatekeeper deities who guard the gates of heaven, and warned him not to eat or drink anything offered there, as it might kill him, but to accept and wear any garments and oil offered. The hero put on mourning garments and told the two gatekeeper deities he mourned because they had disappeared from the land. He was then offered the food of life and water of life but refused them. When garments and oil were offered, he accepted and used them as instructed. Brought before the sky god, he was asked why he refused to eat or drink, and he replied that the wise god had told him not to. The sky god laughed at the wise god's actions and passed judgment, asking rhetorically what harm the hero had brought on mankind, adding that men would now suffer disease, which a healing goddess might relieve. The hero was then sent back down to earth. The ending of the story is missing. In another fragmentary tale, the hero and a legendary king descend nine cubits into the earth and break into an ancient tomb; what occurs there is unclear, but they leave and reseal the tomb.
Adapa.story: After a great flood, humanity was left without guidance, which led to the rise of Adapa, a mortal man and sage or priest of the temple of Ea in the city of Eridu. Ea, sometimes considered his father, had given Adapa great wisdom but not eternal life. While carrying out his duties, Adapa was fishing on the river Tigris when the sea became rough from a strong wind and his boat capsized. Angered, Adapa broke the wings of the south wind, preventing it from blowing for seven days. The god Anu called Adapa to account for this action, but Ea instructed Adapa to gain the sympathy of Dumuzid and Gishzida, who guard the gates of heaven, and warned him not to eat or drink anything offered there, as it might kill him, but to accept and wear any garments and oil offered. Adapa put on mourning garments and told Dumuzid and Gishzida he mourned because they had disappeared from the land. He was then offered the food of life and water of life but refused them. When garments and oil were offered, he accepted and used them as instructed. Brought before Anu, he was asked why he refused to eat or drink, and he replied that Ea had told him not to. Anu laughed at Ea's actions and passed judgment, asking rhetorically what harm Adapa had brought on mankind, adding that men would now suffer disease, which the goddess Ninkarrak might relieve. Adapa was then sent back down to earth. The ending of the story is missing. In another fragmentary tale, Adapa and King Enmerkar descend nine cubits into the earth and break into an ancient tomb; what occurs there is unclear, but they leave and reseal the tomb.

Osiris.title: Osiris
Osiris.blind: The fertility god, god of agriculture and the afterlife, was the eldest child of an earth deity and a sky deity, and was both brother and husband to a goddess. His brother desired his throne and conspired with a foreign queen and seventy-two accomplices to kill him. The brother tricked the god into entering a box, sealed it with lead, and threw it into a great river. The goddess searched for her husband and found him embedded in a tree trunk that was holding up the roof of a palace in a foreign coastal city. She retrieved the body, but the brother found it again and cut it into pieces, scattering them. The goddess, joined by her sister, searched the land and recovered all the pieces except the god's genitals. She reassembled and wrapped the body, then used magic to briefly revive him so she could conceive a child. She later gave birth to their son, who eventually avenged his father by defeating the brother. In another telling, the god was an ancient king who taught his people to abandon cannibalism and travelled the world with his sons, a nature spirit, woodland spirits, and nine goddesses of inspiration, teaching humanity to cultivate a fruiting vine and sow grain crops. After returning home, he was murdered by his evil brother, who divided his body into twenty-six pieces and distributed them among fellow conspirators to implicate them. The goddess and a strong hero (her son) avenged him and slew the murderer. The goddess recovered all the parts except the phallus, secretly buried them, and made replicas that were distributed to various locations, which became centers of his worship. Thereafter, the god ruled as lord of the dead and the underworld.
Osiris.story: Osiris, god of fertility, agriculture, and the afterlife, was the eldest son of the earth god and the sky goddess, and was both brother and husband to Isis. His brother Set desired his throne and conspired with the Queen of Ethiopia and seventy-two accomplices to kill him. Set tricked Osiris into entering a box, sealed it with lead, and threw it into the Nile. Isis searched for her husband and found him embedded in a tamarisk tree trunk that was holding up the roof of a palace in Byblos on the Phoenician coast. She retrieved the body, but Set found it again and cut it into pieces, scattering them. Isis, joined by her sister Nephthys, searched the land and recovered all the pieces except Osiris's genitals. Isis reassembled and wrapped the body, then used magic to briefly revive him so she could conceive a child. She later gave birth to their son, Horus, who eventually avenged his father by defeating Set. In another telling, Osiris was an ancient king who taught his people to abandon cannibalism and travelled the world with his sons, a nature spirit, woodland spirits, and nine goddesses of inspiration, teaching humanity to cultivate the vine and sow wheat and barley. After returning home, he was murdered by his evil brother, who divided his body into twenty-six pieces and distributed them among fellow conspirators to implicate them. Isis and the strong hero (Horus) avenged him and slew the murderer. Isis recovered all the parts except the phallus, secretly buried them, and made replicas that were distributed to various locations, which became centers of Osiris's worship. Thereafter, Osiris ruled as lord of the dead and the underworld.

Thoth.title: Thoth
Thoth.blind:
A moon deity, depicted as ibis-headed or baboon-headed, served as scribe and counselor to a sun god, standing beside him on his solar barge alongside a goddess of truth and order, who was also his wife. The moon deity invented writing and picture-script, and was credited with authoring works of science, religion, magic and law.

In one myth, the year originally had only 360 days, and a sky goddess was unable to bear children during that year. The moon deity gambled with the moon itself for a portion of its light—one seventy-second of it, equal to five days—and won. During these five additional days, the sky goddess and an earth god gave birth to four deities: a god who would later be slain, a rival god, a goddess who was the slain god's wife, and another goddess.

Later, when the first god was killed, the moon deity gave the wife-goddess the magic words needed to restore her dead husband, enabling her to conceive a son, a young god. After a battle between the young god and the rival god, the moon deity offered counsel and wisdom to resolve their conflict.

In the underworld, the moon deity appeared in the form of an ape, serving as a god of equilibrium, who reported when the scale weighing the heart of the deceased against a feather representing truth balanced exactly even, determining the judgment of the dead.

In another tale, the moon deity demonstrated a new invention, writing, to a king. The king replied that writing would not strengthen memory but only remind, giving people the appearance of wisdom without its substance, since they would hear much without being properly taught.
Thoth.story:
Thoth, a moon deity depicted as ibis-headed or baboon-headed, served as scribe and counselor to the sun god Ra, standing beside him on his solar barque alongside the goddess Ma'at, truth and order personified, who was also his wife. Thoth invented writing and hieroglyphs, and was credited with authoring works of science, religion, magic and law.

In one myth, the year originally had only 360 days, and the sky goddess Nut was unable to bear children during that year. Thoth gambled with the moon for a portion of its light—one seventy-second of it, equal to five days—and won. During these five additional days, Nut and the earth god Geb gave birth to four deities: Osiris, Set, Isis, and Nephthys.

Later, when Osiris was killed, Thoth gave Isis the magic words needed to restore her dead husband, enabling her to conceive a son, Horus. After a battle between Horus and Set, Thoth offered counsel and wisdom to resolve their conflict.

In the underworld, Thoth appeared in the form of an ape, serving as the god of equilibrium, who reported when the scale weighing the heart of the deceased against a feather representing truth balanced exactly even, determining the judgment of the dead.

In another tale, Thoth demonstrated a new invention, writing, to King Thamus, praising it as a remedy for memory. The king replied that writing would not strengthen memory but only remind, giving people the appearance of wisdom without its substance, since they would hear much without being properly taught.

Tunupa.title: Tunupa
Tunupa.blind: A mountain is personified in the legends of a people as a deity possessing varying attributes. The stories about this deity are often linked to explaining the origin of a great salt flat that surrounds the mountain on one side. Partway up the mountain there is a cave containing several mummies, and at the foot of the mountain lies an ancient village.
Tunupa.story: Tunupa is a mountain personified in Aymara legends as a deity possessing varying attributes. The stories about this deity are often linked to explaining the origin of the great salt flat that surrounds the mountain on its southern side. Partway up the mountain there is a cave containing several mummies, and at the foot of the mountain lies an ancient village.

Nommo.title: Nommo
Nommo.blind:
According to a people's religion and creation mythology, a primordial being was the first living creature created by a sky god. Shortly after his creation, this being underwent a transformation and multiplied into four pairs of twins. One of the twins rebelled against the universal order created by the sky god. To restore order to his creation, the sky god sacrificed another of the being's progeny, whose body was dismembered and scattered throughout the universe. This dispersal of body parts is seen by the people as the source for the proliferation of shrines throughout their traditional territory; wherever a body part fell, a shrine was erected.

According to additional secret mythologies related to foreign researchers, the primordial beings were inhabitants of a world circling a certain star. They descended from the sky in a vessel accompanied by fire and thunder. After arriving, they created a reservoir of water and subsequently dived into the water. The legends state that these beings required a watery environment in which to live. The being divided his body among men to feed them; that is why it is also said that as the universe had drunk of his body, he also made men drink. He gave all his life principles to human beings.

These beings are also thought to be the origin of the first religious leader of the people.
Nommo.story:
According to Dogon religion and creation mythology, Nommo was the first living creature created by the sky god Amma. Shortly after his creation, Nommo underwent a transformation and multiplied into four pairs of twins. One of the twins rebelled against the universal order created by Amma. To restore order to his creation, Amma sacrificed another of the Nommo progeny, whose body was dismembered and scattered throughout the universe. This dispersal of body parts is seen by the Dogon as the source for the proliferation of Binu shrines throughout the Dogons' traditional territory; wherever a body part fell, a shrine was erected.

According to additional secret mythologies related to French anthropologists, the Nommos were inhabitants of a world circling the star Sirius. The Nommos descended from the sky in a vessel accompanied by fire and thunder. After arriving, the Nommos created a reservoir of water and subsequently dived into the water. The Dogon legends state that the Nommos required a watery environment in which to live. The Nommo divided his body among men to feed them; that is why it is also said that as the universe had drunk of his body, the Nommo also made men drink. He gave all his life principles to human beings.

The Nommo are also thought to be the origin of the first Hogon.

Itzamna.title: Itzamna
Itzamna.blind: The figure was an upper deity of the sky, regarded as a creator being. It was invoked in yearly rituals: in one month a ritual sprinkling of sacred books was performed in its honor as 'the first priest'; in another it was called on as a deity of medicine; and in a further month the very old venerated it alongside the rain deities. One year in a four-year cycle was placed under its patronage. The figure was credited with inventing the priestly art of writing. It was said to have once been a priestly figure who divided the land and gave names to all its features. It was regarded as the creator of humankind and as parent of a fourfold deity dwelling in the interior of the earth. In another tradition, it fathered thirteen offspring with a goddess, two of whom created the earth and humankind. In pictorial scenes it could be shown clinging to the back of a wild pig or a deer, held ready for sacrifice, or shot at while in the form of a bird. It was also shown seated on a celestial throne, governing agriculture and the hunt. Its head sometimes appeared within the jaws of a two-headed reptile representing the earth, seen as its transformation in a creation account. It could take the shape of a great bird that carried a two-headed serpent in its beak, associated with rain; this bird was one of four such spirits seated atop four world trees, re-erected after the sky once collapsed. Its shooting was a major episode in a twin heroes' myth. Human rulers took its name as part of their titles, and in one scene a dignitary wearing its bird form's headdress bestowed a royal headband upon a ruler, acting as the creator deity granting rulership.
Itzamna.story: Itzamná was an upper god of the sky, regarded as a creator deity. He was invoked in yearly rituals: in one month a ritual sprinkling of sacred books was performed in his honor as 'the first priest'; in another he was called on as a god of medicine; and in a further month the very old venerated him alongside the rain deities. One year in a four-year cycle was placed under his patronage. Itzamná was credited with inventing the priestly art of writing. He was said to have once been a priestly figure who divided the land and gave names to all its features. He was regarded as the creator of humankind and as father of a fourfold deity dwelling in the interior of the earth. In another tradition, he fathered thirteen sons with a goddess, two of whom created the earth and humankind. In pictorial scenes he could be shown clinging to the back of a peccary or a deer, held ready for sacrifice, or shot at while in the form of a bird. He was also shown seated on a celestial throne, governing agriculture and the hunt. His head sometimes appeared within the jaws of a two-headed caiman representing the earth, seen as his transformation in a creation account. He could take the shape of a great bird that carried a two-headed serpent in its beak, associated with rain; this bird was one of four such spirits seated atop four world trees, re-erected after the sky once collapsed. Its shooting was a major episode in a twin heroes' myth. Human rulers took his name as part of their titles, and in one scene a dignitary wearing his bird form's headdress bestowed a royal headband upon a king, acting as the creator god granting rulership.

Manco C\u00e1pac.title: Manco Cápac
Manco C\u00e1pac.blind: The hero, also called by another name, was said to have emerged from a cave at a sacred site with his three brothers and four sisters, one of whom would become his wife, carrying a golden staff given to him by his father, a creator god. Traveling together, the siblings joined with other peoples they met and sought to conquer the tribes of a fertile valley. The hero caused his three brothers to be trapped or turned to stone, leaving him sole leader. He then married his elder sister, and together they defeated three small local tribes and settled in a marshy area between two streams, founding a city, later divided into four districts. Though small, the city was surrounded by larger tribes, including a confederated group to the north, who often attacked it, forcing the hero and later his son to defend it. After his natural death, his son succeeded him, and his mummified body remained in the city until a later ruler ordered it moved to a temple on an island in a great lake, leaving only a statue in the city. In another version, the hero was the son of a sun god and a moon goddess, sent to earth with his siblings to build a temple where the golden staff sank into the ground; they traveled through caves to the valley and built the temple there. A further account holds that the hero was the son of a sorceress, who tricked the people of the city into making her queen, secretly bore and hid her son, then revealed him as a divine child destined to rule; she married him, and they reigned together.
Manco C\u00e1pac.story: Manco Cápac, also called Ayar Manco, was said to have emerged from a cave at Tamputoco (Paqariq Tampu) with his three brothers, Ayar Auca, Ayar Cachi, and Ayar Uchu, and four sisters, including Mama Ocllo, carrying a golden staff given to him by his father, the creator god Viracocha. Traveling together, the siblings joined with other peoples they met and sought to conquer the tribes of the Cusco Valley. Manco Cápac caused his three brothers to be trapped or turned to stone, leaving him sole leader. He then married his elder sister, Mama Ocllo, and together they defeated three small tribes—the Sahuares, Huallas, and Alcahuisas—and settled in a marshy area between two streams, founding the city of Cusco, later divided into four districts. Though small, the city was surrounded by larger tribes, such as the confederated Ayarmacas and Pinaguas, who often attacked it, forcing Manco Cápac and later his son Sinchi Roca to defend it. After his natural death, his son succeeded him, and his mummified body remained in Cusco until Pachacuti ordered it moved to the Temple of the Sun on Isla del Sol, leaving only a statue in the city. In another version, Manco Cápac was the son of the sun god Inti and the moon goddess Mama Killa, sent to earth with his siblings to build a temple where the golden staff, called tapac-yauri, sank into the ground; they traveled through caves to Cusco and built the temple there. A further account holds that Manco Cápac was the son of the sorceress Mama Waqu, who tricked the people of Cusco into making her queen, secretly bore and hid her son, then revealed him as a divine child destined to rule; she married him, and they reigned together.

Pachacamac.title: Pachacamac
Pachacamac.blind: The creator god was worshipped by the people of this land before a great empire conquered them. When the empire conquered them, they added him to their own pantheon, though they considered him less powerful than their own supreme god. The myths about him are contradictory. Some accounts claim he was the cowardly brother of a legendary founder-hero, called by another name in that version. Other accounts say that he, the founder-hero, and the empire's supreme god were the three sons of the sun god. Another myth relates that the creator god made the first man and the first woman but forgot to give them food, so the man died. The woman then prayed over the creator god's head to the sun god, his father, asking to be made the mother of all the peoples of the earth. The creator god became furious, and as her children were born one by one, he tried to kill them. He was ultimately beaten and thrown into the sea by her hero-son. After this defeat, the creator god gave up his violent struggle and instead became content to rule as the supreme god of fish.
Pachacamac.story: The creator god Pacha Kamaq was worshipped by the people of Peru before the Inca conquest. When the Inca conquered them, they added him to their own pantheon, though they considered him less powerful than their supreme god Viracocha. The myths about him are contradictory. Some accounts claim he was the cowardly brother of Manco Cápac, called Ayca. Other accounts say that he, Manco Cápac, and Viracocha were the three sons of Inti, the sun god. Another myth relates that Pacha Kamaq made the first man and the first woman but forgot to give them food, so the man died. The woman then prayed over Pacha Kamaq's head to Inti, his father, asking to be made the mother of all the peoples of the earth. Pacha Kamaq became furious, and as her children were born one by one, he tried to kill them. He was ultimately beaten and thrown into the sea by her hero-son, Wichama. After this defeat, Pacha Kamaq gave up his violent struggle and instead became content to rule as the supreme god of fish.

Enki.title: Enki
Enki.blind:
The hero was a deity of wisdom, crafts, fresh subterranean waters, magic, and incantations, who ruled over a subterranean water realm. His wife was a goddess, and their children included four other deities. His attendant was another deity, and his servants included several kinds of minor beings and a group of sages.

The hero was credited as the creator of mankind, fashioned from clay. In one myth, he devised the plan to create a new being meant to take over the labor of the gods. In another, he worked together with a goddess to create man from clay mixed with divine blood. When another god later sought to destroy humanity by sending a flood, the hero had sworn an oath not to reveal this plan, so instead he warned his human protégé by speaking to a reed wall, allowing humanity to survive. In a later account, the creation of man was instead described as a joint effort between the hero and his son.

The hero also acted as a clever problem-solver among the gods. In one story, to calm the heart of a warlike goddess, he fashioned a double of her out of clay to serve as her adversary. In another, he outwitted a warrior god who had been plotting against him. In the story of a human figure, the hero gave instructions that allowed that human to ingratiate himself with three gods. In another story cycle, the hero served as a problem solver and kingmaker among the gods.
Enki.story:
Enki was the Mesopotamian god of wisdom, crafts, fresh subterranean waters, magic, and incantations, who ruled the Abzû. His wife was Damgalnuna, and their children included Nanshe, Asalluhi, Marduk, and Enbilulu. His attendant deity was Isimud, and his servants included the lahmu, the kulullû, and the Seven Sages.

Enki was credited as the creator of mankind, fashioned from clay. In one myth, Enki devised the plan to create a new being meant to take over the labor of the gods. In another, he worked together with the goddess Belet-ili to create man from clay mixed with divine blood. When the god Enlil later sought to destroy humanity by sending a flood, Enki had sworn an oath not to reveal this plan, so instead he warned his human protégé by speaking to a reed wall, allowing humanity to survive. In a later account, the creation of man was instead described as a joint effort between Enki and his son Marduk.

Enki also acted as a clever problem-solver among the gods. In one story, to calm the heart of the warlike goddess Ishtar, he fashioned a double of her out of clay to serve as her adversary. In another, he outwitted the warrior god Ninurta, who had been plotting against him. In the story of Adapa, Enki gave instructions that allowed Adapa to ingratiate himself with three gods. In the Kumarbi cycle, Enki served as a problem solver and kingmaker among the gods.

Isis.title: Isis
Isis.blind: The protagonist deity was sister and wife to the storm-brother king, both children of the earth god and the sky goddess, part of a divine family descended from a creator god. When the creator passed down rule through the male line, the storm-brother became king and the protagonist his queen. Their brother killed the king and dismembered his corpse. The protagonist and her sister, aided by another deity, searched for the scattered pieces and reassembled them. The protagonist's grief, sexual desire, and magical spells stirred the king back to life; she restored his breath, copulated with him, and conceived their son, though afterward the king could live only in the underworld. The protagonist gave birth to her son in the reed thickets of a river delta after a long, difficult labor, then had to protect the infant from the hostile brother and from snakes, scorpions, and illness. Seven minor scorpion spirits guarded her; when a wealthy woman refused her shelter, the scorpions stung the woman's son, and the protagonist healed the innocent child out of compassion. The protagonist and her son were sometimes shown in conflict: once the son beheaded her, and she replaced her head with that of a cow. As the son grew, he challenged the hostile brother for the kingship, and the protagonist helped him by using cunning and magic—once transforming into a young woman to trick the brother into condemning his own usurpation of the throne, and later using her powers of transformation to destroy him and his followers. In another tale, the protagonist served as a midwife alongside other goddesses at the birth of three future kings, calling out their names as each was born.
Isis.story: Isis was sister and wife to Osiris, both children of the earth god Geb and the sky goddess Nut, part of a divine family descended from a creator god. When the creator passed down rule through the male line, Osiris became king and Isis his queen. Their brother Set killed Osiris and dismembered his corpse. Isis and her sister Nephthys, aided by another deity, searched for the scattered pieces and reassembled them. Isis's grief, sexual desire, and magical spells stirred Osiris back to life; she restored his breath, copulated with him, and conceived their son Horus, though afterward Osiris could live only in the underworld. Isis gave birth to Horus in the papyrus thickets of a river delta after a long, difficult labor, then had to protect the infant from Set and from snakes, scorpions, and illness. Seven minor scorpion deities guarded her; when a wealthy woman refused Isis shelter, the scorpions stung the woman's son, and Isis healed the innocent child out of compassion. Isis and Horus were sometimes shown in conflict: once Horus beheaded her, and she replaced her head with that of a cow. As Horus grew, he challenged Set for the kingship, and Isis helped him by using cunning and magic—once transforming into a young woman to trick Set into condemning his own usurpation of the throne, and later using her powers of transformation to destroy Set and his followers. In another tale, Isis served as a midwife alongside other goddesses at the birth of three future kings, calling out their names as each was born.

Idris (prophet).title: Idris (prophet)
Idris (prophet).blind:
The prophet was the second holy messenger after the first man. He was described as trustworthy and patient, and said to have been raised to a high station. He was born in a great city. Before receiving revelation, he followed the teachings passed down from an earlier holy man, the son of the first man. When he grew older, the deity made him a prophet. At that time, the people did not follow the deity's message and instead worshipped fire. The prophet urged his people to give up their wrongdoing, but many refused, so he left the city; some of his people, though reluctant, went with him. They asked him where they would find a place like their home city; he told them that if they migrated for the sake of the deity, the deity would provide for them. They traveled to a foreign land and saw a great river, where the prophet stood at its bank and glorified the deity.

The prophet divided his time: three days a week preaching to his people, four days devoted entirely to worship. He was among the first to use a writing instrument, the first to observe the movement of the stars, and he established measures and weights. He was also credited with inventing the art of making garments.

Concerning his being raised to a high station: the deity told the prophet that he would credit him daily with the good deeds of all descendants of the first man. Wanting to increase his own good deeds, the prophet asked a friend among the heavenly messengers to help him speak with the angel who takes souls. This heavenly being carried him on its wings up through the heavens. In the fourth heaven they met the angel who takes souls, who was descending toward the earth to take the prophet's soul. Astonished, the angel took the prophet's soul then and there, in the fourth heaven, fulfilling the words that he was raised to a high station.

During another holy messenger's night journey through the heavens, that messenger encountered the prophet in the fourth heaven.
Idris (prophet).story:
Idris was the second prophet after Adam, described in the Quran as trustworthy and patient, and said to have been "exalted to a high station." He was born in Babylon. Before receiving divine revelation, he followed the teachings that had been given to Seth, the son of Adam. When he grew older, God made him a prophet. At that time the people did not follow God's message and instead worshipped fire. Idris urged his people to abandon their wrongdoing, but many refused to listen, so he left Babylon; some of his people, though reluctant to leave their home, went with him. They asked him where they would find a place as good as Babylon; he told them that if they migrated for God's sake, God would provide for them. They traveled to Egypt and saw the Nile River, where Idris stood on its bank and glorified God.

Idris divided his time: three days a week he preached to his people, and four days he devoted entirely to worship. He was among the first men to write with a pen, the first to observe the movement of the stars, and he set out weights and measures. He was also credited with inventing the art of making garments.

Concerning his being raised to a high station: God told Idris that he would credit him daily with the good deeds of all of Adam's descendants. Wanting to increase his own good deeds further, Idris asked a friend among the angels to help him speak with the angel of death. This angel carried Idris on its wings up through the heavens. In the fourth heaven they met the angel of death, who was descending toward the earth to take Idris's soul. Astonished, the angel of death took Idris's soul there in the fourth heaven, fulfilling the words that he was raised to a high station.

During Muhammad's Night Journey through the heavens, he encountered Idris in the fourth heaven.

Enoch (ancestor of Noah).title: Enoch
Enoch (ancestor of Noah).blind: The figure, son of a patriarch, was father of another future patriarch. He lived 365 years, walking with the deity, until the deity took him so that he was no more and did not experience death like other ancestors. Traditions say he was raised to a heavenly realm and appointed guardian of celestial treasures, made chief of the angels, and set as an attendant before the deity's throne. There he was taught all secrets and mysteries, and with angels at his command he carried out whatever the deity decreed. He was identified as the being who communicates the deity's word, and through this role he was said to have conveyed divine revelation to a later prophet and dictated a sacred book of laws. He was also given the title of "Great Scribe" for his piety. One tradition holds that though righteous, he was easily tempted toward evil, so the deity took him away before his time to preserve his righteousness. Another story tells that the earth had been corrupted by two demons, and the figure was carried to the heavenly realm to demonstrate that the deity was not cruel. A further account describes him as a pious ascetic who preached repentance, gathered many disciples despite the world's small population, and was made king; under his rule peace reigned until he was summoned to the heavenly realm to govern beings called divine beings. In another version, he founded an exceedingly righteous city; its entire people were taken to the heavenly realm without dying, due to their piety. He also foretold that a descendant would survive a great flood with his family, preserving mankind and sacred writings. He performed miracles and witnessed wars and disasters in his lifetime.
Enoch (ancestor of Noah).story: Enoch, son of the patriarch Jared, was father of Methuselah. He lived 365 years, walking with God, until God took him so that he was no more and did not experience death like other ancestors. Traditions say he was raised to heaven and appointed guardian of celestial treasures, made chief of the angels, and set as an attendant before God's throne. There he was taught all secrets and mysteries, and with angels at his command he carried out whatever God decreed. He was identified as the being who communicates God's word, and through this role he was said to have conveyed divine revelation to Moses and dictated the Book of Jubilees. He was also given the title of "Great Scribe" for his piety. One tradition holds that though righteous, he was easily tempted toward evil, so God took him away before his time to preserve his righteousness. Another story tells that the earth had been corrupted by the demons Shammazai and Azazel, and Enoch was carried to heaven to demonstrate that God was not cruel. A further account describes him as a pious ascetic who preached repentance, gathered many disciples despite the world's small population, and was made king; under his rule peace reigned until he was summoned to heaven to govern the sons of God. In another version, he founded an exceedingly righteous city named Zion; its entire people were taken to heaven without dying, due to their piety. He also foretold that his descendant Noah would survive a great flood with his family, preserving mankind and sacred writings. He performed miracles and witnessed wars and disasters in his lifetime.

Gilgamesh flood myth.title: Gilgamesh flood myth
Gilgamesh flood myth.blind: The hero journeys to meet the flood hero, who tells him a secret story. In a certain city, a group of great gods swore to send a flood, but one wise god secretly warned the flood hero through a reed wall, commanding him to demolish his house and build a boat to preserve living things. The flood hero built a large boat with six decks, sealed with a tar-like substance, and loaded it with silver, gold, his relatives, craftsmen, and all the beasts and animals of the field. A storm arose, sent by the gods, with thunder, wind, and flood lasting six days and nights, destroying all humans and covering the land. The gods, frightened by their own act, wept in the heavens. When the storm calmed, the flood hero's boat rested on a mountain. He released a dove, a swallow, and finally a raven, which did not return, showing the waters had receded. He then offered a sacrifice, and the gods gathered around it. The storm god was angry that anyone survived, but the wise god rebuked him for the disproportionate punishment. The storm god then blessed the flood hero and his wife, granting them immortality, and sent them to live far away at the mouth of the rivers. Later, the flood hero challenges the hero to stay awake six days and nights, but the hero fails, falling asleep immediately. The flood hero then tells him of a plant at the bottom of the sea that restores youth. The hero retrieves it but loses it to a serpent while bathing, which sheds its skin and departs rejuvenated. The hero returns empty-handed to his home city, where he admires its great walls.
Gilgamesh flood myth.story: Gilgamesh journeys to meet the flood hero Utnapishtim, who tells him a secret story. In the city of Shuruppak, the great gods Anu, Enlil, Ninurta, Ennugi, and Ea swore to send a flood, but Ea secretly warned Utnapishtim through a reed wall, commanding him to demolish his house and build a boat to preserve living things. Utnapishtim built a large boat with six decks, sealed with bitumen, and loaded it with silver, gold, his relatives, craftsmen, and all the beasts and animals of the field. A storm arose, sent by the gods, with thunder, wind, and flood lasting six days and nights, destroying all humans and covering the land. The gods, frightened by their own act, wept in the heavens. When the storm calmed, Utnapishtim's boat rested on a mountain. He released a dove, a swallow, and finally a raven, which did not return, showing the waters had receded. He then offered a sacrifice, and the gods gathered around it. Enlil was angry that anyone survived, but Ea rebuked him for the disproportionate punishment. Enlil then blessed Utnapishtim and his wife, granting them immortality, and sent them to live far away at the mouth of the rivers. Later, Utnapishtim challenges Gilgamesh to stay awake six days and nights, but Gilgamesh fails, falling asleep immediately. Utnapishtim then tells him of a plant at the bottom of the sea that restores youth. Gilgamesh retrieves it but loses it to a serpent while bathing, which sheds its skin and departs rejuvenated. Gilgamesh returns empty-handed to Uruk, where he admires the city's great walls.

Genesis flood narrative.title: Genesis flood narrative
Genesis flood narrative.blind: Ten generations after the creation of the first man, the creator god saw that the earth was corrupt and filled with violence, and that every intention of the thoughts of humanity's heart was only evil continually, so he decided to destroy what he had created. But the creator god found one righteous man, the hero, and confided in him his intention to bring a great flood to eliminate everywhere all flesh in which there is the breath of life. The creator god instructed the hero to build a large vessel, and the hero entered the vessel in his six hundredth year of life. On a certain day of a certain month of that year, the fountains of the great deep burst apart and the floodgates of the sky broke open, and rain fell for forty days and forty nights until the highest mountains were covered to a certain depth, and all life perished except the hero and those with him in the vessel. After a set number of days, the creator god remembered the hero, and the waters subsided until the vessel rested on a range of mountains. On a certain day of a certain month of the hero's six hundred and first year, the earth was dry. The hero released a large black bird, which went to and fro until the waters dried up, and also released a small white bird, which on the third occasion did not return to him again. Then the hero built an altar and made a sacrifice, and the creator god made a covenant with him that living beings would be allowed to eat every living thing but not its blood, and that the creator god would never again destroy all life by a flood.
Genesis flood narrative.story: Ten generations after the creation of Adam, God saw that the earth was corrupt and filled with violence, and that every intention of the thoughts of man's heart was only evil continually, so he decided to destroy what he had created. But God found one righteous man, Noah, and confided in him his intention to bring a Flood to eliminate everywhere all flesh in which there is the breath of life. God instructed Noah to build an ark, and Noah entered the Ark in his six hundredth year of life. On the 17th day of the second month of that year, the fountains of the Great Deep burst apart and the floodgates of heaven broke open, and rain fell for forty days and forty nights until the highest mountains were covered to a depth of 15 cubits, and all life perished except Noah and those with him in the Ark. After 150 days, God remembered Noah, and the waters subsided until the Ark rested on the mountains of Ararat. On the 27th day of the second month of Noah's six hundred and first year, the earth was dry. Noah released a raven, which went to and fro until the waters dried up, and also released a dove, which on the third occasion did not return to him again. Then Noah built an altar and made a sacrifice, and God made a covenant with Noah that man would be allowed to eat every living thing but not its blood, and that God would never again destroy all life by a flood.

Atra-Hasis.title: Atra-Hasis
Atra-Hasis.blind: When the divine workers had to labor like humans, the lower group of gods dug canals and rivers to sustain the land, while the upper group of gods ruled over them. After 40 years the lower gods rebelled, surrounding the dwelling of the chief god. The chief god consulted two other high gods; his messenger failed to negotiate peace. To avoid battle, the chief god proposed creating humans to do the gods' hard labor. He asked the mother goddess, leader of seven divine wombs, to help; she required the aid of a clever god. The gods purified themselves, then the clever god slaughtered a lesser god, mixing his blood with clay to form the first human. The mother goddess gave the creature a basket and taught it to labor. A woman was placed beside the man, and at the mother goddess's command they reproduced. The mother goddess had them celebrate a seven-day feast for a goddess of war and sexuality, and after nine months the first child was born. After 1200 years, humans multiplied and grew noisy, so the chief god sent the god of death to kill many with plague. The clever god told his priest, a wise man, to have people worship only the death god, who grew ashamed and stopped. After another 1200 years, humans multiplied again; the chief god sent a storm god, then a fertility goddess, to bring storms and famine. The clever god again advised the wise man to redirect worship, shaming these gods into stopping. Enraged, the chief god decreed a flood to destroy humanity and forced the clever god to swear silence. The clever god secretly instructed the wise man, speaking to a reed wall, to build a cube-shaped, waterproof ship, gather food and animals, and prepare for seven days of flood. The wise man built the ship with neighbors' help, promising future rewards, then he and his family and a fertile couple boarded and sealed the ship as storms began.
Atra-Hasis.story: When the gods had to work like humans, the lower gods (the Igigu) dug canals and rivers to sustain the land, while the upper gods (the Anunnaki) ruled over them. After 40 years the lower gods rebelled, surrounding the dwelling of Enlil, chief of the gods. Enlil consulted Anu and Enki; his messenger Nusku failed to negotiate peace. To avoid battle, Enlil proposed creating humans to do the gods' hard labor. He asked Mami, leader of seven divine wombs, to help; she required Enki's aid. The gods purified themselves, then Enki slaughtered a lesser god, Geshtu-E, mixing his blood with clay to form the first human. Mami gave the creature a basket and taught it to labor. A woman was placed beside the man, and at Mami's command they reproduced. Mami had them celebrate a seven-day feast for Ishtar, and after nine months the first child was born. After 1200 years, humans multiplied and grew noisy, so Enlil sent Namtar to kill many with plague. Enki told his priest Atrahasis to have people worship only Namtar, who grew ashamed and stopped. After another 1200 years, humans multiplied again; Enlil sent Adad, then Nisaba, to bring storms and famine. Enki again advised Atrahasis to redirect worship, shaming these gods into stopping. Enraged, Enlil decreed a flood to destroy humanity and forced Enki to swear silence. Enki secretly instructed Atrahasis, speaking to a reed wall, to build a cube-shaped, waterproof ship, gather food and animals, and prepare for seven days of flood. Atrahasis built the ship with neighbors' help, promising future rewards, then he and his family and a fertile couple boarded and sealed the ship as storms began.

Ramayana.title: Ramayana
Ramayana.blind: A sage asks another sage if a truly righteous man exists in the world, and learns of a prince. A king with three wives has no son; he performs a fire sacrifice, and the gods ask a great god to take mortal birth to destroy a demon king who terrorizes the universe. Four sons are born to the king's wives, the eldest being the hero. As a youth, the hero and his brother receive weapons from a sage and destroy demons. At a neighboring kingdom, the hero strings and breaks a legendary bow, winning the hand of a princess who had been found in a field, and marries her. Before the hero can be crowned, his stepmother, provoked by a servant, demands he be exiled fourteen years and her own son be made king instead. The old king dies of grief. The wife and the loyal brother join the hero in exile. The half-brother refuses the throne and rules only as regent. In the forest, a demoness tries to seduce the brothers and harm the wife; the loyal brother cuts off her nose and ears. Her brothers attack and are defeated. The demon king sends a demon disguised as a golden deer to lure the hero away, then abducts the wife while the loyal brother is tricked into leaving her unguarded. A large bird tries to rescue her but is mortally wounded. The hero allies with monkey-people, kills their king's usurping brother to restore him to the throne, and gains the aid of a devoted ally, who helps find the wife, held captive by the demon king, who wants to marry her but she refuses, remaining faithful. The hero ultimately wins the battle against the demon king and returns to his capital with his wife to be crowned king amid celebration.
Ramayana.story: A sage asks another sage if a truly righteous man exists in the world, and learns of a prince named Rama. A king with three wives has no son; he performs a fire sacrifice, and the gods ask the god Vishnu to take mortal birth to destroy a demon king who terrorizes the universe. Four sons are born to the king's wives, the eldest being Rama. As a youth, Rama and his brother Lakshmana receive weapons from a sage and destroy demons. At a neighboring kingdom, Rama strings and breaks a legendary bow, winning the hand of princess Sita, who had been found in a field, and marries her. Before Rama can be crowned, his stepmother Kaikeyi, provoked by a servant, demands he be exiled fourteen years and her son Bharata be made king instead. The old king dies of grief. Sita and Lakshmana join Rama in exile. Bharata refuses the throne and rules only as regent. In the forest, a demoness tries to seduce the brothers and harm Sita; Lakshmana cuts off her nose and ears. Her brothers attack and are defeated. The demon king Ravana sends a rakshasa disguised as a golden deer to lure Rama away, then abducts Sita while Lakshmana is tricked into leaving her unguarded. A vulture tries to rescue her but is mortally wounded. Rama allies with monkey-people, kills their king's usurping brother to restore him to the throne, and gains the aid of the devoted Hanuman, who helps find Sita, held captive by Ravana, who wants to marry her but she refuses, remaining faithful. Rama ultimately wins the battle against Ravana and returns to his capital with Sita to be crowned king amid celebration.

Reamker.title: Reamker
Reamker.blind: The hero is sent into exile by a queen mother who wants her own son to inherit the throne. His faithful wife joins him, having been won when he alone succeeded in a challenge of firing arrows through a spinning wheel. His younger brother also joins them out of concern. In a forest, a female demon tries to seduce first the hero, then his brother, who cuts off her ear and nose in anger. She flees to her ten-headed brother, a demon ruler of an island, who travels to the forest with his uncle. Awed by the wife's beauty, the demon ruler has his uncle transform into a golden deer to lure the brothers away, then imitates the hero's voice to draw the brother off too, despite a protective magic circle drawn around the wife. Disguised as an old beggar, the demon ruler tricks her outside the circle and abducts her. The brothers ally with a leader of monkey-like beings, helping him defeat a rival, and in gratitude he sends a warrior of his kind to help search for the wife, discovering she is held on the demon's island. The warrior orders a bridge built to the island; mermaids sabotage the work, but he falls in love with their princess, who then stops interfering. The hero and demon ruler battle; only by piercing the demon's navel is he finally slain. The hero returns triumphant but suspects his wife's fidelity after a magical incident with a portrait. She passes a trial by fire but, hurt by his distrust, leaves to live with a wise man, bearing twin sons who are later reunited with their father.
Reamker.story: The hero-prince is sent into exile by a queen mother who wants her own son to inherit the throne. His faithful wife joins him, having been won when he alone succeeded in a challenge of firing arrows through a spinning wheel. His younger brother also joins them out of concern. In the forest, a female demon tries to seduce first the prince, then his brother, who cuts off her ear and nose in anger. She flees to her ten-headed brother, a demon king ruling an island, who travels to the forest with his uncle. Awed by the wife's beauty, the demon king has his uncle transform into a golden deer to lure the brothers away, then imitates the prince's voice to draw the brother off too, despite a protective magic circle drawn around the wife. Disguised as an old beggar, the demon king tricks her outside the circle and abducts her. The brothers ally with a monkey king, helping him defeat a rival, and in gratitude the monkey king sends a monkey warrior to help search for the wife, discovering she is held on the demon's island. The monkey warrior orders a bridge built to the island; mermaids sabotage the work, but he falls in love with their princess, who then stops interfering. The prince and demon king battle; only by piercing the demon's navel is he finally slain. The prince returns triumphant but suspects his wife's fidelity after a magical incident with a portrait. She passes a trial by fire but, hurt by his distrust, leaves to live with a wiseman, bearing twin sons who are later reunited with their father.

Ramakien.title: Ramakien
Ramakien.blind: A great sky god incarnates in various forms. As an animal he defeats a demon. Later, another high god grants his servant a magical finger that kills anyone he points at; when tricked by the sky god disguised as a dancing woman, the servant points at himself and dies, later reborn as a multi-headed demon king of an island kingdom. The demon king marries a woman and receives another wife as a gift from the high god, fathering a son. Meanwhile two monkey princes are born from a queen's adultery with gods, becoming monkeys after a river test. The elder gains a magic weapon and steals his brother's bride and later the demon king's wife, fathering a son, then banishes his brother, who meets a monkey general born from divine weapons placed in a maiden's mouth. A hero, an incarnation of the sky god, falls in love with a princess (secretly the demon king's daughter, and an incarnation of a goddess) at an archery contest. Exiled to the forest with his brother, the hero spurns a demoness, prompting the demon king to abduct the princess. The hero allies with the monkey general, the exiled brother-prince, and a bear-prince; the monkey general finds the princess, burns the island kingdom, and helps build a causeway. The hero kills the demon king and his son, frees the princess, who passes a fire ordeal, and they return home. Later, doubting her fidelity, the hero orders her killed, but his brother spares her; she bears twin sons in exile with a hermit. The hero seeks her return; she vanishes into the underworld, until the high god finally reunites them.
Ramakien.story: A great god, Phra Narai, incarnates in various forms. As a boar he defeats a demon. Later, the god Phra Isuan grants his servant Nonthok a diamond finger that kills anyone he points at; when tricked by Phra Narai disguised as a dancing woman, Nonthok points at himself and dies, later reborn as the ten-faced demon king Thotsakan of Lanka. Thotsakan marries Kala Akhi and receives Nang Montho from Phra Isuan, fathering Intharachit. Meanwhile monkey princes Phali and Sukhrip are born from a queen's adultery with gods, becoming monkeys after a river test. Phali gains a magic trident and steals Sukhrip's bride and later Thotsakan's wife, fathering Ongkhot, then banishes Sukhrip, who meets Hanuman, born from divine weapons placed in a maiden's mouth. Phra Ram, an incarnation of Phra Narai, falls in love with Nang Sida (Laksami reborn, secretly Thotsakan's daughter) at an archery contest. Exiled to the forest with his brother Phra Lak, Phra Ram spurns the demoness Sammanakha, prompting Thotsakan to abduct Nang Sida. Phra Ram allies with Hanuman, Sukhrip, and Chomphuphan; Hanuman finds Sida, burns Lanka, and helps build a causeway. Phra Ram kills Thotsakan and Intharachit, frees Sida, who passes a fire ordeal, and they return home. Later, doubting her fidelity, Phra Ram orders her killed, but Phra Lak spares her; she bears twin sons in exile with a hermit. Phra Ram seeks her return; she vanishes into the underworld, until Phra Isuan finally reunites them.

Barlaam and Josaphat.title: Barlaam and Josaphat
Barlaam and Josaphat.blind: A ruler in a certain land persecuted the religious community in his realm, a community founded by a traveling teacher. Diviners predicted that the ruler's own child would one day adopt the persecuted faith, so the ruler had the young heir isolated from all outside contact and confined. Despite this isolation, the heir met a solitary holy man and converted to the faith through him. The heir kept this new faith even in the face of the parent's anger and attempts at persuasion. Eventually the ruler himself converted to the faith, handed over rule to the child, and withdrew into the wilderness to live as a solitary holy man. The child, now ruler, later gave up rule as well and went into seclusion together with the old teacher who had converted him.
Barlaam and Josaphat.story: An Indian king persecuted the Christian Church in his realm, a church founded by an apostle. Astrologers predicted that the king's own son would one day become a Christian, so the king had the young prince isolated from all outside contact and imprisoned. Despite this isolation, the prince met a hermit, a holy man, and converted to Christianity through him. The prince kept his new faith even in the face of his father's anger and attempts at persuasion. Eventually the king himself converted to Christianity, turned over his throne to his son, and retired to the desert to live as a hermit. The son, now king, later abdicated his own throne and went into seclusion together with his old teacher, the hermit who had converted him.

Gautama Buddha.title: The Buddha
Gautama Buddha.blind: A wandering religious teacher was born in a certain town to royal parents of a ruling clan. He renounced his home life to live as a wandering ascetic. After a period of mendicancy, asceticism, and meditation, he attained a state of awakening at a certain place. He then wandered through a nearby plain, teaching others and building a monastic order. He taught a middle way between sensual indulgence and severe asceticism, leading to freedom from ignorance, craving, rebirth, and suffering. His core teachings were summarized in a set of four truths and an eightfold path, a training of the mind that included ethical training, kindness toward others, and meditative practices such as sense restraint, mindfulness, and meditation proper. He also taught concepts describing how all phenomena—both mental states and concrete things—come into being and cease to be depending on other phenomena, lacking an existence of their own. He frequently referred to himself by a special title meaning one who is beyond all coming and going. He was also known by many other epithets reflecting his perfected qualities, such as the Blessed One, the Well-Gone, the Knower of Worlds, and the Teacher of gods and humans. His followers compiled his teachings into two collections: one containing codes for monastic discipline, and another containing discourses attributed to him. Later generations composed additional texts, including systematic treatises, biographies, stories of his past lives, and further discourses. Tradition holds that he died in a certain town and reached a final release from conditioned existence.
Gautama Buddha.story: A wandering religious teacher was born in Lumbini to royal parents of the Shakya clan. He renounced his home life to live as a wandering ascetic. After a period of mendicancy, asceticism, and meditation, he attained nirvana at Bodh Gaya. He then wandered through the lower plain, teaching others and building a monastic order known as the sangha. He taught a Middle Way between sensual indulgence and severe asceticism, leading to freedom from ignorance, craving, rebirth, and suffering. His core teachings were summarized in the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path, a training of the mind that included ethical training, kindness toward others, and meditative practices such as sense restraint, mindfulness, and meditation proper. He also taught the concepts of the five aggregates and dependent origination, describing how all phenomena—both mental states and concrete things—come into being and cease to be depending on other phenomena, lacking an existence of their own. He frequently referred to himself by a special title meaning one who is beyond all coming and going. He was also known by many other epithets reflecting his perfected qualities, such as the Blessed One, the Well-Gone, the Knower of Worlds, and the Teacher of gods and humans. His followers compiled his teachings into two collections: one containing codes for monastic discipline, and another containing discourses attributed to him. Later generations composed additional texts, including systematic treatises, biographies, stories of his past lives, and further discourses. Tradition holds that he died in Kushinagar and reached final release from conditioned existence.

Panchatantra.title: Panchatantra
Panchatantra.blind: An elderly wise man was tasked with teaching the principles of good governance and wise conduct to three ignorant princes, sons of a king ruling a kingdom. He did so through five interlinked collections of animal fables. In the first, a jackal minister, unemployed in a lion king's court, conspired with his sidekick to break apart close friendships and alliances among the animals, illustrating how trust is lost. The second followed four weak animals—a crow, a mouse, a turtle, and a deer—who, by working together and supporting one another, escaped every threat and prospered, showing that cooperation among the weak can achieve what strength alone cannot. The third told of a war between crows and owls: the crow king heeded the wise counsel of his advisor, while the owl king ignored his own advisor, and so the crows triumphed. This collection also told of an old man who married a young woman who despised him; when a thief entered their home one night, she embraced her husband from fear, delighting him so much that he thanked the thief and offered him anything he wished. The fourth and fifth, shorter and focused on human folly, warned against haste. One fable told of a woman who left her child with a loyal mongoose; finding blood on its mouth upon her return, she killed it in anger, only to discover it had saved her child from a snake, and she grieved her hasty act.
Panchatantra.story: An elderly Brahmin named Vishnusharma was tasked with teaching the principles of good governance and wise conduct to three ignorant princes, sons of King Amarasakti of Mahilaropya. He did so through five interlinked books of animal fables. In the first book, a jackal minister named Damanaka, unemployed in a lion king's court, conspired with his sidekick Karataka to break apart close friendships and alliances among the animals, illustrating how trust is lost. The second book followed four weak animals—a crow, a mouse, a turtle, and a deer—who, by working together and supporting one another, escaped every threat and prospered, showing that cooperation among the weak can achieve what strength alone cannot. The third book told of war between crows and owls: the crow king heeded the wise counsel of his advisor, while the owl king ignored his own advisor, and so the crows triumphed. This book also told of an old man who married a young woman who despised him; when a thief entered their home one night, she embraced her husband from fear, delighting him so much that he thanked the thief and offered him anything he wished. The fourth and fifth books, shorter and focused on human folly, warned against haste. One fable told of a woman who left her child with a loyal mongoose; finding blood on its mouth upon her return, she killed it in anger, only to discover it had saved her child from a snake, and she grieved her hasty act.

Kalila wa-Dimna.title: Kalīla wa-Dimna
Kalila wa-Dimna.blind:
A ruler summons an advisor to answer his requests for guidance by telling him a great cycle of animal fables, each nested inside another. Two small canines serve at the court of a lion ruler; one is content with his station, the other constantly schemes for advancement. The advisor tells how a large horned animal, once terrified of the lion, becomes his trusted friend, until the ambitious canine poisons the lion's trust, provoking a war that ends in the horned animal's death. For this treachery the canine is tried and put to death, though the tale warns that mercy has limits, since unchecked wrongdoing breeds more wrongdoing.

Asked for a story of true friendship, the advisor tells of a small rodent who frees a flock of birds caught in a hunter's net, then befriends a black bird, a shelled reptile, and a horned grazing animal; the four repeatedly rescue one another from hunters and danger.

Asked about false submission, he tells of a war between a ruler bird of prey and a band of black birds, in which one black bird feigns loyalty to the birds of prey, learns their secrets, and delivers victory to his own kind.

He tells of an exiled ruler of a group of primates who befriends a shelled reptile, is betrayed by him, escapes, and recounts a tale of a pack animal, a small wild canine, and a sick large predator to explain why he can no longer trust his friend.

A trapped small rodent frees a snared feline in exchange for protection from hunters, after which the two part ways.

A small songbird whose chicks are killed by a ruler's son blinds him in revenge and refuses a false reconciliation.

A canine who conspired against another advisor is punished and then restored to the lion ruler's favor.

A female large predator whose cubs are killed swears off meat, then all food, living out her life in mourning.

A black bird, envying another bird's call, tries to imitate it, forgets his own cry, and is left with neither.
Kalila wa-Dimna.story:
A king summons a philosopher to answer his requests for guidance by telling him a great cycle of animal fables, each nested inside another. Two jackals serve at the court of a lion king; one is content with his station, the other constantly schemes for advancement. The philosopher tells how an ox, once terrified of the lion, becomes his trusted friend, until the ambitious jackal poisons the lion's trust, provoking a war that ends in the ox's death. For this treachery the jackal is tried and put to death, though the tale warns that mercy has limits, since unchecked wrongdoing breeds more wrongdoing.

Asked for a story of true friendship, the philosopher tells of a mouse who frees a flock of doves caught in a hunter's net, then befriends a crow, a tortoise, and a gazelle; the four repeatedly rescue one another from hunters and danger.

Asked about false submission, he tells of a war between an owl king and a band of crows, in which one crow feigns loyalty to the owls, learns their secrets, and delivers victory to his own people.

He tells of an exiled monkey king who befriends a tortoise, is betrayed by him, escapes, and recounts a tale of a donkey, a fox, and a sick lion to explain why he can no longer trust his friend.

A trapped mouse frees a snared cat in exchange for protection from hunters, after which the two part ways.

A lark whose chicks are killed by a prince blinds him in revenge and refuses a false reconciliation.

A jackal who conspired against another advisor is punished and then restored to the lion king's favor.

A lioness whose cubs are killed swears off meat, then all food, living out her life in mourning.

A crow, envying a partridge's call, tries to imitate it, forgets his own cry, and is left with neither.

Deucalion.title: Deucalion
Deucalion.blind: The hero was the child of a primordial being, and ruled over a certain region. The chief god grew angry at humanity's wickedness after a king sacrificed a boy to him, and decided to destroy that age of mankind with a great flood. The hero's father forewarned him of the coming deluge, so the hero built a wooden chest and provisioned it carefully; no animals were saved in this version. He and his wife, daughter of another primordial being, entered the chest together. The rivers ran in torrents and the sea flooded the coastal plains until, after nine days, the waters receded and the chest came to rest on a mountain. Once safe, the couple gave thanks to the chief god. The hero then consulted an oracle of a goddess about how to repopulate the earth, and was told to cover his head and throw the bones of his mother behind his shoulder. The couple understood that 'mother' meant the earth itself, and 'bones' meant stones. As they walked, they threw stones behind their shoulders: those thrown by the hero became men, and those thrown by his wife became women. These new people were given a certain name, and they settled a nearby region. The hero and his wife also had children of their own, including a son who became ancestor of a people who ruled a wider land, and daughters. One daughter, by a sea god, became mother of a figure who founded a city. The hero later fled his kingdom with his sons to another city, where he built a sanctuary to the chief god and eventually died and was buried.
Deucalion.story: Deucalion was the son of the Titan Prometheus, and ruled over a region called Phthia. Zeus, the king of the gods, grew angry at humanity's wickedness after King Lycaon sacrificed a boy to him, and decided to destroy the Bronze Age of mankind with a great flood. Prometheus forewarned his son Deucalion of the coming deluge, so Deucalion built a wooden chest and provisioned it carefully; no animals were saved in this version. He and his wife Pyrrha, daughter of the Titan Epimetheus, entered the chest together. The rivers ran in torrents and the sea flooded the coastal plains until, after nine days, the waters receded and the chest came to rest on a mountain. Once safe, the couple gave thanks to Zeus. Deucalion then consulted an oracle of the goddess Themis about how to repopulate the earth, and was told to cover his head and throw the bones of his mother behind his shoulder. The couple understood that 'mother' meant Gaia, the earth itself, and 'bones' meant stones. As they walked, they threw stones behind their shoulders: those thrown by Deucalion became men, and those thrown by Pyrrha became women. These new people were called the Leleges, and they settled the region of Locris. Deucalion and Pyrrha also had children of their own, including a son named Hellen, ancestor of a people who ruled Thessaly, and daughters. One daughter, by the sea god Poseidon, became mother of Delphus, founder of a city. Deucalion later fled his kingdom with his sons to Athens, where he built a sanctuary to Zeus and eventually died and was buried.

Manu (Hinduism).title: Manu (Hinduism)
Manu (Hinduism).blind: The central figure is the archetypal first human and progenitor of humanity. In later tradition, this figure becomes the title of fourteen successive rulers, each heading a great age within a cosmic cycle; when one age ends, a new ruler begins the next. The first ruler was born from the mind of a creator god and married to a woman formed alongside him. Their daughters married sages and gods, producing many divine and human lines, and two of their grandsons were incarnations of a preserver god. The first ruler and his wife practiced austerities in a forest by a river until demon-like beings attacked them; his grandson, aided by minor gods, killed the attackers and then took the throne of the king of heaven. Each subsequent ruler had his own sons, sages, and guardian deities, and the preserver god appeared in a different incarnation during each age to protect the world. The seventh ruler ruled a kingdom before a great flood. A fish-avatar of the preserver god warned him of the coming deluge and instructed him to build a boat. He loaded the boat with sacred scriptures, his own family, and seven sages, and the fish towed the boat to safety, preserving humanity and knowledge through the flood. This tale of warning, boat-building, and rescue is repeated with variations in other sacred texts.
