Later rulers continued the pattern: each had sons who became kings, each age had its own heavenly king and seven sages, and each was watched over by a fresh incarnation of the preserver god, some of whom performed heroic deeds such as slaying demons or liberating devotees, until the fourteenth and final ruler of the current cosmic cycle.
Manu (Hinduism).story: Manu is the archetypal first man and progenitor of humanity. In later tradition, Manu becomes the title of fourteen successive rulers, each heading a great age (manvantara) within a cosmic cycle; when one age ends, a new Manu begins the next. The first Manu, Svayambhuva, was born from the mind of the creator god Brahma and married to Shatarupa. Their daughters married sages and gods, producing many divine and human lines, and two of their grandsons were incarnations of the god Vishnu. Svayambhuva and his wife practiced austerities in a forest by a river until demon-like Rakshasas attacked them; his grandson Yajna, aided by minor gods, killed the attackers and then took the throne of the king of heaven, Indra. Each subsequent Manu had his own sons, sages, and guardian deities, and Vishnu appeared in a different incarnation during each age to protect the world. The seventh Manu, Vaivasvata, ruled a kingdom before a great flood. The fish-avatar of Vishnu warned him of the coming deluge and instructed him to build a boat. Manu loaded the boat with sacred scriptures, his own family, and seven sages, and the fish towed the boat to safety, preserving humanity and knowledge through the flood. This tale of warning, boat-building, and rescue is repeated with variations in other sacred texts. Later Manus continued the pattern: each had sons who became kings, each age had its own Indra and seven sages, and each was watched over by a fresh incarnation of Vishnu, some of whom performed heroic deeds such as slaying demons or liberating devotees, until the fourteenth and final Manu of the current cosmic cycle.

Matsya.title: Matsya
Matsya.blind: A god took the form of a fish and is described as rescuing the first man from a great flood. In the earliest account, the man, performing a ritual, finds a tiny fish in his hands. The fish says it fears being eaten by larger fish and asks for protection, promising in return to save the man from a coming flood. The man agrees, placing the fish first in a pot, then in a larger ditch, and finally, once it has grown large enough, releasing it into a great sea. The fish thanks him, warns him of the exact day of the flood, and tells him to build a boat that can be tied to its horn. When the flood arrives, the man ties his boat to the fish's horn, and the fish tows the boat through the storm to the high ground of a mountain range, saving him. Afterward, the man performs sacrifices, and from these a goddess appears; together they produce a new race of humans. In later versions, the fish reveals itself to be a great creator god, and grants the man creative power. Other tellings add that the man gathers seven wise men, plant seeds, and pairs of animals into the boat before the flood, preserving them all. In another cycle of stories, a demon steals the sacred scriptures from a sleeping creator god. The fish god descends to earth as a small fish, is found and nurtured by a king in the same growing manner, reveals its identity, warns of a flood, and after guiding the king's boat to safety, kills the demon and returns the stolen scriptures to the creator. The king is then made ruler of the current age of humanity.
Matsya.story: Matsya, the fish form of the god Vishnu, is described as rescuing the first man, Manu, from a great flood. In the earliest account, Manu, performing a ritual, finds a tiny fish in his hands. The fish says it fears being eaten by larger fish and asks for protection, promising in return to save Manu from a coming flood. Manu agrees, placing the fish first in a pot, then in a larger ditch, and finally, once it has grown large enough, releasing it into the ocean. The fish thanks him, warns him of the exact day of the flood, and tells him to build a boat that can be tied to its horn. When the flood arrives, Manu ties his boat to the fish's horn, and the fish tows the boat through the storm to the high ground of the Himalayas, saving him. Afterward, Manu performs sacrifices, and from these the goddess Ida appears; together they produce a new race of humans. In later versions, the fish reveals itself to be Brahma, and grants Manu creative power. Other tellings add that Manu gathers seven sages, plant seeds, and pairs of animals into the boat before the flood, preserving them all. In another cycle of stories, a demon named Hayagriva steals the sacred Vedas from a sleeping Brahma. Vishnu descends to earth as a small fish, is found and nurtured by a king named Satyavrata in the same growing manner, reveals its identity, warns of a flood, and after guiding the king's boat to safety, kills the demon and returns the stolen scriptures to Brahma. Satyavrata is then made Vaivasvata Manu, ruler of the current age of humanity.

Utnapishtim.title: Utnapishtim
Utnapishtim.blind: A mortal ruler of a certain city was tasked by a deity to abandon his possessions and build a giant vessel to survive a coming flood that would destroy all life. The vessel was made of solid timber so sunlight would not shine in, equal in length and width, its design drawn on the ground by the deity. The frame was built in five days, measuring 200 feet in length, width, and height, with a floor-space of one acre. It had seven floors, each divided into nine sections, and was finished on the seventh day. Once everyone had boarded, the entrance was sealed. The ruler brought his wife, family, relatives, craftsmen of his village, baby animals, and grains aboard. The flood wiped out all who were not on the vessel. After twelve days on the water, the ruler opened the hatch and saw the slopes of a mountain, where he rested the vessel for seven days. He sent out a dove, which found nothing and returned; then a swallow, which also returned; finally a raven, which saw the waters had receded and did not return. The ruler freed the animals and made a sacrifice to the gods. Because he had preserved mankind's seed and remained loyal, the gods granted the ruler and his wife immortality and a place among the heavenly gods. Later, a hero, mourning his friend, sought out the ruler to learn the secret of eternal life. The ruler told him to abandon his quest, then set him a trial to stay awake, which the hero failed. The ruler then revealed a plant that could restore youth. The hero retrieved it from the sea bottom, but a serpent stole it, and he returned home without immortality or renewed youth.
Utnapishtim.story: Uta-napishtim, a mortal king of the city of Shuruppak, was tasked by the god Enki to abandon his possessions and build a giant ship called Preserver of Life to survive a coming flood that would destroy all life. The ship was made of solid timber so sunlight would not shine in, equal in length and width, its design drawn on the ground by Enki. The frame was built in five days, measuring 200 feet in length, width, and height, with a floor-space of one acre. It had seven floors, each divided into nine sections, and was finished on the seventh day. Once everyone had boarded, the entrance was sealed. Uta-napishtim brought his wife, family, relatives, craftsmen of his village, baby animals, and grains aboard. The flood wiped out all who were not on the ship. After twelve days on the water, Uta-napishtim opened the hatch and saw the slopes of Mount Nisir, where he rested the ship for seven days. He sent out a dove, which found nothing and returned; then a swallow, which also returned; finally a raven, which saw the waters had receded and did not return. Uta-napishtim freed the animals and made a sacrifice to the gods. Because he had preserved mankind's seed and remained loyal, the gods granted Uta-napishtim and his wife immortality and a place among the heavenly gods. Later, the hero Gilgamesh, mourning his friend Enkidu, sought out Uta-napishtim to learn the secret of eternal life. Uta-napishtim told him to abandon his quest, then set him a trial to stay awake, which Gilgamesh failed. Uta-napishtim then revealed a plant that could restore youth. Gilgamesh retrieved it from the sea bottom, but a serpent stole it, and he returned home without immortality or renewed youth.

Ziusudra.title: Ziusudra
Ziusudra.blind: A ruler governed a city, having inherited rulership from his father, a former ruler. Before this time, the first cities had been founded. The divine beings decided to send a flood to destroy humankind, and a god of fresh waters warned the ruler to build a large boat. A terrible storm raged for seven days, tossing the huge boat upon the great waters. Then a sun deity appeared, and the ruler opened a window, prostrated himself, and sacrificed two kinds of livestock. After the flood subsided, the ruler prostrated himself before a sky god and another high god, who granted him eternal breath and took him to dwell in a distant paradise-land where the sun rises. Afterward, the flood swept over the land, and when it ended, kingship descended again from the heavens and came to rest in another city. In another telling of this story, the hero bore a different name, son of another figure, and was said to have reigned for eighteen great cycles of years. In this version, the god of fresh waters was identified with another deity, father of the chief sky god of a foreign pantheon, and the reed boat built by the hero was said to have survived long afterward in a distant mountain range.
Ziusudra.story: Ziusudra was king of Shuruppak, having inherited rulership from his father Ubara-Tutu. Before this time, the first cities—Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larak, Sippar, and Shuruppak—had been founded. The gods decided to send a flood to destroy mankind, and the god Enki warned Ziusudra to build a large boat. A terrible storm raged for seven days, tossing the huge boat upon the great waters. Then the sun-god Utu appeared, and Ziusudra opened a window, prostrated himself, and sacrificed an ox and a sheep. After the flood subsided, Ziusudra prostrated himself before the sky god An and the god Enlil, who granted him eternal breath and took him to dwell in Dilmun, the place where the sun rises. Afterward, the flood swept over the land, and when it ended, kingship descended again from heaven and came to rest in the city of Kish. In another telling of this story, the hero was called Xisuthros, son of Ardates, said to have reigned for eighteen great cycles of years. In this version, the god Enki was identified with the god Cronus, father of Zeus, and the reed boat built by Xisuthros was said to have survived long afterward in the Corcyrean Mountains of Armenia.

Noah.title: Noah
Noah.blind: The hero, son of an elder man, was the last patriarch before a great flood in a line of long-lived ancestors. His father had hoped his son would bring relief from toil upon a cursed ground. When the hero was five hundred years old, his three sons were born. A supreme deity, seeing the wickedness of mankind, resolved to destroy the earth with a flood, returning it to watery chaos. The hero alone found favor and was commanded to build a large boat to save his family and every kind of land animal. He obeyed faithfully, and when the flood came, he, his family, and the animals were preserved while the rest of mankind perished. After the waters receded, the hero offered burnt offerings to the deity, who accepted them and made a covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood, setting a rainbow in the clouds as a sign. The deity blessed the hero and his sons, commanding them to be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth again. Certain laws were given: not to eat living animals, not to shed human blood, and other moral commands. Afterwards, the hero became a farmer and planted a vineyard. He drank of its wine, grew drunk, and lay uncovered in his tent. One of his sons saw his father's nakedness and told his brothers, who covered him without looking. When the hero awoke, he cursed that son's child to be a servant to his brothers. From the hero's three sons came all the peoples that spread across the earth after the flood.
Noah.story: Noah, son of Lamech, was the tenth and last patriarch before the flood. Lamech had hoped his son would bring relief from toil upon the cursed ground. When Noah was five hundred years old, his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth were born. God, seeing the wickedness of mankind, resolved to destroy the earth with a flood, returning it to watery chaos. Noah alone found favor and was commanded to build an ark to save his family and every kind of land animal. Noah obeyed faithfully, and when the flood came, he, his family, and the animals were preserved while the rest of mankind perished. After the waters receded, Noah offered burnt offerings to God, who accepted them and made a covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood, setting a rainbow in the clouds as a sign. God blessed Noah and his sons, commanding them to be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth again. Certain laws were given: not to eat living animals, not to shed human blood, and other moral commands. Afterwards, Noah became a farmer and planted a vineyard. He drank of its wine, grew drunk, and lay uncovered in his tent. His son Ham saw his father's nakedness and told his brothers, who covered Noah without looking. When Noah awoke, he cursed Ham's son Canaan to be a servant to his brothers. From Noah's three sons came all the nations that spread across the earth after the flood.

Prometheus.title: Prometheus
Prometheus.blind: The hero, a member of an older race of divine beings, was responsible for creating humanity from clay and aiding it in its earliest days. He was regarded as the father of human arts and sciences, and in some accounts the father of a flood hero. At a sacrificial meal meant to settle accounts between mortals and immortals, the hero tricked the sky god, ruler of the gods, by offering him a choice between meat hidden inside an animal's stomach and bones wrapped in glistening fat. The sky god chose the fat-wrapped bones, and this became the precedent for future sacrifices, with humans keeping the meat and burning bones for the gods. Angered by the trick, the sky god hid fire from humanity. The hero stole the fire back, hidden in a hollow plant stalk, and restored it to humanity. In retaliation, the sky god had a craftsman god fashion the first woman out of clay, with a goddess of skill helping to adorn her. She carried a container which, when opened, released mischief, sorrow, plague, and disease into the world; only Hope remained trapped inside because the container was sealed before it could escape. For his crimes, the sky god bound the hero to a rock in a mountain range and sent an eagle to eat his liver daily; the liver regrew each night, prolonging the torment. Eventually, a strongman hero killed the eagle and freed the hero, with the sky god's permission. In another tradition, the hero was also credited with establishing the form of animal sacrifice practiced in religious ritual.
Prometheus.story: Prometheus, a Titan, was responsible for creating humanity from clay and aiding it in its earliest days. He was regarded as the father of human arts and sciences, and in some accounts the father of Deucalion, the hero of a flood story. At a sacrificial meal meant to settle accounts between mortals and immortals, Prometheus tricked Zeus, king of the Olympian gods, by offering him a choice between beef hidden inside an ox's stomach and bones wrapped in glistening fat. Zeus chose the fat-wrapped bones, and this became the precedent for future sacrifices, with humans keeping the meat and burning bones for the gods. Angered by the trick, Zeus hid fire from humanity. Prometheus stole the fire back, hidden in a fennel stalk, and restored it to humanity. In retaliation, Zeus had Hephaestus fashion the first woman out of clay, with Athena helping to adorn her. She carried a jar which, when opened, released mischief, sorrow, plague, and disease into the world; only Hope remained trapped inside because the jar was sealed before it could escape. For his crimes, Zeus bound Prometheus to a rock in the Caucasus Mountains and sent an eagle to eat his liver daily; the liver regrew each night, prolonging the torment. Eventually, the hero Heracles killed the eagle and freed Prometheus, with Zeus's permission. In another tradition, Prometheus was also credited with establishing the form of animal sacrifice practiced in religious ritual.

Cadmus.title: Cadmus
Cadmus.blind: The hero, a prince of a foreign land, son of a king and queen of a coastal city, was sent by his father to find his sister after she was carried off by the sky god, and told not to return without her. Unable to find her, he traveled with his mother and his nephew to a sacred island, where he took a bride, daughter of the sky god and a star-nymph; the gods attended their wedding and gave gifts. The hero then went to a sacred oracle site, where he was told to follow a special cow and build a city where it lay down. The cow, given by a neighboring king, led him to a region, where he founded a great city. Sending companions to fetch water from a spring, he found them slain by a water-dragon sacred to a war god; the hero killed the dragon and, on a wisdom goddess's instruction, sowed its teeth in the earth. Armed men sprang up from the ground; the hero threw a stone among them, causing them to fight until only five survived, who helped build the citadel of the city. For killing the dragon, the hero served the war god for eight years, after which he married his bride, receiving a robe from the wisdom goddess and a necklace from a craftsman god that brought misfortune to its owners. They had two sons and four daughters. After troubles befell his family and city, the hero abdicated to his grandson and went with his wife to another land, founding two more cities. Grieving over the dragon's death, he wished to become a serpent himself; he and his wife were both transformed into snakes, their souls eventually passing to the blessed fields.
Cadmus.story: Cadmus, a prince of Phoenicia, son of King Agenor and Queen Telephassa of Tyre, was sent by his father to find his sister Europa after she was carried off by Zeus, and told not to return without her. Unable to find her, he traveled with his mother and his nephew Thasus to Samothrace, where he took Harmonia, daughter of Zeus and the Pleiad Electra, as his bride; the gods attended their wedding and gave gifts. Cadmus then went to Delphi, where the oracle told him to follow a special cow and build a city where it lay down. The cow, given by Pelagon, King of Phocis, led him to Boeotia, where he founded Thebes. Sending companions to fetch water from a spring, he found them slain by a water-dragon sacred to Ares; Cadmus killed the dragon and, on Athena's instruction, sowed its teeth in the earth. Armed men called the Spartoi sprang up; Cadmus threw a stone among them, causing them to fight until only five survived, who helped build the citadel of Thebes. For killing the dragon, Cadmus served Ares for eight years, after which he married Harmonia, receiving a robe from Athena and a necklace from Hephaestus that brought misfortune to its owners. They had sons Polydorus and Illyrius and daughters Agave, Autonoë, Ino, and Semele. After troubles befell his family and city, Cadmus abdicated to his grandson Pentheus and went with Harmonia to Illyria, founding Lychnidos and Bouthoe. Grieving over the dragon's death, he wished to become a serpent himself; he and Harmonia were both transformed into snakes, their souls eventually passing to the blessed fields.

Triptolemus.title: Triptolemus
Triptolemus.blind: The hero, later worshipped as the inventor of agriculture, first became known to a great goddess as she searched, disguised as an old woman, for her daughter, who had been abducted by the god of the underworld. The goddess was welcomed by a king and asked to nurse his two sons. Finding one son sick, she fed him her own milk and placed him among hot coals, restoring his strength and making him grow instantly into a man. In gratitude she tried to make the other son immortal by placing him in the hearth fire, but was discovered and stopped. Instead she gave the healed son a chariot drawn by winged serpents, gifted him a grain crop, and taught him agriculture and her secret rites so he could spread them across the earth, aided by the goddess and her restored daughter. The hero traveled to a foreign land to teach its king and people to farm, but the king grew jealous and tried to kill him in his sleep; the goddess turned the king into a lynx and sent the hero back into the sky. He then went to another kingdom, where its king seized him and killed one of his chariot serpents; the goddess restored the serpent and chariot. He also traveled to a city, teaching its ruler to grow a grain crop and found a new city, later founding a second city after the ruler's son died trying to drive the chariot himself. The hero likewise taught agriculture to another people and their prince. As one of the first priests of the goddess, the hero learned her secret rites and received three commandments: honor parents, honor the gods with produce, and spare animals. After death, he became one of the judges of the underworld, ruling over those initiated into the mysteries.
Triptolemus.story: Triptolemus, later worshipped as the inventor of agriculture, first became known to the goddess Demeter as she searched, disguised as an old woman named Doso, for her daughter Persephone, who had been abducted by Hades. Demeter was welcomed by King Celeus of Eleusis and asked to nurse his sons, Demophon and Triptolemus, born to him and Metanira. Finding Triptolemus sick, Demeter fed him her own milk and placed him among hot coals, restoring his strength and making him grow instantly into a man. In gratitude she tried to make Demophon immortal by placing him in the hearth fire, but was discovered and stopped. Instead she gave Triptolemus a chariot drawn by winged serpents, gifted him wheat, and taught him agriculture and her mysteries so he could spread them across the earth, aided by Demeter and the restored Persephone. Triptolemus traveled to Scythia to teach King Lyncus and his people to farm, but Lyncus grew jealous and tried to kill him in his sleep; Demeter turned Lyncus into a lynx and sent Triptolemus back into the sky. He then went to the Getae, where King Charnabon seized him and killed one of his chariot serpents; Demeter restored the serpent and chariot. He also traveled to Patrae, teaching King Eumelus to grow corn and found the city of Aroe, later founding Antheia after Eumelus's son Antheias died trying to drive the chariot himself. Triptolemus likewise taught agriculture to Arcas and the Pelasgians. As one of the first priests of Demeter, Triptolemus learned her secret rites and received three commandments: honor parents, honor the gods with produce, and spare animals. After death, he became one of the judges of the underworld, ruling over those initiated into the Mysteries.

Palamedes (mythology).title: Palamedes (mythology)
Palamedes (mythology).blind: A prince, son of a king, joined a coalition of allied peoples in an expedition against a foreign city. He was credited with inventing dice, numbers, and letters. When a foreign prince took a queen to his city, the alliance's leader sent word to all the allied kings to honor their oaths and defend the marriage. One king, wishing to avoid the war, feigned madness by yoking two different pack animals together to plow his fields, causing the plow to move chaotically. The hero, realizing the deception, placed the man's infant son in front of the plow, forcing him to swerve and reveal his sanity. This act showed the hero's cleverness and began a rivalry between the two men. The hero later fought alongside other warriors, killing a son of a war deity, and stood his ground in battle to conquer a city after another great warrior was wounded and retreated. Accounts differ on his death: in one, his rival hid gold in his tent and forged a letter implicating him in treason, leading the allied forces to stone him to death. In another, he was drowned by two men during a fishing trip. In yet another, he was lured into a well seeking treasure and crushed with stones. In a different version, instead of dying early, he convinced the allied forces to make him their leader instead of the original commander, killed two enemy warriors in battle, but was then shot in the neck and killed by an enemy archer. He was remembered for his wisdom, his invention of counting and writing, and for the injustice of his death.
Palamedes (mythology).story: Palamedes was a prince, son of a king, who joined the Greeks in their expedition against Troy. He was credited with inventing dice, numbers, and letters. When Paris took Helen to Troy, the Greek leader sent word to all the kings to honor their oaths and defend the marriage. One king, wishing to avoid the war, feigned madness by yoking a donkey and an ox together to plow his fields, causing the plow to move chaotically. Palamedes, realizing the deception, placed the man's infant son in front of the plow, forcing him to swerve and reveal his sanity. This act showed Palamedes' cleverness and began a rivalry between the two men. Palamedes later fought alongside other heroes, killing a son of a war god, and stood his ground in battle to conquer a city after another great warrior was wounded and retreated. Accounts differ on his death: in one, his rival hid gold in his tent and forged a letter implicating him in treason, leading the Greeks to stone him to death. In another, he was drowned by two men during a fishing trip. In yet another, he was lured into a well seeking treasure and crushed with stones. In a different version, instead of dying early, he convinced the Greeks to make him their leader instead of the original commander, killed two enemy warriors in battle, but was then shot in the neck and killed by an enemy archer. He was remembered for his wisdom, his invention of counting and writing, and for the injustice of his death.

Orpheus.title: Orpheus
Orpheus.blind: The hero, son of a regional king and a divine muse, was a legendary musician, poet, and prophet. A god of music gave him a golden stringed instrument and taught him to play, while his mother taught him to compose verses. His music could charm birds, fish, and wild beasts, move trees and rocks to dance, and divert rivers. The hero joined a band of adventurers in search of a legendary treasure. When their ship passed dangerous singing creatures who lured sailors to wreck on rocky islands, the hero played his instrument louder and more beautifully, drowning out their voices and saving the crew. Later, the hero married a woman. While walking among her people at her wedding, she was pursued by a wild woodland spirit and fled into a nest of venomous snakes, dying from a fatal bite. Grief-stricken, the hero played such mournful songs that nature spirits and gods wept. He traveled to the underworld, where his music softened the hearts of its rulers, who agreed to let the woman return with him on the condition that he walk ahead and not look back until both reached the upper world. As the hero emerged, he turned to look at her too soon, before she had crossed over, and she vanished forever. Toward the end of his life, the hero abandoned worship of other gods, honoring only the sun as the greatest deity. Rising early to greet the sunrise atop a mountain, he angered his former patron, who sent frenzied female worshippers to tear him limb from limb. He was buried afterward, his death mirroring that of another figure similarly destroyed by the same maddened women.
Orpheus.story: Orpheus, son of the Thracian king Oeagrus and the Muse Calliope, was a legendary musician, poet, and prophet. Apollo gave him a golden lyre and taught him to play, while his mother taught him to make verses. His music could charm birds, fish, and wild beasts, move trees and rocks to dance, and divert rivers. Orpheus joined Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece. When the ship passed the Sirens, whose songs lured sailors to wreck on rocky islands, Orpheus played his lyre louder and more beautifully, drowning out their voices and saving the crew. Later, Orpheus married Eurydice. While walking among her people at her wedding, she was pursued by a satyr and fled into a nest of vipers, dying from a fatal bite. Grief-stricken, Orpheus played such mournful songs that nymphs and gods wept. He traveled to the underworld, where his music softened the hearts of its rulers, who agreed to let Eurydice return with him on the condition that he walk ahead and not look back until both reached the upper world. As Orpheus emerged, he turned to look at her too soon, before she had crossed over, and she vanished forever. Toward the end of his life, Orpheus abandoned worship of other gods, honoring only the sun as the greatest deity. Rising early to greet the sunrise atop a mountain, he angered his former patron, who sent frenzied female worshippers to tear him limb from limb. He was buried afterward, his death mirroring that of another figure similarly destroyed by the same maddened women.

Romulus and Remus.title: Romulus and Remus
Romulus and Remus.blind: Two twin brothers were born in a smaller city to a woman who was a consecrated priestess and daughter of a deposed ruler. She conceived them after a war god visited her in a sacred grove. Fearing them as threats to his power, the usurping king who had overthrown her father ordered the infants killed and had them abandoned on the bank of a great river. A river god saved them, and they survived because a she-wolf suckled them in a cave. A shepherd found and raised them, and they grew up as leaders among the local herding community, unaware of their true heritage. As young men, they became involved in a conflict between supporters of their grandfather and the usurping king. One brother was captured and taken to the smaller city, where his identity was suspected. The other organized a rescue, and the brothers learned of their true parentage. Joining forces with their grandfather, they overthrew and killed the usurper, restoring the grandfather to the throne. The twins then set out to found their own city near a group of hills. They quarreled over which hill to build on, each favoring a different one, and sought divine approval through bird-omen divination. One brother saw six birds, but the other saw twelve and claimed victory. The dispute escalated, and the losing brother was killed, either by his twin or by one of the twin's supporters, after insulting the new city. The surviving brother went on to found the city, establishing its government, army, religious traditions, and institutions, ruling as its first king for many years.
Romulus and Remus.story: Romulus and Remus were twin brothers born in Alba Longa to Rhea Silvia, a Vestal Virgin and daughter of the deposed king Numitor. She conceived them after the god Mars visited her in a sacred grove. Fearing them as threats to his rule, King Amulius, who had overthrown Numitor, ordered the infants killed and had them abandoned on the bank of the river Tiber. The god Tiberinus saved them, and they survived thanks to a she-wolf who suckled them in a cave, the Lupercal. A shepherd named Faustulus found and raised them, and they grew up as leaders among the local shepherd community, unaware of their true heritage. As young men, they became involved in a conflict between supporters of Numitor and Amulius. Remus was captured and taken to Alba Longa, where his identity was suspected. Romulus organized a rescue, and the brothers learned of their true parentage. Joining forces with their grandfather Numitor, they overthrew and killed Amulius, restoring Numitor to the throne. The twins then set out to found their own city near the seven hills. They quarreled over which hill to build on—Romulus favoring the Palatine, Remus the Aventine—and sought divine approval through augury. Remus saw six birds, but Romulus saw twelve and claimed victory. The dispute escalated, and Remus was killed, either by Romulus or by one of his supporters, after insulting the new city. Romulus went on to found Rome, establishing its government, army, religious traditions, and institutions, ruling as its first king for many years.

Aeneas.title: Aeneas
Aeneas.blind:
A mortal prince, cousin to a king, fathered a son by a goddess of love. The king of the gods had made the goddess desire the prince; she appeared to him disguised as a mortal princess, seduced him, then revealed her true identity, warning him never to tell anyone he had lain with a goddess. She bore a son, gave him to mountain nymphs to raise until age five, then delivered him to his father. The father later boasted of the affair and was struck lame in one foot by a thunderbolt from the king of the gods, so that in later years his son had to carry him.

In a great war, the son was an honorable warrior, twice saved from death by the gods. He led an attack to recover the body of his brother-in-law and commanded allied troops as cousin to the chief warrior on his side. His mother and a god of prophecy rescued him from a duel with an enemy hero and healed him; a sea god also saved him from another great hero, declaring he was destined to become king of his people. He was said to be the one household spared destruction for his piety.

When his city fell, the gods commanded him to flee. He gathered companions, carried the city's sacred household images, and bore his lame father from the flames. His father died during their travels. A storm drove them to a foreign city, where its queen fell in love with him and proposed joint rule; but a divine messenger reminded him of his destiny, and he departed secretly. The grieving queen cursed his descendants and killed herself upon a pyre.

After another storm, the group held funeral games for the dead father on an island, then reached a new land, where the son descended to the underworld, met the dead queen (who turned away from him) and his father, who showed him the future of his descendants. A local king welcomed the exiles, and despite his daughter's betrothal to a rival king, a prophecy destined her to marry the newcomer instead. War followed, aided by hostile gods and allied kings, but the newcomer prevailed and killed the rival. He founded a city named for his wife, welcomed his lost queen's sister, who later killed herself from jealousy, and after his own death was made a god: a river god cleansed his mortal parts and his mother anointed him with divine substances. He became ancestor of the twin founders of a great city, raised in infancy by a she-wolf.

V\u00e4in\u00e4m\u00f6inen.title: Väinämöinen
V\u00e4in\u00e4m\u00f6inen.blind:
The hero was a demigod born to a primal goddess. He remained in his mother's womb for seven hundred and thirty years while she floated in the sea and the earth was formed. A bird laid eggs upon her knee; when the eggs fell and broke, they formed the earth and the sky. After praying to the sun, the moon, and a group of stars, the hero was able to leave his mother's womb and dive into the sea.

He became an eternal bard, bringing order over chaos and establishing his homeland. He was old and wise, possessing a potent magical singing voice. He defeated a younger rival in a singing contest, since the hero had witnessed and shaped the events of creation while the rival only remembered that they had happened. The hero then sang the rival down into a bog.

The hero's search for a wife brought his land into contact with a dark, hostile northern land. This conflict led to the creation and theft of a magical artifact, made by a smith. A mission to recapture it ended in battle, and the artifact was shattered, its pieces scattered across the world. The hero also slew a great fish and made a magical stringed instrument from its jawbones, playing it so beautifully that goddesses came to listen. He possessed a magical fire sword, crafted by the smith, which shone like the sun and was extraordinarily sharp.

His end came when a maiden bore a child after eating a berry. The infant was brought before the hero to be judged, and he ruled that the strangely born child should be put to death. The two-week-old infant rebuked the old man for his past sins, including causing a maiden's drowning. The child was then baptized and made king. Defeated and ashamed, the hero sang for himself a boat of copper and sailed away from the mortal realm, promising that he would return when his crafts and might were needed again.
V\u00e4in\u00e4m\u00f6inen.story:

Väinämöinen then sang Joukahainen down into a bog.

Väinämöinen's search for a wife brought his land into contact with a dark, hostile northern land called Pohjola. This conflict led to the creation and theft of a magical artifact, the Sampo, made by a smith named Ilmarinen. Väinämöinen also slew a great pike and made a magical kantele from its jawbones, playing it so beautifully that goddesses came to listen. He possessed a magical fire sword, crafted by the smith, which shone like the sun and was extraordinarily sharp.

His end came when a maiden named Marjatta bore a child after eating a berry. The infant was brought before Väinämöinen to be judged, and he ruled that the strangely born child should be put to death. Ilmarinen.title: Ilmarinen
Ilmarinen.blind: The smith-god is an immortal artificer who works several known metals of the time, including copper and precious metals. He forged the dome of the sky and once forged an iron tool for a bird so it could gather pieces of its broken eggs, which became the sun, moon, and clouds. Elsewhere, an island at the center of the world was born when a drop of boiling gold fell from his pot into the sea. He also struck the first spark of fire using feathers from a great bird, and forged the first iron, which swore never to hurt anyone but broke its promise after an insect brought venom into its quenching water. In one tale, the smith-god forged a weapon and a horse, then worked the bellows himself and created a maiden of gold, but she was cold to lie beside, teaching that men should never make a maiden of gold and silver. In the great tale of the magic mill, a sage was held captive by an enchantress, mistress of a northern land, who demanded a magic mill be forged in exchange for safe passage and her daughter's hand. The sage tricked the smith-god into traveling to the northern land. There, seeing the maiden's beauty, the smith-god agreed to forge the mill. Over days he cast a crossbow, a ship, a cow, and a plow from his forge, each one flawed and destroyed. Finally, after conjuring four winds, the magic mill emerged, producing grain, salt, and gold. The enchantress locked it away, and though the smith-god asked the maiden to marry him, she refused, and he returned home alone. Later, after losing his wife to a curse, he forged a new wife of gold, but she was cold; his brother refused to marry her and told him to melt her down into trinkets instead.
Ilmarinen.story: Ilmarinen is an immortal artificer god who works brass, copper, iron, gold, and silver. He forged the dome of the sky and once forged an iron rake for a swallow so it could gather pieces of its broken eggs, which became the sun, moon, and clouds. Elsewhere, an island at the center of the world was born when a drop of boiling gold fell from his pot into the sea. He also struck the first spark of fire using three eagle feathers, and forged the first iron, which swore never to hurt anyone but broke its promise after a hornet brought snake poison into its quenching water. In one tale, Ilmarinen forged a sword and a stallion, then worked the bellows himself and created a maiden of gold, but she was cold to lie beside, teaching that men should never make a maiden of gold and silver. In the great tale of the Sampo, the sage Väinämöinen was held captive by Louhi, mistress of Pohjola, who demanded a magic Sampo be forged in exchange for safe passage and her daughter's hand. Väinämöinen tricked Ilmarinen into traveling to Pohjola. There, seeing the maiden's beauty, Ilmarinen agreed to forge the Sampo. Over days he cast a crossbow, a ship, a cow, and a plow from his forge, each one flawed and destroyed. Finally, after conjuring four winds, the Sampo emerged as a mill producing grain, salt, and gold. Louhi locked it away, and though Ilmarinen asked the maiden to marry him, she refused, and he returned home alone. Later, after losing his wife to a curse, he forged a new wife of gold, but she was cold; his brother refused to marry her and told him to melt her down into trinkets instead.

Bran the Blessed.title: Brân the Blessed
Bran the Blessed.blind:
A giant king ruled over an island realm. He was brother to a woman, and to several half-brothers, one of whom was prone to violent jealousy. A foreign king sailed with a fleet of ships to ask for the king's sister in marriage, seeking an alliance between the two lands. The giant king agreed, and a wedding feast was held in tents, since no house could hold his massive body. Furious that he had not been consulted, the jealous half-brother mutilated all the foreign king's horses. To make amends, the giant king gave the offended king a magic cauldron that could restore the dead to life, though the revived could not speak. Pleased, the foreign king sailed home with his new wife.

The wife bore a son, but resentment over the maimed horses lingered, and the foreign court forced her into the kitchen, where she was abused for three years. She tamed a bird and sent it with a message to her brother, who declared war. He waded across the sea himself, since no ship could bear him, while his army sailed behind. When the enemy blocked a river crossing, the giant king lay down his own body as a bridge for his troops. The enemy, seeming to yield, offered his nephew the kingship and built a great house to host the giant, but hid a group of armed men in sacks to ambush the feast. The suspicious half-brother crushed the skulls of the hidden men. At the feast he also flung his sister's young son into the fire, sparking battle. The enemy revived their dead with the magic cauldron until the half-brother hid among the corpses and let himself be thrown in, shattering the cauldron and dying in the act. The giant king was mortally wounded in the foot. He ordered his men to cut off his head and carry it to be buried facing the enemy's homeland to ward off invasion. The survivors feasted with the still-speaking head for years before completing the burial. The sister, grieving, died of a broken heart.

Wayland the Smith.title: Wayland the Smith
Wayland the Smith.blind: A master craftsman, one of three siblings, lived for a time with three supernatural maidens who were companions to him and his siblings. After nine years the maidens departed; the siblings went searching for them and never returned. The craftsman's companion left him a ring before she departed, and he forged many copies of it. A ruler captured the craftsman while he slept, had him crippled so he could not walk, and imprisoned him on an island, forcing him to make treasures for the ruler. The ruler gave the craftsman's ring to his own daughter and wore the craftsman's weapon himself. In revenge, when the ruler's two sons secretly visited the craftsman's workshop, he killed them, then made drinking vessels from their skulls, jewels from their eyes, and an ornament from their teeth. He sent the vessels to the ruler, the jewels to the ruler's spouse, and the ornament to the daughter. When the daughter brought her ring to him for mending, he tricked and seduced her, leaving her pregnant. He then crafted a flying garment and traveled to the ruler's hall, where he revealed everything he had done: the killing of the sons, the ornaments made from their remains, and the seduction of the daughter. The grieving ruler could not stop him, for no archer or rider could reach him in flight, and the craftsman escaped forever. The ruler summoned his daughter and asked if the craftsman's account was true; she confirmed it, saying she had been powerless against him because he was too strong for her.

He sent the goblets to the king, the jewels to the queen, and the brooch to the daughter. When the daughter brought her ring to him for mending, he tricked and seduced her, leaving her pregnant. He then crafted a winged garment and flew to the king's hall, where he revealed everything he had done: the murder of the sons, the jewelry made from their remains, and the seduction of the daughter. The grieving king could not stop him, for no archer or horseman could reach him in flight, and the smith escaped forever. The king summoned his daughter and asked if the smith's account was true; she confirmed it, saying she had been powerless against him because he was too strong for her.

Kvasir.title: Kvasir
Kvasir.blind: In a certain mythology, two tribes of divine beings had fought a long war. To seal peace between them, both sides spat into a vessel. Not wanting the truce-symbol to go to waste, the divine beings shaped the spittle into a man, the wise one. He was extremely wise, able to answer any question put to him, and he traveled far and wide teaching people and spreading knowledge. Eventually two small magical craftsmen invited the wise one to their home for a private talk. When he arrived, they killed him and drained his blood into two vessels and a container. They mixed the blood with honey to create a magical drink, a drink that would make whoever tasted it a poet or scholar. When the divine beings asked after the wise one, the craftsmen lied, saying he had suffocated from his own intelligence, since no one was learned enough to question him. The drink eventually passed through the hands of a chief god and came to humankind, bringing them the gift of poetry. The wise one also played a role in catching a trickster deity, who had turned into a fish to hide from the divine beings after causing the death of another god. When the divine beings reached the trickster's hideout, the wise one was the first to enter, and being the wisest of all, he recognized the shape of a fishing net in the ashes of a fire. He told the divine beings, who used the pattern to fashion a net and capture the trickster from a river, binding him afterward as punishment.
Kvasir.story: In Norse mythology, two tribes of gods, the Æsir and the Vanir, had fought a long war. To seal peace between them, both sides spat into a vat. Not wanting the truce-symbol to go to waste, the gods shaped the spittle into a man named Kvasir. He was extremely wise, able to answer any question put to him, and he traveled far and wide teaching mankind and spreading knowledge. Eventually two dwarfs, Fjalar and Galar, invited Kvasir to their home for a private talk. When he arrived, they killed him and drained his blood into two vats, called Són and Boðn, and a pot called Óðrerir. They mixed the blood with honey to create the Mead of Poetry, a drink that would make whoever tasted it a poet or scholar. When the Æsir asked after Kvasir, the dwarfs lied, saying he had suffocated from his own intelligence, since no one was learned enough to question him. The mead eventually passed through the hands of the god Odin and came to mankind, bringing them the gift of poetry. Kvasir also played a role in catching the trickster god Loki, who had turned into a salmon to hide from the gods after causing the death of the god Baldr. When the gods reached Loki's hideout, Kvasir was the first to enter, and being the wisest of all, he recognized the shape of a fishing net in the ashes of a fire. He told the gods, who used the pattern to fashion a net and capture Loki from a river, binding him afterward as punishment.

R\u00edgs\u00feula.title: Rígsþula
R\u00edgs\u00feula.blind: A wandering deity walked along a shoreline and came to a hut owned by an elderly couple, who gave him poor food and let him sleep between them in their bed. Nine months later the woman bore a dark, ugly son, who married another woman; their many sons and daughters became a class of servants. Traveling on, the deity reached a better house belonging to a second couple, who fed him well and likewise let him sleep between them. Nine months later a ruddy son was born; he married a woman, and their children became free farmers, craftsmen, and herders. Continuing further, the deity came to a splendid mansion belonging to a third couple, who served him a magnificent meal. Nine months later a beautiful, fair-haired son was born. When this son grew skilled with weapons, hunting birds, hounds, and horses, the deity returned, claimed him as his own child, gave him his own title, taught him secret knowledge, and urged him toward lordship. This son won eighteen homesteads through war and married a noblewoman, daughter of a local lord; they had twelve sons, ancestors of a warrior nobility. The youngest of these sons surpassed all others in secret knowledge, magic, understanding the speech of birds, quenching fire, and healing minds, and inherited his father's title as well. While hunting birds in a forest, he was told by a crow that he should instead make war and seek the halls of two rulers who were wealthier than he. The story breaks off at this point.
R\u00edgs\u00feula.story: A god named Ríg wandered along a seashore and came to a farm-hut owned by a couple called Ái and Edda, who gave him poor food and let him sleep between them in their bed. Nine months later Edda bore a dark, ugly son named Þræll, who married a woman named Thír; their many sons and daughters became the race of serfs. Traveling on, Ríg reached a better house belonging to Afi and Amma, who fed him well and likewise let him sleep between them. Nine months later a ruddy son, Karl, was born; he married a woman named Snör, and their children became free farmers, craftsmen, and herdsmen. Continuing further, Ríg came to a splendid mansion of Faðir and Móðir, who served him a magnificent meal. Nine months later a beautiful, fair-haired son, Jarl, was born. When Jarl grew skilled with weapons, hawks, hounds, and horses, Ríg returned, claimed him as his son, gave him his own name, taught him runes, and urged him toward lordship. Jarl won eighteen homesteads through war and married Erna, daughter of a lord named Hersir; they had twelve sons, ancestors of the warrior nobility. The youngest, Konr, surpassed all others in rune-lore, magic, understanding birds' speech, quenching fire, and healing minds, and inherited the name Ríg as well. While hunting birds in a forest, Konr was told by a crow that he should instead make war and seek the halls of two rulers, Dan and Danþír, who were wealthier than he. The poem breaks off at this point.

Sosruko.title: Sosruko
Sosruko.blind: The hero is a central character in many cycles of a people's traditional sagas. He is a powerful but devious man, though he is the smallest of a group of legendary figures, a people whose sagas recount many heroic deeds. Because of his cunning and his power despite his small stature, the hero is sometimes cast in the light of a trickster figure among his people. He is described as a minion of the gods, serving them in some capacity, and he is also the son of a doting mother, a divine or legendary matriarch, who cares for him closely. The central deed attributed to the hero is that he stole fire from a giant. This act of theft, taking fire away from a being far larger and presumably more powerful than himself, stands as his defining accomplishment within the mythology of his people. His smallness in comparison to the other legendary figures makes this feat notable, since he achieves through cleverness and deviousness what might otherwise require great physical strength. His mother's devotion to him is mentioned alongside this feat, suggesting that his family relationship played a role in the stories told about him. The hero's identity as a trickster-like figure, his service to the gods, his relationship with his mother, and his theft of fire from the giant together form the core narrative elements associated with him in the traditional sagas of his people, which are the traditional stories of a regional people.

Amirani.title: Amirani
Amirani.blind: The hero was the child of a goddess of the hunt, but was removed prematurely from her womb and raised by a hunter and his wife, alongside her two natural sons. Raised violently in the wilderness, the three brothers attacked every stranger they met to test their strength. Eager for adventure, the hero fought against demonic giants living at the edges of inhabited lands. Later, to avenge their murdered uncle, the brothers sought out his killer, a three-headed giant. The hero challenged the giant and cut off all three heads; from each head a worm emerged and became a dragon—one white, one red, one black. The hero killed the white and red dragons, but the black dragon swallowed him and fled to a great sea or the underworld. From inside, the hero cut the dragon open and killed it. He then journeyed overseas seeking a woman, daughter of a demon king. The demon army killed his adopted brothers, but the hero slew every enemy, including their king. Grief-stricken, he took his own life, but the woman used magic to revive him and his companions. Wandering alone, the hero met an undead giant he could not lift. He prayed to a sky god, who granted him great strength, making him arrogant enough to challenge the god to a duel. As punishment, the god chained him beneath a mountain, guarded by his winged dog, whose licking of the chains was undone whenever distant blacksmiths struck their anvils. Once yearly the mountain opens, letting the hero see the sky briefly before closing again.
Amirani.story: Amirani, a culture hero, was the son of Dali, a goddess of the hunt, but was removed prematurely from her womb and raised by a hunter named Sulkalmakhi and his wife Darejan, alongside her two natural sons, Badri and Usup. Raised violently in the wilderness, the three brothers attacked every stranger they met to test their strength. Eager for adventure, Amirani fought against Devs, demonic giants living at the edges of inhabited lands. Later, to avenge their murdered uncle, the brothers sought out his killer, a three-headed giant named Baq'-Baq'. Amirani challenged the giant and cut off all three heads; from each head a worm emerged and became a dragon—one white, one red, one black. Amirani killed the white and red dragons, but the black dragon swallowed him and fled to the Black Sea or the underworld. From inside, Amirani cut the dragon open and killed it. He then journeyed overseas seeking kamar, daughter of the demon king Kaji. The demon army killed his adopted brothers, but Amirani slew every enemy, including their king. Grief-stricken, he took his own life, but kamar used magic to revive him and his companions. Wandering alone, Amirani met an undead giant he could not lift. He prayed to Ghmerti (God), who granted him great strength, making him arrogant enough to challenge God to a duel. As punishment, God chained him beneath a mountain, guarded by his winged dog Q'ursha, whose licking of the chains was undone whenever distant blacksmiths struck their anvils. Once yearly the mountain opens, letting Amirani see the sky briefly before closing again.

Fuxi.title: Fuxi
Fuxi.blind: A giant being was said to be the creation figure, sleeping within an egg of chaos. As he awoke, he stood up and divided the sky from the earth. He then died after standing up, and his body turned into rivers, mountains, plants, animals, and everything else in the world, among which was a powerful being. This powerful being gave birth to a twin brother and sister, who had human faces and the bodies of snakes. The two lived together on a mythical mountain. One day they set up two separate piles of fire, and the flames eventually became one; taking this as a sign, they decided to become husband and wife. They used clay to create offspring, and with divine power they made the clay figures come alive, and these became the earliest human beings. The brother looked upward and studied the images in the heavens, and looked downward and studied the occurrences on earth. He united husband and wife and laid down the laws of humanity, devising eight symbolic figures made of two fundamental forces in order to gain mastery over the world, representing heaven, earth, water, fire, thunder, wind, mountain, and lake. He taught people to cook food and to hunt and fish, including fishing with nets and hunting with weapons of bone, wood, and bamboo. He instituted marriage and the family structure and offered the first sacrifices to the sky. He is said to have received the pattern for his symbols from markings on the back of a dragon-horse (or tortoise) that emerged from a river, an event said to be the origin of writing. He is also credited with inventing a stringed musical instrument. His daughter, also said to be his consort, drowned while crossing a river and became its spirit. He is said to have lived 197 years and to have died in a place where a monument to him still stands.

This powerful being gave birth to a twin brother and sister, who had human faces and the bodies of snakes. The two lived together on a mythical mountain. One day they set up two separate piles of fire, and the flames eventually became one; taking this as a sign, they decided to become husband and wife. They used clay to create offspring, and with divine power they made the clay figures come alive, and these became the earliest human beings. The brother looked upward and studied the images in the heavens, and looked downward and studied the occurrences on earth. He united husband and wife and laid down the laws of humanity, devising eight symbolic figures made of two fundamental forces in order to gain mastery over the world, representing heaven, earth, water, fire, thunder, wind, mountain, and lake. He taught people to cook food and to hunt and fish, including fishing with nets and hunting with weapons of bone, wood, and bamboo. He instituted marriage and the family structure and offered the first sacrifices to the sky. He is said to have received the pattern for his symbols from markings on the back of a dragon-horse (or tortoise) that emerged from a river, an event said to be the origin of writing. He is also credited with inventing a stringed musical instrument. His daughter, also said to be his consort, drowned while crossing a river and became its spirit. He is said to have lived 197 years and to have died in a place where a monument to him still stands.

Shennong.title: Shennong
Shennong.blind: The hero's mother swallowed the vapor of a mythical creature, and nine days later she gave birth to him on the banks of a river. He had the head of a bovine animal with the body of a man. He grew rapidly, beginning to speak after only three days, and eventually reached a height of over eight feet. He obtained a mystical book of herbs from a wise teacher and journeyed across the land to record 365 medicinal herbs and fungi. He taught people the use of the plow, the basics of agriculture, and the use of a fibrous plant. He was also called a god of burning wind, and was said to be either the progenitor of, or to have had as a minister, an ox-headed, sharp-horned, bronze-foreheaded, iron-skulled being. He was regarded as the father of a later ruler who carried on the secrets of medicine, immortality, and gold-making. Before his teachings, people were sickly, wanting, starved and diseased; he researched agriculture himself, eating hundreds of plants, and even consumed seventy poisons in a single day to test them, having a transparent body that let him see the effects within himself. He invented a bent-wood plow and cut-wood rake and established a noonday market. He discovered a beverage plant when leaves from a burning twig were carried by hot air into his cooking vessel of boiling water, and thereafter used it as an antidote to poisons. He eventually died after eating the yellow flower of a poisonous weed that ruptured his intestines before he could swallow his antidotal drink, having given his life for humanity. He was afterward worshipped as a healing deity and patron of farmers, grain traders, and medical practitioners. He is also said to have helped create a stringed musical instrument together with two other legendary figures.

He is also said to have helped create a stringed musical instrument together with two other legendary figures.

N\u00fcwa.title: Nüwa
N\u00fcwa.blind: A mother goddess created humanity out of loneliness. She molded people from a yellow clay-like earth by hand, and these became the wealthy and noble. Because shaping each person individually was exhausting, she dragged a string through mud to mass-produce the rest of humanity, who became the commoners. A great battle between deities broke the pillars that held up the sky, causing the sky to collapse partly, fires to rage uncontrollably, floods that would not recede, and fierce beasts to attack ordinary people. The goddess smelted five-colored stones to patch the holes in the sky, cut the legs off a giant turtle to serve as new pillars, killed a great serpent blamed for the flooding, and piled up reeds and ashes to stop the surging waters. Order was restored: the sky was mended, the pillars stood firm, the waters drained, and people were safe. The goddess was the sister, and later wife, of a male culture hero. Before marrying, the two lived on a sacred mountain; ashamed of their feelings for each other, they prayed that if a higher power approved their marriage, mist would gather over the mountain. The mist gathered, confirming their union. When they became intimate, they made a fan from grass to hide their faces, which is said to be why fans are used in marriage customs today. In another version, after surviving a great flood, the pair married by a higher power's command, and the goddess gave birth to a ball of flesh, which was cut into pieces that scattered across the world and became human beings. In a later legend, the goddess was honored for having mended the sky long ago. A ruler who saw her temple statue lusted after her image and wrote a lewd poem on a nearby wall. Enraged, the goddess vowed that his ruling house would fall as punishment, and she sent three spirit subordinates to bewitch him, contributing to the eventual collapse of his rule.
