Yu the Great.title: Yu the Great
Yu the Great.blind:
The hero was a legendary sage-king credited with controlling a great flood and founding a dynasty. He was the son of a father-figure who descended from earlier ancestral rulers and a supreme ancestor-deity. During a former ruler's reign, floods plagued the land, and the father spent over nine years building dikes and dams that failed. The hero, his son, studied the rivers and, working with an agricultural helper, devised irrigation canals that redirected floodwaters and dredged riverbeds, laboring alongside common workers for thirteen years. He famously opened a narrow channel at a certain mountain, later called by a name honoring him. In some versions, a dragon and a turtle assisted him; in others, he cut through a mountain ridge with a divine axe. He sacrificed his body to the work, developing calluses on his hands and feet. Newly married, he left home for the flood work and passed his own doorstep three times over thirteen years without entering, even as his wife bore their son and the boy grew old enough to speak and then reach ten years. The hero also killed a nine-headed snake monster serving a rival deity's minister.

Another ruler, impressed by the hero's diligence, passed the throne to him over his own son. The hero became ruler at 53, established his capital, and founded a new ruling line. He divided the land into nine provinces, collected metal from each, and cast a set of nine ritual vessels. He fought a rebellious leader of a foreign people, defeated but spared him, reforming him for three years until he ruled well. The hero also killed a rival northern leader to secure his throne. He ruled for forty-five years, died of illness during a hunting tour, and was buried at a mountain.
Yu the Great.story:
Yu the Great was a legendary sage-king credited with controlling a great flood and founding the Xia dynasty. He was the son of Gun, who descended from Zhuanxu and the Yellow Emperor. During Emperor Yao's reign, floods plagued the land, and Gun spent over nine years building dikes and dams that failed. Yu, his son, studied the rivers and, working with Hou Ji, devised irrigation canals that redirected floodwaters and dredged riverbeds, laboring alongside common workers for thirteen years. He famously opened a narrow channel at Mount Longmen, later called "Yu's Gateway." In some versions, a yellow dragon and black turtle assisted him; in others, he cut through a mountain ridge with a divine axe. He sacrificed his body to the work, developing calluses on his hands and feet. Newly married, he left home for the flood work and passed his own doorstep three times over thirteen years without entering, even as his wife bore their son Qi and the boy grew old enough to speak and then reach ten years. Yu also killed Xiangliu, a nine-headed snake monster serving Gonggong's minister.

Emperor Shun, impressed by Yu's diligence, passed the throne to him over his own son. Yu became emperor at 53, established his capital, and founded the Xia dynasty. He divided the land into nine provinces, collected bronze from each, and cast the Nine Tripod Cauldrons. He fought a rebellious Miao leader, defeated but spared him, reforming him for three years until he ruled well. Yu also killed a northern leader named Fangfeng to secure his throne. Yu ruled for forty-five years, died of illness during a hunting tour, and was buried at Mount Kuaiji.

Cangjie.title: Cangjie
Cangjie.blind: A legendary figure served as an official historian to a ruler and is credited as the inventor of a system of writing. According to legend he had four eyes, and when he completed his invention, spirits and ghosts wept and the sky rained a grain crop. One version of the legend tells that shortly after unifying a land, the ruler grew dissatisfied with the old method of recording information by tying knots in rope, and charged the figure with creating a system of written symbols. The figure settled on a riverbank and devoted himself to the task, but for a long time could not create even one symbol. One day he saw a large mythical bird flying overhead carrying an object in its beak; the object fell before him and proved to be a hoof-print. Unable to identify the animal, he asked a passing hunter, who told him it was the unmistakable hoof-print of a mythical hoofed beast, distinct from that of any other animal. This exchange inspired the figure to believe that capturing the distinguishing characteristics of things in drawings would produce the ideal form of writing. He began studying the sun, moon, stars, clouds, lakes, rivers, oceans, and every kind of bird and beast, creating symbols based on their special traits, until he had compiled a great many. He presented the completed writing system to the ruler, who summoned the regional leaders of the land's provinces so that the figure could teach them the new symbols. Monuments and shrines were later built in his honor on the riverbank where he had worked. Another version of the legend says the figure was instead inspired by observing the network of veins on a shelled reptile.
Cangjie.story: Cangjie was an official historian serving the Yellow Emperor and is credited as the inventor of Chinese characters. According to legend he had four eyes, and when he completed his invention of the characters, deities and ghosts wept and the sky rained millet. One version of his legend tells that shortly after unifying China, the Yellow Emperor grew dissatisfied with the old method of recording information by tying knots in rope, and charged Cangjie with creating a system of written characters. Cangjie settled on a riverbank and devoted himself to the task, but for a long time could not create even one character. One day he saw a phoenix flying overhead carrying an object in its beak; the object fell before him and proved to be a hoof-print. Unable to identify the animal, he asked a passing hunter, who told him it was the unmistakable hoof-print of a Pixiu, distinct from that of any other beast. This exchange inspired Cangjie to believe that capturing the distinguishing characteristics of things in drawings would produce the ideal form of writing. He began studying the sun, moon, stars, clouds, lakes, rivers, oceans, and every kind of bird and beast, creating characters based on their special traits, until he had compiled a great many. He presented the completed writing system to the Yellow Emperor, who summoned the premiers of the nine provinces so that Cangjie could teach them the new characters. Monuments and temples were later built in his honor on the riverbank where he had worked. Another version of the legend says Cangjie was instead inspired by observing the network of veins on a turtle.

Dangun.title: Tan'gun
Dangun.blind:
The sky god had a son who yearned to live among the earth's valleys and mountains. The sky god permitted his son and 3,000 followers to descend onto a sacred mountain, where the son founded a settlement called "the divine city." Along with his ministers of clouds, rain, and wind, he instituted laws and moral codes, and taught humans various arts, medicine, and agriculture, including two forms of healing practice.

A tiger and a bear prayed to the son of the sky god that they might become human. He gave them a number of cloves of a bulb plant and a bundle of an herb, ordering them to eat only this sacred food and remain out of sunlight for 100 days. The tiger gave up after about twenty days and left the cave, but the bear persevered and was transformed into a woman.

The bear-woman was grateful and made offerings to the son of the sky god, but she lacked a husband and grew sad. She prayed beneath a sacred tree to be blessed with a child. Moved by her prayers, the son of the sky god took her as his wife, and she gave birth to a son.

This son ascended to the throne, built a walled city near a great river, and called his kingdom by a name now referred to as the first kingdom, to distinguish it from a later kingdom of the same name established roughly 2000 years afterward. He later moved his capital to another mountain city. The ruler of this kingdom conducted a yearly ritual in honor of his ancestral god, and the myth became the political ideology of the era, with the ritual serving as a function of political assembly.
Dangun.story:
The Lord of Heaven had a son who yearned to live among the earth's valleys and mountains. The Lord of Heaven permitted his son and 3,000 followers to descend onto a sacred mountain, where the son founded a settlement called the "City of God." Along with his ministers of clouds, rain, and wind, he instituted laws and moral codes, and taught humans various arts, medicine, and agriculture, including acupuncture and moxibustion.

A tiger and a bear prayed to the son of heaven that they might become human. He gave them twenty cloves of garlic and a bundle of mugwort, ordering them to eat only this sacred food and remain out of sunlight for 100 days. The tiger gave up after about twenty days and left the cave, but the bear persevered and was transformed into a woman.

The bear-woman was grateful and made offerings to the son of heaven, but she lacked a husband and grew sad. She prayed beneath a divine birch tree to be blessed with a child. Moved by her prayers, the son of heaven took her as his wife, and she gave birth to a son.

This son ascended to the throne, built a walled city near a great river, and called his kingdom by a name now referred to as the first kingdom, to distinguish it from a later kingdom of the same name established roughly 2000 years afterward. He later moved his capital to another mountain city. The king of this kingdom conducted a yearly ritual in honor of his ancestral god, and the myth became the political ideology of the era, with the ritual serving as a function of political assembly.

Ninigi-no-Mikoto.title: Ninigi-no-Mikoto
Ninigi-no-Mikoto.blind:
The hero, grandson of the sun goddess, was born from a heavenly father-god and a mother-goddess, and was nurtured with special affection by a senior creator deity. The sun goddess sent the hero to rule the earth, giving him three sacred treasures: a sword, a mirror, and a jewel. On his descent to earth, the hero was accompanied by several deities, including a female deity, a guardian deity, and others, who became ancestors of various clans. The guardian deity blocked the hero's path, but the female deity persuaded him to let the hero pass. The hero descended onto a sacred mountain in a mountain range on a large island.

Seeking a wife, the hero met a mountain god, who offered his two daughters. The hero accepted the younger, beautiful daughter but rejected the elder, less attractive daughter for her ugliness. As a result, he was cursed: his descendants, the rulers, would live short, transient lives like blossoms instead of eternal lives like rock, as explained either by the mountain god or by the elder daughter's own curse.

Soon after marrying, the younger daughter became pregnant in a single night, leading the hero to accuse her of adultery. To prove her faithfulness, she entered a hut and set it ablaze, surviving along with her three sons.

The hero later died and was buried at a specific burial site, recorded under a traditional name. Today, a shrine in a specific region is designated as his official burial site. The hero is worshipped at several shrines, including one dedicated jointly to him and another deity.
Ninigi-no-Mikoto.story:
Ninigi, grandson of the sun goddess Amaterasu, was born from Ame no Oshihomimi and Takuhadachijihime, and was nurtured with special affection by Takamimusubi. Amaterasu sent Ninigi to rule the earth, giving him three sacred treasures: the sword Kusanagi no Tsurugi, the mirror Yata no Kagami, and the jewel Yasakani no Magatama. On his descent to earth, Ninigi was accompanied by several gods, including Uzume, Sarutahiko, Koyane, Futodama, Ishikoridome, and Tamanooya, who became ancestors of various clans. Sarutahiko blocked Ninigi's path, but Uzume persuaded him to let Ninigi pass. Ninigi descended onto Mt. Takachiho in the Kirishima Mountains.

Seeking a wife, Ninigi met the mountain god Oyamatsumi, who offered his two daughters, Sakuyahime and Iwanagahime. Ninigi accepted Sakuyahime but rejected Iwanagahime for her ugliness. As a result, he was cursed: his descendants, the emperors, would live short, transient lives like blossoms instead of eternal lives like rock, as explained either by Oyamatsumi or by Iwanagahime's own curse.

Soon after marrying, Sakuyahime became pregnant in a single night, leading Ninigi to accuse her of adultery. To prove her faithfulness, she entered a hut and set it ablaze, surviving along with her three sons: Hoderi, Hosusero, and Hoori.

Ninigi later died and was buried at E no Goriyo, recorded as "Hyūga no Enoyama no misasagi." Today, Nitta Shrine in Satsumasendai is designated as his official burial site. Ninigi is worshipped at shrines such as Amatsu Shrine and Kirishima-jingu Shrine, and alongside Kuni no Tokotachi at Ise Shrine.

\u014ckuninushi.title: Ōkuninushi
\u014ckuninushi.blind: A divine figure originally given one name was one of many brothers, all seeking to marry a certain princess of a certain land. On the way, his brothers cruelly tricked an injured hare, but the hero healed it by telling it to wash in fresh water and roll in pollen. The hare predicted the hero would win the princess, which came true. Enraged, his brothers killed him twice—once with a burning boulder, once by crushing him in a split tree—but his mother revived him each time with divine help. He fled to the underworld to seek counsel from an underworld god, falling in love with that god's daughter. The underworld god set him four deadly trials (snakes, insects, a burning field, lice-picking), which the hero survived with the daughter's magical aid. He then stole the underworld god's weapons and instrument and fled with the daughter; the underworld god, though angry, blessed him with a new name meaning 'Master of the Great Land.' Using the stolen weapons, the hero defeated his brothers and became ruler of the earthly realm. He married multiple goddesses, including the first princess, the underworld god's daughter, and another princess, fathering many children. A tiny god arrived by sea and helped him build and develop the land, until that tiny god departed to another world. The hero then enshrined another god to help him. Eventually the heavenly deities declared his land must be surrendered to them, sending several messengers who failed or defected, before ultimately the hero ceded his rule to the heavenly deities and withdrew to rule the netherworld.
\u014ckuninushi.story: A divine figure originally named Ōnamuji was one of many brothers (the eighty deities) all seeking to marry Princess Yagamihime of Inaba. On the way, his brothers cruelly tricked an injured hare, but Ōnamuji healed it by telling it to wash in fresh water and roll in pollen. The hare predicted Ōnamuji would win the princess, which came true. Enraged, his brothers killed him twice—once with a burning boulder, once by crushing him in a split tree—but his mother revived him each time with divine help. He fled to the underworld to seek counsel from the god Susanoo, falling in love with Susanoo's daughter Suseribime. Susanoo set him four deadly trials (snakes, insects, a burning field, lice-picking), which Ōnamuji survived with Suseribime's magical aid. He then stole Susanoo's weapons and instrument and fled with Suseribime; Susanoo, though angry, blessed him with the name Ōkuninushi, 'Master of the Great Land.' Using the stolen weapons, Ōkuninushi defeated his brothers and became ruler of the earthly realm. He married multiple goddesses, including Yagamihime, Suseribime, and Nunakawahime, fathering many children. A tiny god, Sukunabikona, arrived by sea and helped him build and develop the land, until Sukunabikona departed to another world. Ōkuninushi then enshrined another god, Ōmononushi, to help him. Eventually the heavenly gods declared his land must be surrendered to them, sending several messengers who failed or defected, before ultimately Ōkuninushi ceded his rule to the heavenly deities and withdrew to rule the netherworld.

Gesar.title: Epic of King Gesar
Gesar.blind: The hero was born miraculously, through a divine or magical conception, sometimes said to descend from a father who was both a sky figure and a holy mountain, and a mother who was a goddess of the watery underworld. As a child he was ugly, dark-skinned, snotty, and troublesome, and was despised. He had two uncles: one, an old and wise elder, supported him, while the other, cowardly and greedy, saw the boy as a threat and tried to harm him. This second uncle banished the hero and his mother to a remote plateau, where the boy grew up living a feral life, clothed in animal skins and wearing a hat of antelope horns. When the hero reached the age of twelve, a horse race was held: whoever won would marry the beautiful daughter of a neighboring chieftain and become ruler of a kingdom. The hero won the race on his miraculous horse, married the chieftain's daughter, and ascended the throne, taking a title meaning "Great Lion, Wish-fulfilling Jewel, Subduer of Foes." With thirty companions he then waged war against enemy lands. While he was away fighting a man-eating demon, his wife was kidnapped by a rival king. The hero returned, used magic to infiltrate the enemy's palace, killed the king, and recovered his wife. He then fought two more foreign kings, and set out to conquer eighteen great fortresses, battling various foreign adversaries. In some versions, at age thirty-nine he retreated to a sacred hill. In old age, in his eighties, he descended briefly into an underworld realm before finally leaving the world of men and ascending to a celestial paradise, from which he may return in the future to save his people from their enemies.

Rama.title: Rama
Rama.blind: The hero, an avatar of a great preserving god, was born to a king and his first wife in a capital city, the seat of a kingdom. His half-brothers were three other princes. At a ceremony in another kingdom, a king offered his daughter in marriage to whoever could string the great bow of a storm god. The hero alone succeeded, breaking the bow, and won the king's daughter as his wife. On the journey home another avatar of the great god challenged him to string a second divine bow; the hero did so successfully and was acknowledged as a form of the great god. The hero and his wife lived happily for twelve years until a stepmother, another wife of his father, invoked an old promise and demanded that the hero be exiled for fourteen years. The hero accepted his father's word, and his wife and a younger brother joined him in exile. They crossed a river and stayed at a hermitage with a sage, where a devoted woman offered the hero half-eaten fruit as a sign of devotion, which he ate out of love. Later, in a forest region, a demoness tried to seduce the hero, was rejected, and threatened his wife; the younger brother cut off her nose and ears. Her brother, a demon king, sought revenge, saw the hero's wife, desired her, and had his uncle lure her away disguised as a deer before kidnapping her to his island kingdom. The hero and his brother, discovering the kidnapping, traveled south, allied with a monkey king, and gained a loyal monkey commander.
Rama.story: Rama, an avatar of the god Vishnu, was born to King Dasharatha and his wife Kausalya in Ayodhya, capital of the kingdom of Kosala. His half-brothers were Lakshmana, Bharata, and Shatrughna. At a ceremony in the kingdom of Mithila, King Janaka offered his daughter Sita in marriage to whoever could string the great bow of the god Shiva. Rama alone succeeded, breaking the bow, and won Sita as his wife. On the journey home another avatar, Parashurama, challenged him to string the bow of Vishnu; Rama did so successfully and was acknowledged as a form of Vishnu. Rama and Sita lived happily for twelve years until Kaikeyi, another wife of Dasharatha, invoked an old promise and demanded that Rama be exiled for fourteen years. Rama accepted his father's word, and Sita and Lakshmana joined him in exile. They crossed a river and stayed at a hermitage with the sage Vasishtha, where a devotee named Shabari offered Rama half-eaten fruit as a sign of devotion, which he ate out of love. Later, at Panchavati, a demoness named Shurpanakha tried to seduce Rama, was rejected, and threatened Sita; Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears. Her brother, the demon king Ravana, sought revenge, saw Sita, desired her, and had his uncle Maricha lure her away disguised as a deer before kidnapping her to his island kingdom of Lanka. Rama and Lakshmana, discovering the kidnapping, traveled south, allied with the monkey king Sugriva, and gained the loyal commander Hanuman.

Bhagiratha.title: Bhagiratha
Bhagiratha.blind: A king, the great-grandson of an earlier king, once performed a great horse sacrifice, but the sacrificial horse was stolen by a sky god and hidden in an underworld realm, where a sage was meditating. The earlier king's 60,000 sons found the horse there and disturbed the sage with their noise; enraged, the sage reduced them all to ashes with his fiery gaze. The duty of performing their funeral rites passed down through generations until it fell to the hero. After becoming king, he went to a great mountain range to practice austerities and invoke a river goddess, asking her to descend from heaven to earth. She warned that her fall would be too powerful to bear unless a great god agreed to catch her in his hair. The hero then performed a thousand-year penance to the great god, who agreed and let the goddess flow through his matted locks for a thousand years before releasing a single drop, which became the river on earth. The river flowed to the underworld realm and performed the funeral rites for the earlier king's sons. Along the way, the river flooded the hermitage of another sage, who swallowed it in anger; only after the hero's pleading did that sage release the river through his ear. The hero then ruled again, his people prospering. He was known for gifting many cows to a sage, and he married his daughter to another sage before dying. Separately, it is said his father, a prior king, died childless, so two of that king's widows conceived the hero together, though the child was born deformed until a crippled sage transformed him into a strong youth.
Bhagiratha.story: King Sagara, great-grandfather of Bhagiratha, once performed a great horse sacrifice, but the sacrificial horse was stolen by the god Indra and hidden in the underworld realm of Patala, where the sage Kapila was meditating. Sagara's 60,000 sons found the horse there and disturbed Kapila with their noise; enraged, the sage reduced them all to ashes with his fiery gaze. The duty of performing their funeral rites passed down through generations until it fell to Bhagiratha. After becoming king, he went to the Himalayas to practice austerities and invoke the goddess Ganga, asking her to descend from heaven to earth. She warned that her fall would be too powerful to bear unless the god Shiva agreed to catch her in his hair. Bhagiratha then performed a thousand-year penance to Shiva, who agreed and let Ganga flow through his matted locks for a thousand years before releasing a single drop, which became the river on earth. The river flowed to Patala and performed the funeral rites for Sagara's sons. Along the way, the river flooded the hermitage of the sage Jahnu, who swallowed it in anger; only after Bhagiratha's pleading did Jahnu release the river through his ear. Bhagiratha then ruled again, his people prospering. He was known for gifting many cows to a sage, and he married his daughter to another sage before dying. Separately, it is said his father Dilipa died childless, so two of Dilipa's widows conceived Bhagiratha together, though the child was born deformed until a crippled sage transformed him into a strong youth.

Agastya.title: Agastya
Agastya.blind: A holy man was born from a mud jar after two divine beings, performing a rite, were overcome by the beauty of a supernatural woman and their seed fell into a jar; from this jar the holy man emerged, along with a twin holy man. He grew into a great ascetic and scholar. He asked for the hand of a princess of a certain realm, whose parents feared she could not endure his austere life, but she accepted him, saying his virtue outweighed comfort, and became his wife. After the wedding she demanded worldly comforts before consummating the marriage, forcing him to seek wealth in society. They had a son who learned sacred verses in the womb and was born reciting them. The holy man ran a school of learning with his wife and students. He reconciled a conflict between two divine armies through an offering for mutual understanding. When all beings journeyed to a great mountain range for a wedding of two deities, the earth tilted, and the holy man was asked to travel to a distant region to restore balance; on his way he commanded a mountain range to lower itself so sun, moon, and living beings could pass, and it obeyed, never rising again. He used his ascetic power to kill two demons who had been luring and destroying thousands of men. In a forest he and his wife met an exiled prince, his wife, and his brother; the holy man gave the prince a divine bow and arrow and warned him of the evil of a demon king, advising that beings must love one another. In another tale, when a king of the gods and his demon rival fought and the demons hid in the sea, the holy man drank up the entire ocean to reveal them.

Sang Hyang Tunggal.title: Acintya
Sang Hyang Tunggal.blind: A theological and symbolic figure represents the ineffable, ultimate nature of a supreme divine principle, one that lies beyond thought, form, and direct worship. This figure serves as a personalized representation of the unknowable nature of a higher power, and for a long period it functioned as a conceptual manifestation of a great god within a particular religious tradition, before another name came into common use for the supreme god. The figure is closely associated with a sun deity: just as the blinding light of the sun cannot be looked at directly, the true nature of the divine principle cannot be fully grasped. In its most common graphical form, the figure appears as a naked man surrounded by flames, his nakedness symbolizing pure consciousness and a state beyond attachment to the senses. The figure appears prominently on special shrines within temples, where it is represented either through an empty throne or as a human figure. It also appears in temple carvings and in a classical style of painting, where it is placed at the uppermost part of a composition, reinforcing ideas of transcendence and cosmic hierarchy, with flames, light, and stillness as recurring motifs. Additionally, the figure is depicted in a form of shadow puppet theatre, shown with radiating flames and a frontal, unmoving posture. In these performances, the figure does not act as a character within the story or interact with others; instead, it serves as a symbolic presence representing ultimate reality, cosmic order, and the source of creation, situating the drama within a larger metaphysical framework rather than advancing the plot itself.

M\u0101ui (M\u0101ori mythology).title: Māui (Māori mythology)
M\u0101ui (M\u0101ori mythology).blind: The hero was born prematurely and, fearing he would become a malevolent spirit, his mother cast him into the sea wrapped in her hair. Sea spirits wrapped him in seaweed, and his grandfather found him on the beach and raised him. The hero later joined his family, where his siblings at first distrusted him but came to admire his shapeshifting powers. Noticing his mother vanished each dawn, the hero blocked the light and followed her, transformed into a bird, down into the underworld. There he found his parents, and his father performed his birth ritual incorrectly, causing the gods to curse the hero and all humanity with mortality. Using a magic fishhook made from his grandmother's jawbone, the hero secretly joined his brothers on a fishing trip, baited the hook with his own blood, and hauled up a giant fish that became a great island. His brothers cut into the fish before proper rites were performed, causing it to writhe and form mountains and valleys instead of flat land. The hero also stole fire by exhausting the fingernails of the fire goddess, escaping her wrathful flames with help from weather gods, and brought back fire-making sticks for his people. He transformed his sister's husband into the first dog after a quarrel, causing his sister to drown herself in grief. Finally, seeking immortality for humankind, the hero attempted to pass through the body of the goddess of death while she slept, but a companion laughed and woke her; she crushed him, making him the first to die and dooming all humans to mortality.

M\u0101ui (Hawaiian mythology).title: Māui (Hawaiian mythology)
M\u0101ui (Hawaiian mythology).blind:
The hero was one of several children of a father and mother figure in the old genealogies. He owned a magic fish-hook, baited with the wing of his mother's pet bird. The hero tricked his brothers while fishing: he caught his hook on the ocean floor, claimed he had hooked a great fish, and told them to paddle hard without looking back. As they strained at the paddles, new landmasses rose from the sea behind them, and thus he created a chain of islands. In another telling, the hero tried to fish up a fish deity, but his mother rose from the water first as a gourd and then as a beautiful woman; his brothers disobeyed his order not to look back, the line broke, and the islands he sought to join into one landmass remained separate.

Next, because his mother complained that her cloth material could not dry since the sun crossed the sky too quickly, the hero climbed a mountain and lassoed the sun's rays with a rope made from his sister's hair, forcing the sun to agree to move more slowly, giving longer days in one season and shorter ones in another.

Though he owned a magic hook, the hero was a poor ordinary fisherman and endured his brothers' teasing, repaying them with tricks.

Seeing that the sky hung too low for people to stand upright, the hero sought his father, traveled to a certain town, and together they braced themselves and pushed the sky up high enough for humanity to live comfortably.

After fishing up the islands, the hero explored them and found them uninhabited despite standing houses. He returned home, pursued a woman, and married her. While fetching water, she was struck and slimed by a long eel. The hero set traps, killed the eel with a stone tool, and buried it; from the burial grew a palm tree, producing the first coconuts.
M\u0101ui (Hawaiian mythology).story:
Māui, a culture hero, was one of four sons of ʻAkalana and his wife Hina. He owned a magic fish-hook called Manaiakalani, baited with the wing of Hina's pet bird. Māui tricked his brothers while fishing: he caught his hook on the ocean floor, claimed he had hooked a great fish, and told them to paddle hard without looking back. As they strained at the paddles, new islands rose from the sea behind them, and thus he created the islands of Hawaii. In another telling, Māui tried to fish up the god of fish, Pimoe, but Hina rose from the water first as a gourd and then as a beautiful woman; his brothers disobeyed his order not to look back, the line broke, and the islands he sought to join into one landmass remained separate.

Next, because his mother Hina complained that the sun crossed the sky too quickly for her bark cloth to dry, Māui climbed the mountain Haleakala and lassoed the sun's rays with a rope made from his sister's hair, forcing the sun to agree to move more slowly, giving longer days in summer and shorter ones in winter.

Though he owned a magic hook, Māui was a poor ordinary fisherman and endured his brothers' teasing, repaying them with tricks.

Seeing that the sky hung too low for people to stand upright, Māui sought his father, traveled to Lahaina, and together they braced themselves and pushed the sky up high enough for humanity to live comfortably.

After fishing up the islands, Māui explored them and found them uninhabited despite standing houses. He returned home, pursued Hina, and married her. While fetching water, Hina was struck and slimed by the Long Eel, Tuna. Māui set traps, killed Tuna with a stone axe, and buried him; from the burial grew a palm tree, producing the first coconuts.

T\u0101ne.title: Tāne
T\u0101ne.blind: A god of forests and birds was the son of the sky father and the earth mother, who once lay in a tight embrace, their many children living in darkness between them. The children grew frustrated at their confinement. One brother, the future god of war, proposed killing their parents, but this god disagreed, suggesting instead that they separate them, sending the sky father upward and leaving the earth mother below. Several brothers tried and failed to part them. Finally, this god lay on his back and pushed with his strong legs, forcing his parents apart, and the sky father rose high above. The god then searched for heavenly lights so his father would be properly adorned, obtaining the stars, moon, and sun and casting them into the sky. Another brother, god of storms, was angry at the separation and joined the sky father, punishing the earth with violent storms, attacking the forests and shattering trees, then attacking the sea, causing the sea god to flee. The sea god's descendants split, some fleeing into the sea as fish, others into the forests as reptiles. Ever since, the sea god has resented the forest god for hiding his children. The forest god gave humans canoes, hooks, and nets to catch fish, while the sea god retaliated with floods and overturned canoes. Later, this god sought a wife, first fathering insects, birds, and plants with non-human females, then molding a woman from soil. He married his daughter without her knowing his identity; upon discovering the truth, she fled to the underworld and became the goddess of death, telling him to raise their children while she awaited them below. He also brought down three baskets of knowledge from the heavens.

Tangaroa.title: Tangaroa
Tangaroa.blind:
The sea deity, a great atua of the sea, is child of the sky father and the earth mother. Together with his brothers—one associated with cultivated food, one with war, one with wild food, and one with forests—he forces apart their parents. Afterward, his brother, the storm deity, attacks him, driving him to hide in the sea. The sea deity becomes father of many sea creatures. His son has two children, one who becomes ancestor of fish and one who becomes ancestor of reptiles. Terrified by the storm deity's assault, the fish flee to the sea while the reptiles flee to the forests. Because the forest deity shelters the runaway reptiles, the sea deity holds a lasting grudge against him. Ever after, people who travel on the sea, acting as representatives of the forest deity, enter the sea deity's hostile realm and must make offerings to him before doing so.

In another account, the sea deity is instead son of a different ancestor figure, and the earth mother is his wife; while he is away she commits adultery with the sky father, and in the battle that follows on the beach the sea deity spears the sky father through both thighs before the earth mother marries the sky father. In yet another tradition the sea deity marries a personification of chilling cold, and they parent several fish-class deities; elsewhere he is said to have a son and nine daughters.

In one island tradition, the sea deity is the origin of fire. A trickster hero travels to obtain fire from him, deliberately takes a forbidden path, angering the sea deity, who tries to kick him to death. The hero overcomes him, forces him to give fire, then kills him, before reviving him again with incantations to comfort his horrified parents.
Tangaroa.story:
Tangaroa, the great atua of the sea, is son of Ranginui (Sky) and Papatūānuku (Earth). Together with his brothers Rongo, Tū, Haumia, and Tāne he forces apart their parents. Afterward his brother Tāwhirimātea, atua of storms, attacks him, driving him to hide in the sea. Tangaroa becomes father of many sea creatures. His son Punga has two children, Ikatere, ancestor of fish, and Tū-te-wehiwehi, ancestor of reptiles. Terrified by Tāwhirimātea's assault, the fish flee to the sea while the reptiles flee to the forests. Because Tāne shelters the runaway reptiles, Tangaroa holds a lasting grudge against him. Ever after, people who travel on the sea, acting as representatives of Tāne, enter Tangaroa's hostile realm and must make offerings to him before doing so.

In another account, Tangaroa is instead son of Temoretu, and Papatūānuku is his wife; while he is away she commits adultery with Rakinui, and in the battle that follows on the beach Tangaroa spears Rakinui through both thighs before Papatūānuku marries Rakinui. In yet another tradition Tangaroa marries Te Anu-matao, and they parent several fish-class deities; elsewhere he is said to have a son, Tinirau, and nine daughters.

In one island tradition, Tangaroa is the origin of fire. The trickster Māui travels to obtain fire from him, deliberately takes a forbidden path, angering Tangaroa, who tries to kick him to death. Māui overcomes him, forces him to give fire, then kills him, before reviving him again with incantations to comfort his horrified parents.

Qat (deity).title: Qat (deity)
Qat (deity).blind: The hero was born when his father, a stone, exploded. He had several brothers, all sharing one title with different epithets (one foolish, one wise, and so on), and a companion, a trickster spirit who could take the form of a spider. The hero created islands and filled them with plants and animals. He carved the first three pairs of men and women from a sacred type of wood and brought them to life by playing drums and making them dance. The trickster companion, envious, carved his own figures, brought them to life, then buried them for a week; when dug up they had rotted, and this is how death began. When his brothers tired of endless daylight, the hero created Night and taught them to sleep, later slicing through Night with a piece of red volcanic glass to make Dawn. One day the hero found sky maidens bathing after removing their wings; he hid one pair so that one maiden had to stay, becoming his wife, later given another name. The hero's mother made her cry, her tears washed away the earth hiding her wings, and she flew off. The hero shot a roped arrow into a great tree reaching into the sky and climbed after her, but the root snapped and he fell to his death, while she escaped. Other versions say he sailed away instead, promising to return, or that he climbed a tall fruit tree to escape his hostile brothers, the tree growing endlessly until his companion blew him a thread to descend. In the most popular version, the hero built a canoe with his companion's help; his brothers stole it, sailed to another island, and together they defeated a giant.
Qat (deity).story: Qat was born when his father, a stone, exploded. He had eleven brothers, all called Tagaro (Tagaro the Foolish, Tagaro the Wise, and so on), and a companion, Marawa, who could take the form of a spider. Qat created islands and filled them with plants and animals. He carved the first three pairs of men and women from dracaena wood and brought them to life by playing drums and making them dance. Marawa, envious, carved his own figures, brought them to life, then buried them for a week; when dug up they had rotted, and this is how death began. When his brothers tired of endless daylight, Qat created Night and taught them to sleep, later slicing through Night with red obsidian to make Dawn. One day Qat found sky maidens bathing after removing their wings; he hid one pair so that a girl named Vinmara had to stay, becoming his wife, later called Ro-Lei. Qat's mother made her cry, her tears washed away the earth hiding her wings, and she flew off. Qat shot a roped arrow into a banyan tree in the sky and climbed after her, but the root snapped and he fell to his death, while she escaped. Other versions say he sailed away instead, promising to return, or that he climbed a nutmeg tree to escape his hostile brothers, the tree growing endlessly until Marawa blew him a thread to descend. In the most popular version, Qat built a canoe with Marawa's help; his brothers stole it, sailed to another island, and together they defeated a giant named Qasavara.

Tagaro.title: Tangaroa
Tagaro.blind: The sea god is the child of the sky god and the earth goddess. Together with his siblings, the gods of forests, cultivated foods, wild foods, and war, he helped forcibly separate their parents. Afterward, the storm god attacked him in fury, forcing the sea god to flee and hide within the sea. The sea god became the father of many sea creatures. His son had two children: one became the ancestor of all fish, the other the ancestor of all reptiles. Terrified by the storm god's onslaught, the fish took refuge in the sea while the reptiles fled to the forests. Because the forest god sheltered these runaway reptiles, the sea god has held a lasting grudge against him. This rivalry reflects a belief that the sea and the land are opposed realms, so people who go fishing or travel by sea are seen as entering the domain of the sea god, the enemy of the forest god who claims humans as his own; for this reason, offerings must be made to the sea god before any sea voyage. In another tradition, a trickster hero seeks fire from the sea god, who is said to be the origin of fire. Advised to reach the sea god's home by the safe path, the hero instead takes the forbidden path of death, enraging the sea god, who tries to kick him to death. The hero fights back, forces the sea god to give him fire, and kills him. When the parents of the hero are horrified, he uses magical chants to bring the sea god back to life.

Kilibob and Manup.title: Kilibob and Manup
Kilibob and Manup.blind: Two brothers, the younger brother and the older brother, lived on an island. The younger brother was a hunter and carver; the older brother was a fisherman. Conflict began when the older brother's wife persuaded the younger brother to carve his identifying pattern on her thighs in exchange for his missing arrow. The older brother interpreted this as adultery. Fighting broke out between the followers of the two brothers. The younger brother escaped by turning into a lizard and hiding inside a tree. The tree was cut down and fell into a bay. From the fallen tree, the younger brother built a great canoe and smaller craft. In one version, a large ship with a funnel and foreign goods rose from the water. The younger brother loaded the vessel with valuable artifacts, animals, and food plants, released beautiful young people from bamboo containers, and sailed away. When the older brother tried to imitate him, his canoes sank and their crews drowned. In some versions, the younger brother offered the older brother a choice between local and foreign goods; the older brother chose bows, arrows, canoes, a root crop, and pigs rather than firearms, small boats, a grain staple, and preserved food — explaining why the outsiders possess ships, guns, and manufactured wealth while local people retained older technologies. The capsized canoe became the island, and its outrigger became a neighboring island. The younger brother's travels also distributed practical knowledge: he rewarded a man with gifts of food plants, house-building plans, canoe-building plans, and cooking instructions, explaining how skills and resources came to be unevenly distributed across the region.
Kilibob and Manup.story: Two brothers, Kulbob (the younger) and Manub (the older), lived on Karkar Island. Kulbob was a hunter and carver; Manub was a fisherman. Conflict began when Manub's wife persuaded Kulbob to carve his identifying pattern on her thighs in exchange for his missing arrow. Manub interpreted this as adultery. Fighting broke out between the followers of the two brothers. Kulbob escaped by turning into a lizard and hiding inside a ngaul tree. The tree was cut down and fell into a bay. From the fallen tree, Kulbob built a great canoe and smaller craft. In one version, a large ship with a funnel and European goods rose from the water. Kulbob loaded the vessel with valuable artifacts, animals, and food plants, released beautiful young people from bamboo containers, and sailed away. When Manub tried to imitate him, his canoes sank and their crews drowned. In some versions, the younger brother offered the older brother a choice between local and European goods; the older brother chose bows, arrows, canoes, taro, and pigs rather than firearms, dinghies, rice, and canned food — explaining why Europeans possess ships, guns, and manufactured wealth while local people retained older technologies. The capsized canoe became Karkar Island, and its outrigger became Bagbag Island. Kulbob's travels also distributed practical knowledge: he rewarded a man named Buroi with gifts of food plants, house-building plans, canoe-building plans, and cooking instructions, explaining how skills and resources came to be unevenly distributed across the region.

Baiame.title: Baiame
Baiame.blind: A creator deity and sky father descended from the sky to the land, shaping rivers, mountains, and forests throughout the lands. He then gave the people their laws of life, traditions, songs, and culture, and created the first initiation site, a sacred ground where boys were initiated into manhood. When he had finished his work, he returned to the sky, and thereafter people called him the Sky Hero, the All Father, or the Sky Father. He is said to have had two wives, one of whom is often identified with a large flightless bird, and with her he had a child, who in other tellings is instead said to be his sibling. It was forbidden to speak his name publicly, and women were forbidden to view drawings of him or to approach his sacred sites, which were often male initiation grounds. In rock paintings he is depicted as a human figure with a large head-dress or hairstyle, shown always in front view with lines of footprints nearby, decorated with waistbands, vertical lines down the body, bands, and dots, while his child or sibling is drawn in profile beside him. In one region, he was believed to have created all the mountains, lakes, rivers, and caves of that area. After finishing his creations there, he leapt back up into the spirit world from a particular mountain, which he flattened with his leap; its flat top remains visible to this day. A nearby cave contains rock paintings, including a large figure of a man thought to represent him, and the site is regarded as sacred.

Djanggawul.title: Djang'kawu
Djanggawul.blind: Three sibling creation ancestors—two sisters and one brother—created the landscape of a continent and covered it with plants and animals. They journeyed by canoe from an island in the east during the night, guided by a bright star, and landed at a coastal site. The sisters were custodians of ceremonial law and carried with them digging sticks, feathered headwear, and sacred objects hidden in a basket and in mats. As they traveled, these objects transformed into various landforms. At the coastal site, they created freshwater wells by plunging their digging sticks into the sand; the sticks then turned into a variety of plant species, while their clap sticks turned into rock formations. At another site, high among the sand dunes, the sisters gave birth to the first members of a clan and performed the first major ceremony of the region. During their journey, the siblings encountered a foreign people cooking a sea creature on an island in a bay; the siblings asked them to leave the land. The ancestors then continued westward, producing more offspring, who became the ancestors of other clans belonging to the same group.
Djanggawul.story: The Djang'kawu were three sibling creation ancestors—two sisters and one brother—who created the landscape of Australia and covered it with plants and animals. They journeyed by canoe from the island of Baralku in the east during the night, guided by the Morning Star, and landed at a place called Yalangbara. The sisters, named Bitjiwurrurru and Madalatj, were the custodians of ceremonial law and carried with them digging sticks, feathered headwear, and sacred objects hidden in a basket and in mats. As they traveled, these objects transformed into various landforms. At Yalangbara, they created freshwater wells by plunging their digging sticks into the sand; the sticks then turned into a variety of plant species, while their clap sticks turned into rock formations. At a site called Balma, high among the sand dunes, the sisters gave birth to the first members of the Rirratjingu clan and performed the first ngarra ceremony, one of the region's major ceremonies. During their journey, the siblings encountered a foreign people cooking a sea creature on an island in a bay; the siblings asked them to leave the land. The Djang'kawu then continued westward, producing more offspring, who became the ancestors of other clans belonging to the same moiety.

Wandjina.title: Wandjina
Wandjina.blind: According to origin stories, the beings were cloud and rain spirits who created the landscape and all its inhabitants, and who continued to hold influence over both. When each spirit found the place where it would die, it painted its own image on a cave wall and then entered a nearby waterhole. The local people later refreshed these paintings as a way of regenerating the life force of the spirits. The beings were said to punish those who broke the law by sending floods, lightning, and cyclones. A closely related creator being was described as a more diffuse life force underlying all things, comparable to a serpent creator figure found in other belief systems; one aspect of this being was embodied in a sacred snake known by its own name. In rock art, the beings were painted in black, red, and yellow on a white background, shown alone or in groups, sometimes alongside figures such as the serpent creator or a root vegetable. They were typically depicted with large upper bodies and heads showing eyes and a nose but no mouth, because they were said to be so powerful they did not need speech, and because if they had mouths the rain would never cease. Around their heads, lines or blocks of color represented lightning emerging from transparent helmets. Each painting and site had its own name, and communities repainted the images, especially in a particular part of the year, to ensure both the continued presence of the spirits and the arrival of the seasonal rains.

Kutkh.title: Kutkh
Kutkh.blind: A raven spirit is central to creation myths. In some tales he is created by a creator being and lets dawn onto the earth by chipping away stones surrounding her. In others he creates himself, sometimes out of an old fur coat, taking pride in his independence. A rugged peninsula is created when he drops a feather while flying over the earth. Islands and continents are created by his defecation, rivers and lakes from his waters. He brings light in the form of the sun and moon—sometimes tricking an evil spirit who captured the celestial bodies, sometimes being tricked himself into releasing them from his bill. His children mate with other animal spirits, creating the peoples that populate the world. He interacts with a wolf spirit, a fox spirit, a bear spirit, a wolverine spirit, a mouse spirit, an owl spirit, a dog spirit, a seal spirit, a walrus spirit, and other spirits, often involving trickery, sometimes winning, sometimes being fooled. In one legend, the mighty raven flew through the cosmos. Tired, he regurgitated the earth from his gut, transformed into an old man, and landed on the empty land to rest. From his first footsteps emerged the first mice. Curious and fearless, they entered his nose while he slept. His sneeze buckled the earth, creating mountains and valleys. His attempts to stamp them out formed the ocean. Further harassment led to a battle between snow and fire, creating the seasons. Thus the variable world emerged from interaction between the raven spirit and the mice. He gave mankind light, fire, language, fresh water, and skills like net-weaving and mating, though he is also portrayed as foolish, hungry, thieving, and selfish.

Nanabozho.title: Nanabozho
Nanabozho.blind:
The trickster spirit, belonging to a certain people, is one of four sons born to a human mother and a spirit father associated with a cardinal direction. The spirit is a shapeshifter, able to take the form of male or female animals or humans, though it most often appears as a rabbit, called by names meaning "Great rabbit" or "Big rabbit." It was sent to Earth by a great spirit to teach its people. One of its first tasks upon arriving was to name all the plants and animals. It is credited as the founder of a religious society, and as the inventor of fishing and of a writing system. As a co-creator of the world, it is called by a name meaning "the Great Hare who created the Earth." As a trickster, the spirit often creates chaos, being greedy and manipulative, but through forming deep relationships with others it becomes more balanced.

In a later legend, the trickster spirit encounters a giant lumberjack, who has been cutting down forests across the land. The spirit confronts the lumberjack in a certain region and asks him to leave without logging any more timber. The two fight for forty days and forty nights. The spirit ends the battle by slapping the lumberjack across the face with a fish from a lake. The lumberjack stumbles, and the spirit pulls at his whiskers, forcing him to promise to leave the area. In another version of the story, the lumberjack falls onto his rear end at the fight's end, and the shape of his buttocks creates a lake.
Nanabozho.story:
Nanabozho, a spirit of the Ojibwe people, is one of four sons born to a human mother and a spirit father called E-bangishimog ("In the West"). Nanabozho is a shapeshifter, able to take the form of male or female animals or humans, though he most often appears as a rabbit, called Mishaabooz ("Great rabbit") or Gitchii-waabooz ("Big rabbit"). He was sent to Earth by Gitche Manidoo to teach the Ojibwe people. One of his first tasks upon arriving was to name all the plants and animals. He is credited as the founder of the Midewiwin, and as the inventor of fishing and of hieroglyphs. As a co-creator of the world, he is called Michabo Ovisaketchak, "the Great Hare who created the Earth." As a trickster, Nanabozho often creates chaos, being greedy and manipulative, but through forming deep relationships with others he becomes more balanced.

In a later legend, Nanabozho encounters the lumberjack Paul Bunyan, who has been cutting down forests across the land. Nanabozho confronts Bunyan in Minnesota and asks him to leave without logging any more timber. The two fight for forty days and forty nights. Nanabozho ends the battle by slapping Bunyan across the face with a Red Lake walleye fish. Bunyan stumbles, and Nanabozho pulls at his whiskers, forcing him to promise to leave the area. In another version of the story, Bunyan falls onto his rear end at the fight's end, and the shape of his buttocks creates Lake Bemidji.

Glooscap.title: Glooscap
Glooscap.blind: After a creator deity formed the first humans, dust from his body became a hero and his twin brother, opposite in nature. The creator gave the hero power to shape a good world, while the twin brother sought only evil. The hero learned that hunters who killed too much would ruin the world he wished to preserve, so he sought out an old grandmother animal spirit, who wove her own body hair into a magical bag. The hero had hidden all the game animals in a river, boasting that people would never need to hunt again, but the grandmother scolded him, saying humans needed hunting to stay strong, so he released the animals. Later, the hero captured a great bird resting on a mountain peak whose wingbeats caused storms; he bound its wings until the air grew too still and hot to breathe, then loosened them just enough to allow bearable weather. In another account, the hero lay motionless for 365 days facing the rising sun, arms outstretched; afterward an old woman was born from dew on stone, a young man from sea foam, and a woman, mother of a people, from plants of the earth. The hero was said to have shaped valleys and other landforms, turned his evil twin to stone, and, as a giant beaver, slapped his tail to raise five islands from the sea. He painted the world's colors, dipping his brush to create his favorite island. He also slew a monstrous frog that had swallowed all the water, releasing rivers and lakes, and gave people earthenware, knowledge of good and evil, fire, tobacco, fishing nets, and canoes.

Wisakedjak.title: Wisakedjak
Wisakedjak.blind: The trickster figure is a spirit being, known by a descriptive title referencing a bird, who appears in the storytelling traditions of a northern indigenous people. He is a figure much like other trickster beings found among neighboring peoples, and his name takes many different forms depending on the language and community telling his story. As with many mythological figures of this kind, the trickster figure's tales are used to explain how various animals came to be as they are, and how certain geographical features of the land came into existence. He is most often portrayed as the one responsible for bringing about a great flood that destroyed the entire world. In other versions of his story, the trickster figure is also credited as one of the beings who took part in creating the world as it exists now, in the aftermath of that destruction. Some accounts say he accomplished this act of creation entirely on his own, relying on his own trickster power and cleverness. Other accounts say instead that he was given a special magic by a supreme creator being, a higher power above him, specifically so that he could use it to remake the world after the flood had destroyed the old one. Thus the trickster figure stands as both a destroyer, through the flood he caused, and a creator, through his role in rebuilding the world afterward, and his adventures continue to be told as explanations for the natural world as it now appears, including its animals and its landscapes.

Coyote (mythology).title: Coyote (mythology)
Coyote (mythology).blind:
The trickster, a clever, animal-like being, appears throughout many traditional stories. In one account, a primal being floating on endless waters is joined by the trickster, and together they sing the world into being. After people are created, the trickster vows to bring evil into the world; the primal being orders the people to destroy him, but the trickster outwits them with cunning, forcing the being to admit the trickster's power equals his own. In another tale, the trickster saves the world from several evil moons that had caused endless winter. In another, after creating all the animals, the trickster calls a council to decide what qualities humans should have; when the animals argue over whose traits to use, the trickster mocks them and secretly destroys the human models the other animals had shaped overnight, leaving only his own model to come alive. In another story, while a creator shapes beings from clay, the trickster tries to do the same but keeps laughing and fails; accused of laughing, he denies it, telling the world's first lie.

In another myth, the trickster's grandson disobeys his mother, enters a forbidden cave, and is transformed into a giant, hairy horned animal. Two sky-dwelling beings kill and eat him. The trickster, aided by a spider, a bird, and an advisor animal's counsel, hides water, sets a trap, and strikes the beings with a hot stone so the spider can catch and kill them. Returning to his grandson's remains, the trickster finds them gone and realizes the boy has become the first riding animal.

Elsewhere, the trickster repeatedly fails to catch fish until his own excrement begins speaking, giving him detailed instructions for fishing, which he then follows successfully. In a related story, a trickster figure climbs a tree to spin a web like a spider but only leaves behind clumps of hair, which become a lichen. In a creation account, the trickster and another transformer reshape the earth's mountains and valleys and turn ancient magical beings into animals, while virtuous descendants become people. In an emergence story, the trickster guides the first humans up from the underworld to the earth, while another creature continues downward, and the trickster alone remains above with the people.

Sky Woman.title: Atahensic
Sky Woman.blind: According to a people's legend, at the time of creation a sky goddess lived in the world above. While digging up a tree she left a hole in the ground that opened onto a great sky beneath which lay water, and she fell through it. Birds caught her and carried her down onto the water, where a giant turtle rose from the depths for her to rest upon. There she gave birth to twin sons, a good twin and an evil twin. The good twin was born normally, but the evil twin burst from her side, killing her. From her death, the good twin created the sky and, from her head, the sun; the evil twin then made darkness to drive the sun away. The good twin made the moon and stars from her breasts and set them, as his sisters, to guard the night. He gave the rest of her body to the earth, calling her the Great Mother, and planted a seed in her corpse from which a grain crop grew as a gift to mankind. In another version, the sky goddess is instead the grandmother of the twins; her daughter was impregnated by the west wind and died giving birth to them. Wishing her body to sustain the people, or through seeds the sky goddess sowed on her grave, the daughter's remains grew into a grain crop, a bean crop, and a squash-like vegetable from her breasts, hands, and navel; a flowering plant from her legs; a berry plant from her heart; a smoking herb from her head; and a root vegetable from her feet.
Sky Woman.story: According to Iroquois legend, at the time of creation the sky goddess Atahensic, also called Sky Woman, lived in the Upper World. While digging up a tree she left a hole in the ground that opened onto a great sky beneath which lay water, and she fell through it. Birds caught her and carried her down onto the water, where a giant turtle rose from the depths for her to rest upon. There she gave birth to twin sons, Hahgwehdiyu (the good twin, called Sapling) and Hahgwehdaetgah (the evil twin, called Flint). Hahgwehdiyu was born normally, but Hahgwehdaetgah burst from her side, killing her. From her death, Hahgwehdiyu created the sky and, from her head, the sun; Hahgwehdaetgah then made darkness to drive the sun away. Hahgwehdiyu made the moon and stars from her breasts and set them, as his sisters, to guard the night. He gave the rest of her body to the earth, calling her the Great Mother, and planted a seed in her corpse from which corn grew as a gift to mankind. In another version, Atahensic is instead the grandmother of the twins; her daughter Tekawerahkwa was impregnated by the west wind and died giving birth to them. Wishing her body to sustain the people, or through seeds Atahensic sowed on her grave, Tekawerahkwa's remains grew into corn, beans, and squash from her breasts, hands, and navel; sunflowers from her legs; strawberries from her heart; tobacco from her head; and purple potatoes from her feet.

Great Peacemaker.title: Great Peacemaker
Great Peacemaker.blind: A figure known as the peacemaker arose among a group of Native peoples in a wooded region. Some said he was born to a mother of one people as a virgin birth; others said he was born into a second people and later adopted by a third. He traveled from settlement to settlement announcing that he came from the west, going east, to spread peace so that the shedding of blood might cease. His first ally was a woman, who became known as the Mother of Nations; she lent her home for meetings of rival tribal leaders and advised him which leaders to approach. His follower, a man famed for oratory from one of the peoples, helped him win the tribes to his vision. When one tribe at first rejected his message, the peacemaker climbed a tree above a great waterfall and had warriors chop it down; he vanished into the rapids below and was presumed dead, but was found alive by a campfire the next morning. Impressed, that tribe became the founding tribe of a confederacy of tribes. The assembled tribes gathered at a lake, planted a tree symbolizing peace, and proclaimed a binding law. He also walked upon a great lake, possessed a canoe that could fly, and traveled healing the sick. He established a council of chiefs, with power shared between men and women in a matrilineal system, women able to depose unfit chiefs. He prophesied that a white serpent would befriend his people then betray them, a red serpent would fight it, a chosen boy would be given great power, and finally a black serpent would defeat both, until a blinding light—himself—ended the conflict and his people accepted the white serpent as a long-lost brother.
Great Peacemaker.story: A prophet known as the Great Peacemaker (also called Deganawida) arose among the Native peoples of the northeast woodlands. Some said he was born to a Huron mother as a virgin birth; others said he was born Onondaga and later adopted by the Mohawk. He traveled from settlement to settlement announcing that he came from the west, going east, to spread peace so that the shedding of blood might cease. His first ally was a woman called Jigonhsasee, who became known as the Mother of Nations; she lent her home for meetings of rival tribal leaders and advised him which leaders to approach. His follower Hiawatha, an Onondaga famed for oratory, helped him win the tribes to his vision. When the Mohawk at first rejected his message, the Peacemaker climbed a tree above a great waterfall and had warriors chop it down; he vanished into the rapids below and was presumed dead, but was found alive by a campfire the next morning. Impressed, the Mohawk became the founding tribe of a confederacy of tribes. The assembled tribes gathered at a lake, planted a Tree of Peace, and proclaimed a Great Binding Law. He also walked upon a great lake, possessed a canoe that could fly, and traveled healing the sick. He established a council of chiefs, with power shared between men and women in a matrilineal system, women able to depose unfit chiefs. He prophesied that a white serpent would befriend his people then betray them, a red serpent would fight it, a chosen boy would be given great power, and finally a black serpent would defeat both, until a blinding light—himself—ended the conflict and his people accepted the white serpent as a long-lost brother.

Hiawatha.title: Hiawatha
Hiawatha.blind: A great spiritual leader and prophet came to a confederation of peoples, and one of the first he met was a wild man who was a cannibal, known as "the man who eats humans." The prophet climbed onto the roof of the man's dwelling and looked down through the smoke hole, where a large vessel of water sat for cooking human flesh. When the wild man came home, he looked into the water and saw the prophet's face reflected back, mistaking it for his own. In that face he saw beauty, wisdom, and strength, and felt shame for his cannibalism. The prophet came down, sat with him, and taught him a law of peace. The man accepted the message and agreed to help spread it among his own people, while the prophet, who suffered a speech impediment, went to convert other groups. The chief of one group was a cruel tyrant, twisted in body and mind, with living snakes in his hair. The prophet charged the reformed man with converting this tyrant, giving him a new name meaning "he who combs." The tyrant, through magic, caused the deaths of the man's three daughters and his wife. Grief-stricken, he wandered stringing shell beads, seeking someone to perform a ceremony of condolence. He found the prophet among another people, who comforted him with words of healing, gifted him shells as symbols of purity, and had him place them on his eyes, ears, and throat. Together they composed laws and a peace hymn, then traveled to unite five groups. A solar eclipse helped convince one reluctant group, and the tyrant was persuaded to join by being offered the position of principal chief; his mind was made straight and the snakes combed from his hair.

White Buffalo Calf Woman.title: White Buffalo Calf Woman
White Buffalo Calf Woman.blind: During a time of famine, the leader sent out two scouts to hunt for food. As they traveled, they saw a white cloud in the distance, and from it emerged a beautiful young woman in white hide clothing, with dark hair, dark skin, and dark eyes. One of the men was filled with lust for her and approached her, telling his companion he intended to claim her as a wife. The companion warned him she seemed to be a sacred woman and that disrespecting her would be dangerous, but he ignored this advice. The second man watched as the first embraced the woman, and a cloud enveloped them both. When it cleared, only the woman remained, along with a pile of the first man's bones. Frightened, the second man began to draw his bow, but the woman beckoned him forward, saying she could see into his heart and knew he did not share the first man's motives. Since she spoke his language, he believed she was of his people and approached. She revealed she was holy, possessing spiritual and supernatural power, and told him that if his people followed her instructions, they would rise again. He promised to obey. She instructed him to return to his camp, summon the council, and prepare a feast for her arrival. She then taught the people seven sacred ceremonies meant to protect the Earth, and gave them a sacred ceremonial pipe. The ceremonies included a purification rite, a vision-seeking rite, a sun dance, a rite of making relatives, a female puberty rite, a ball-throwing rite, and a soul-keeping rite. Each part of the pipe—the stem, bowl, tobacco, breath, and smoke—symbolized the relationships between the natural world, the elements, humans, and the spiritual beings maintaining the cycle of the universe.

Corn Mother.title: Corn dolly
Corn Mother.blind:
In a traditional belief system, the spirit of a grain crop was thought to live amongst the crop as it grew. When the harvest came and the crop was cut down, this spirit was made homeless. To give it shelter, harvesters fashioned the last sheaf of the grain crop into a hollow figure called a straw figure, or an old woman figure. This figure would then house the crop spirit through the winter, until it was ploughed into the first furrow of the new planting season, returning the spirit to the earth.

Different communities practiced their own versions of this custom. Near one city, the person who cut the last ears of the crop shaped them into a doll called the old woman figure, which was carried home on the last wagon of the harvest. In another region, the last sheaf was dressed in women's clothing, called the same figure, brought home on the final wagon, and then thoroughly drenched with water as a charm to bring rain. In a district further south, the oldest married woman of the village shaped the last sheaf into a woman's form; the finest ears were plucked and woven into a wreath, which the prettiest girl in the village carried on her head to present to the local landowner, while the figure itself was laid in the barn to ward off mice. In neighboring villages of that district, two young men carried the figure atop a pole behind the wreath-bearing girl to the landowner's house; he received the wreath and hung it in his hall, while the figure was set atop a woodpile to preside over the harvest supper and dance.
Corn Mother.story:
In traditional pagan European belief, the spirit of the corn was thought to live amongst the grain crop as it grew. When the harvest came and the crop was cut down, this spirit was made homeless. To give it shelter, harvesters fashioned the last sheaf of wheat or other cereal into a hollow figure called a corn dolly, corn mother, or Old Woman. This figure would then house the corn spirit through the winter, until it was ploughed into the first furrow of the new planting season, returning the spirit to the earth.

Different communities practiced their own versions of this custom. Near one city, the person who cut the last ears of corn shaped them into a doll called the Corn-mother or Old Woman, which was carried home on the last wagon of the harvest. In another region, the last sheaf was dressed in women's clothing, called the Corn-mother, brought home on the final wagon, and then thoroughly drenched with water as a charm to bring rain. In a district further south, the oldest married woman of the village shaped the last sheaf into a woman's form; the finest ears were plucked and woven into a wreath, which the prettiest girl in the village carried on her head to present to the local squire, while the Corn-mother herself was laid in the barn to ward off mice. In neighboring villages of that district, two young men carried the Corn-mother atop a pole behind the wreath-bearing girl to the squire's house; he received the wreath and hung it in his hall, while the Corn-mother was set atop a woodpile to preside over the harvest supper and dance.

Kokopelli.title: Kokopelli
Kokopelli.blind: The trickster figure is a fertility deity, usually depicted as a humpbacked flute player, often with feathers or antenna-like protrusions on his head, venerated by certain Indigenous cultures in a desert region. He presides over both childbirth and agriculture, and is also a trickster god who represents the spirit of music. Among one Indigenous people, he carries unborn children on his back and distributes them to women, which is why young girls often fear him. He takes part in rituals relating to marriage, and is sometimes depicted with a consort, a female figure associated with him by that same people. He can be seen on the full and waning moon, much like the figures some see on the moon's surface. He also presides over the reproduction of game animals, and is often shown with animal companions such as wild sheep and deer. He is also associated with sun-bathing animals such as snakes, and water-loving creatures such as lizards and insects. In his role over agriculture, his flute-playing chases away winter and brings about spring. Some tribes, including another Indigenous people, associate him with the rains. He frequently appears alongside another flute-playing deity in depictions of grain-grinding ceremonies. Some tribes say he carries both seeds and babies on his back.
Kokopelli.story: Kokopelli is a fertility deity, usually depicted as a humpbacked flute player, often with feathers or antenna-like protrusions on his head, venerated by some Native American cultures in the Southwestern United States. He presides over both childbirth and agriculture, and is also a trickster god who represents the spirit of music. Among the Hopi, Kokopelli carries unborn children on his back and distributes them to women, which is why young girls often fear him. He takes part in rituals relating to marriage, and is sometimes depicted with a consort, a woman called Kokopelmimi by the Hopi. He can be seen on the full and waning moon, much like the figures some see on the moon's surface. Kokopelli also presides over the reproduction of game animals, and is often shown with animal companions such as rams and deer. He is also associated with sun-bathing animals such as snakes, and water-loving creatures such as lizards and insects. In his role over agriculture, his flute-playing chases away winter and brings about spring. Some tribes, such as the Zuni, associate him with the rains. He frequently appears alongside Paiyatamu, another flutist, in depictions of maize-grinding ceremonies. Some tribes say he carries both seeds and babies on his back.

Maya Hero Twins.title: Maya Hero Twins
Maya Hero Twins.blind: Two brothers were invited to a land of the dead by its two ruling figures for a ballgame, and were defeated and killed. One brother's severed head was placed in a tree, where it spoke to a young woman passing by and impregnated her with its spittle. When she was found to be pregnant, her father and the rulers of that realm accused her of lying and ordered messenger birds to kill her and bring back her heart as proof. The birds spared her instead, presenting the rulers with a fake heart made of tree sap. The young woman then fled to the world above, to the home of the grandmother of the slain brothers, who set trials before accepting her, including gathering a full net of a grain crop from a garden containing only a single plant, which was accomplished with the help of guardian spirits. The young woman gave birth to twin sons, who were mistreated by their grandmother and jealous older half-brothers, until the twins tricked the half-brothers into climbing a tree that grew impossibly tall, transforming them into monkeys. The twins then defeated a boastful bird deity who falsely claimed to be a great celestial body, tricking him into losing his jeweled teeth and ornaments, causing his death from shame. They also destroyed his two arrogant sons, one by trapping him beneath a mountain, the other by poisoning and burying him. The twins later recovered their father's ballgame equipment, hidden by their grandmother, with help from a rodent. Summoned to the land of the dead to play ball against its rulers, they eventually defeated them, avenging their father and uncle. The twins turned their half-brothers into patrons of artists, and were themselves transformed into the sun and the moon.
Maya Hero Twins.story: Two brothers were invited to the underworld by its two ruling lords for a ballgame, and were defeated and killed. When she was found to be pregnant, her father and the lords of the underworld accused her of lying and ordered owl messengers to kill her and bring back her heart as proof.
