Tezcatlipoca.title: Tezcatlipoca
Tezcatlipoca.blind:
The central figure was one of four offspring born to a primordial lord and lady of duality. Together with three sibling deities, given color designations of black, white, blue, and red, he helped create all the other gods, the world, and humanity. His animal counterpart was a great spotted wildcat, and in that form he became known by another name, meaning "mountain heart."

In a myth of successive world-ages, the central figure ruled the first creation, the age of Earth, but a rival culture-hero deity struck him down, destroying that world and transforming him into the wildcat. The rival deity then ruled the next creation, the age of Water, until the central figure struck him down in turn, destroying the third creation, the age of Wind. The two gods were rivals but also collaborators, both instrumental in the various creations of the world.

In legends of a certain city, the central figure deceived the rival deity, who ruled that city, and forced him into exile.

In another creation account, the rival deity and the central figure joined forces to make the world. Before their act, there was only the sea and a primordial crocodilian earth monster. To lure her, the central figure offered his own foot as bait, and the monster ate it, losing him his foot. The two gods then captured her and distorted her body to form the land.
Tezcatlipoca.story:
Tezcatlipoca was one of four sons born to Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl, the primordial lord and lady of duality. Together with his brothers Quetzalcoatl, Huitzilopochtli, and Xipe Totec, called the Black, White, Blue, and Red Tezcatlipocas, he helped create all the other gods, the world, and humanity. His animal counterpart was the jaguar, and in that form he became known as Tepeyollotl.

In the myth of the Five Suns, Tezcatlipoca ruled the first creation, the Sun of Earth, but Quetzalcoatl struck him down, destroying that world and transforming Tezcatlipoca into a jaguar. Quetzalcoatl then ruled the next creation, the Sun of Water, until Tezcatlipoca struck him down in turn, destroying the third creation, the Sun of Wind. The two gods were rivals but also collaborators, both instrumental in the various creations of the world.

In the legends of the city of Tollan, Tezcatlipoca deceived Quetzalcoatl, who ruled that city, and forced him into exile.

In another creation account, Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca joined forces to make the world. Before their act, there was only the sea and a primordial crocodilian earth monster called Cipactli. To lure her, Tezcatlipoca offered his own foot as bait, and Cipactli ate it, losing him his foot. The two gods then captured her and distorted her body to form the land.

Huitzilopochtli.title: Huītzilōpōchtli
Huitzilopochtli.blind:
In the beginning, a creator couple had four sons: the smallest was a war and sun deity, and his brothers were named Precious Serpent, Our Lord Flayed, and Smoking Mirror. The parents ordered the smallest son and Precious Serpent to bring order to the world. Together they made fire, the first man and woman, the Earth, and the Sun.

In another telling, a fierce goddess was sweeping atop a sacred mountain when a ball of feathers fell and impregnated her. Her other children, four hundred sons and a daughter, were enraged at this and conspired to kill her. As they attacked, the youngest son burst from her womb fully armed and grown. He fought his brothers and beheaded his sister, casting her body down the mountain, then chased his brothers until they scattered across the sky as stars. He became the sun, his sister the moon, and his brothers the stars, and ever after the sun chases the moon and stars.

Later, this god led his people from their original home, ordering them to abandon it and take a new name. He left them briefly under his sister's rule; she founded a settlement, but the people resented her, so he put her to sleep and had the people leave without her. She awoke, enraged, and bore a son who later confronted the god and was killed by him; the god tore out his heart and threw it into a lake. He then commanded his people to find that heart and build their city where they saw an eagle on a cactus eating a serpent. They found this sign on a lake island and founded their city there.
Huitzilopochtli.story:
In the beginning, a creator couple had four sons: the smallest was a war and sun deity, and his brothers were named Precious Serpent, Our Lord Flayed, and Smoking Mirror. The parents ordered the smallest son and Precious Serpent to bring order to the world. Together they made fire, the first man and woman, the Earth, and the Sun.

In another telling, a fierce goddess was sweeping atop a sacred mountain when a ball of feathers fell and impregnated her. Her other children, four hundred sons and a daughter, were enraged at this and conspired to kill her. As they attacked, the youngest son burst from her womb fully armed and grown. He fought his brothers and beheaded his sister, casting her body down the mountain, then chased his brothers until they scattered across the sky as stars. He became the sun, his sister the moon, and his brothers the stars, and ever after the sun chases the moon and stars.

Later, this god led his people from their original home, ordering them to abandon it and take a new name. He left them briefly under his sister's rule; she founded a settlement, but the people resented her, so he put her to sleep and had the people leave without her. She awoke, enraged, and bore a son who later confronted the god and was killed by him; the god tore out his heart and threw it into a lake. He then commanded his people to find that heart and build their city where they saw an eagle on a cactus eating a serpent. They found this sign on a lake island and founded their city there.

Mama Ocllo.title: Mama Ocllo
Mama Ocllo.blind:
The goddess was a mother and fertility deity. In one legend she was daughter of a sun god and a moon goddess; in another she was daughter of a creator god and a water goddess. In all versions she was the older sister and wife of the hero-founder, with whom she founded a great city. In some variants they also had a son, and all later rulers were believed descended from the pair.

Most stories say the sun god sent the goddess and the hero-founder to help a people, whose lives he saw were poor, by teaching them. After being created, the siblings journeyed to find the ideal place to settle, knowing they had found it when a golden rod the sun god gave them sank into the ground. Once it sank, they began teaching the people: together they taught better house construction, while the goddess taught the women spinning, sewing, and household duties.

Accounts of her origin vary: in one, she emerges with the hero-founder from an island or cave in a great lake after the sun god created them, sometimes alongside siblings and ten kin-groups who journey together briefly. In another, they originate at a sacred rock. Another account has all the siblings emerge from the middle window of three at a sacred cave, guided by a sign instead of a rod. Historical chroniclers described the goddess and the hero-founder as leaders of a clan from a certain region.

To found the city, the pair carried the golden scepter, descended into a valley, and built the city where the rod sank and vanished. They gathered people, taught them human customs, divided them into food-gatherers and house-builders, and built a temple to the sun at the city's center, where the rod had disappeared.
Mama Ocllo.story:
Mama Ocllo was a mother and fertility goddess. In one legend she was daughter of the sun god Inti and the moon goddess Mama Killa; in another she was daughter of the creator god Viracocha and Mama Qucha. In all versions she was the older sister and wife of Manco Cápac, with whom she founded the city of Cusco. In some variants they also had a son, Sinchi Roca, and all later Inca rulers were believed descended from the pair.

Most stories say Inti sent Mama Ocllo and Manco Cápac to help the Inca people, whose lives he saw were poor, by teaching them. After being created, the siblings journeyed to find the ideal place to settle, knowing they had found it when a golden rod Inti gave them sank into the ground. Once it sank, they began teaching the people: together they taught better house construction, while Mama Ocllo taught the women spinning, sewing, and household duties.

Accounts of her origin vary: in one, she emerges with Manco Cápac from an island or cave in Lake Titicaca after Inti created them, sometimes alongside siblings and ten ayllus who journey together briefly. In another, they originate at the sacred Rock of Origins. Another account has all the siblings emerge from the middle window of three at a cave called Pacariqtambo, guided by a sign instead of a rod. Historical chroniclers described Mama Ocllo and Manco Cápac as leaders of a clan from the Tampu Tocco area.

To found Cuzco, the pair carried the golden scepter, descended into a valley, and built the city where the rod sank and vanished. They gathered people, taught them human customs, divided them into food-gatherers and house-builders, and built the Temple of the Sun at the city's center, where the rod had disappeared.

Bachu\u00e9.title: Bachué
Bachu\u00e9.blind: According to the religion of a people, a goddess—whose name in a local language means "the one with the naked breast"—was a mother goddess and the mother of humanity. She emerged from the waters of a sacred lake carrying a baby in her arms. This child grew up to become her husband, and together they populated the Earth. She was worshipped in a temple located in an area later renamed, which had formerly been called by another name. According to the legend, after the goddess accomplished her goal of giving birth to humanity, she and her husband, a bird deity, transformed into snakes and returned to the sacred lake from which she had first emerged. The story of the goddess was recorded by a foreign chronicler in his book. He wrote that the indigenous people also called her by another name, meaning "the good woman" in their language, and that they worshipped her as one of their principal deities. The chronicler further noted that the people believed the goddess would sometimes return from the underworld to guide her people.
Bachu\u00e9.story: According to Muisca religion, the goddess Bachué—whose name in the Chibcha language means "the one with the naked breast"—was a mother goddess and the mother of humanity. She emerged from the waters of Iguaque Lake carrying a baby in her arms. This child grew up to become her husband, and together they populated the Earth. She was worshipped in a temple located in what is now the municipality of Chíquiza, an area formerly called "San Pedro de Iguaque." According to the legend, after Bachué accomplished her goal of giving birth to humanity, she and her husband, the parrot god, transformed into snakes and returned to the sacred lagoon from which she had first emerged. The story of Bachué was recorded by the Spanish chronicler Pedro Simón in his book Noticias Historiales. He wrote that the indigenous people also called her "Furachogua," a Chibcha term meaning "the good woman," and that they worshipped her as one of their principal deities. Simón further noted that the Muisca believed Bachué would sometimes return from the underworld to guide her people.

Makunaima.title: Makunaima
Makunaima.blind: A figure known by several variant names is recognized as a creator god among various peoples living in a large river-basin region of a continent.
Makunaima.story: Makunaima, also known by variant names, is recognized as a creator god among various ethnic groups living in the Amazon region of South America.

Anansi.title: Anansi
Anansi.blind:
The trickster is a spider figure who outsmarts more powerful beings through cunning. He has a wife and several sons and a daughter, and is said to be related to a sky deity, sometimes even taking on that role himself.

In one tale, the trickster wants to own all the world's stories, which are held by the sky deity. The sky deity sets four tasks: capture a python, a swarm of hornets, a leopard, and a small magical being, betting the trickster's own mother as part of the wager. With his wife's help, the trickster tricks each creature into capture and brings them, along with his mother, to the sky deity, who gathers his chiefs and generals and declares that the stories will now be called by the trickster's name.

In another tale, the trickster tries to hoard all wisdom in a container, hiding it in a tree, but keeps falling. One of his sons mocks him for not tying the container behind him, and in anger the trickster breaks it, scattering wisdom into the rivers so that everyone can now find wisdom.

In another, during a famine, the trickster finds spirits draining a stream using their skulls; he joins them, loses his skull twice by singing their forbidden song, and finally catches his falling skull with his rear end and flees.

In another, the sky deity wants his favorite son to inherit his ceremonial seat by guessing the name of his secretly harvested root vegetable. The trickster tricks the other sons into revealing information, learns the vegetable's name, and secretly teaches it to the favored son, receiving food as thanks along the way.
Anansi.story:
Anansi is a spider trickster figure who outsmarts more powerful beings through cunning. He has a wife and several sons and a daughter, and is said to be related to the creator sky god, sometimes even taking on that role himself.

In one tale, Anansi wants to own all the world's stories, which are held by the sky god. The sky god sets four tasks: capture a python, a swarm of hornets, a leopard, and a dwarf spirit, betting Anansi's own mother as part of the wager. With his wife's help, Anansi tricks each creature into capture and brings them, along with his mother, to the sky god, who gathers his chiefs and generals and declares that the stories will now be called spider stories.

In another tale, Anansi tries to hoard all wisdom in a pot, hiding it in a tree, but keeps falling. His son mocks him for not tying the pot behind him, and in anger Anansi breaks it, scattering wisdom into the rivers so that everyone can now find wisdom.

In another, during a famine, Anansi finds spirits draining a stream using their skulls; he joins them, loses his skull twice by singing their forbidden song, and finally catches his falling skull with his rear end and flees.

In another, the sky god wants his favorite son to inherit his stool by guessing the name of his secretly harvested yam. Anansi tricks the other sons into revealing information, learns the yam's name, and secretly teaches it to the favored son, receiving food as thanks along the way.

Ogun.title: Ogun
Ogun.blind: A powerful deity of war, iron, hunting, and metalworking was among the primordial deities who first came to a world. Using a metal cutting tool and aided by an animal companion, he cleared a path so that the other primordial deities could enter the world, earning him a title meaning "first of the primordial deities to arrive." According to some legends, after the death of a ruler who had reigned twice, once before and once after another ruler, this deity attempted to seize the throne of an empire, but was ousted by a rival successor and sent into exile. In his earthly life, he became the first king of a city. He fought throughout his life on behalf of the people of that city, and was also known by a name associated with that city. According to the stories, when some of his subjects failed to show him proper respect, he killed them, and then killed himself with his own weapon. However, his followers do not believe he died; instead they say he "disappeared into the earth's surface." He vanished into the ground at a specific place, promising to help anyone who called upon his name. He continues to be venerated in several regions associated with his legend.
Ogun.story: A powerful deity of war, iron, hunting, and metalworking was among the primordial deities who first came to Earth. Using a metal machete and aided by a dog, he cleared a path so that the other primordial deities could enter the world, earning him the epithet "first of the primordial deities to come to Earth." According to some legends, after the death of a ruler who had reigned twice, once before and once after another ruler, this deity attempted to seize the throne of an empire, but was ousted by a rival successor and sent into exile. In his earthly life, he became the first king of a city called Ire. He fought throughout his life on behalf of the people of that city, and was also known by a name meaning "of Ire." According to the stories, when some of his subjects failed to show him proper respect, he killed them, and then killed himself with his own sword. However, his followers do not believe he died; instead they say he "disappeared into the earth's surface." He vanished into the ground at a specific place called Ire-Ekiti, promising to help anyone who called upon his name. He continues to be venerated in several regions associated with his legend.

Obatala.title: Ọbatala
Obatala.blind: The hero, king of all divine beings and the oldest among them, was granted by the supreme creator the task of creating the Earth. Given a bag of tools for creation, he was tempted by a trickster spirit and became drunk on a fermented palm drink, failing in his task. His younger sibling seized the bag, used it to create land upon the primeval ocean, and was rewarded with the title "Ruler of the Earth." The hero was then given a new task: to create human beings. Assisted by a helper figure, he took a long metal chain, a snail's shell filled with sand, a white bird, a black animal, and a palm seed, and descended from the sky on the chain. He released the white bird, which scattered the sand to form mountains and valleys, and planted the seed, which grew into a forest. Content with his work, he began molding humans from clay and water, but drank a fermented drink made from the forest he had created, growing drunk and shaping deformed figures. Upon sobering, he vowed never to drink again and to protect people with disabilities forever after. The finished humans were given a metal blade, a farming tool, and a life-force, and they prospered, with the supreme creator breathing life into them, making the hero the father of humanity. In another telling, the hero was a mortal king, founder and ruler of a great city. His rule was disrupted when his rival led a usurpation against him. With the help of his supporters, the hero overcame his rival, caused his death, and retrieved his throne, ruling again as king.
Obatala.story: Obatala, king of all the orishas and the oldest among them, was granted by the Supreme Deity the task of creating the Earth. Given a satchel of tools for creation, he was tempted by the trickster deity Eshu and became drunk on palm wine, failing in his task. His younger brother Oduduwa seized the satchel, used it to create land upon the primeval ocean, and was rewarded with the title "God of the Earth." Obatala was then given a new task: to create human beings. Assisted by Yemoo, he took a long gold chain, a snail's shell filled with sand, a white hen, a black cat, and a palm nut, and descended from Heaven on the chain. He released the white hen, which scattered the sand to form mountains and valleys, and planted the palm nut, which grew into a forest. Content with his work, he began molding humans from clay and water, but drank palm wine made from the forest he had created, growing drunk and shaping deformed figures. Upon sobering, he vowed never to drink again and to protect people with disabilities forever after. The finished humans were given a copper knife, a wooden hoe, and ase (life-force), and they prospered, with the Supreme Deity breathing life into them, making Obatala the father of humanity. In another telling, Obatala was a mortal king, founder and ruler of a great city. His rule was disrupted when Oduduwa led a usurpation against him. With the help of his supporters, Obatala overcame Oduduwa, caused his death, and retrieved his throne, ruling again as king.

Oduduwa.title: Oduduwa
Oduduwa.blind: The founding ancestor was a divine king and progenitor figure who came from a hilltop village and became holder of the title of ruler of a holy city. He served as progenitor of many independent royal lineages among a people. Tradition holds that the founding ancestor and his group disrupted the political structure of thirteen communities led by a rival deity, causing conflict across several generations until a great disease outbreak forced a truce, uniting the communities into a single state under the founding ancestor. Some of the opposing faction left to found new communities near the coast, while others stayed to continue the conflict. Later, a grandson prince, son of a god of iron and war and youngest grandson of the founding ancestor, was the most warlike of the princes. The city suffered raids from remnants of the opposing faction, but the grandson prince learned their secrets from a heroine and ended the raids, bringing lasting peace with her help. The grandson prince spread the model of kingship through his own offspring, establishing dynasties in two prominent kingdoms, then returned home to claim the sacred crown. Up to sixteen princes left the city to found their own kingdoms, all remembered as descendants of the founding ancestor, who is still revered as ancestor by the people. In the creation tradition, the founding ancestor was sent from heaven by the supreme god to create the earth upon the waters, a mission taken from the sibling-consort, the rival deity, who had been given a shell filled with sand and a bird to scatter it. The founding ancestor is symbolized as the bottom half of a gourd vessel, the rival deity as the top. In another story, the rival deity discovered the secret of his spouse, the founding ancestor, and stole her ceremonial robes to wear himself. A separate, outside tradition claims the founding ancestor was son of an ancestral prince, son of a magician king, who fought in a great battle against a religious leader, lost, and migrated from a distant land into another region, founding many kingdoms and dynasties along the way.
Oduduwa.story: Oduduwa was a divine king and progenitor figure who came from the village of Oke Ora and became holder of the title of ruler of Ile-Ife, the Yoruba holy city. He served as progenitor of many independent royal dynasties among the Yoruba. Tradition holds that Oduduwa and his group disrupted the political structure of thirteen communities led by Obatala, causing conflict across several generations until a great smallpox outbreak forced a truce, uniting the communities into a single state under Oduduwa. Some of the opposing faction left to found new communities near the coast, while others stayed to continue the conflict. Later, Oranyan, son of Ogun and youngest grandson of Oduduwa, was the most warlike of the princes. The city suffered raids from remnants of the opposing faction, but Oranyan learned their secrets from Moremi and ended the raids, bringing lasting peace with her help. Oranyan spread the model of kingship through his own offspring, establishing dynasties in two prominent kingdoms, then returned home to claim the crown of Oduduwa. Up to sixteen princes left the city to found their own kingdoms, all remembered as descendants of Oduduwa, who is still revered as ancestor by the Yoruba people. In the creation tradition, Oduduwa was sent from heaven by the supreme god Olodumare to create the earth upon the waters, a mission taken from the sibling-consort Obatala, who had been given a snail shell filled with sand and a rooster to scatter it. Oduduwa is symbolized as the bottom half of a calabash, Obatala as the top. In another story, Obatala discovered the secret of his wife Oduduwa and stole her masquerade robes to wear himself. A separate, non-Yoruba tradition claims Oduduwa was son of Damerudu (also called Lamurudu), son of a magician king named Kisra, who fought in a great battle against a religious leader, lost, and migrated from Arabia into Africa, founding many kingdoms and dynasties along the way.

Mwari.title: Mwari
Mwari.blind: According to a people's tradition, a supreme creator deity is the author of all things and all life, in whom all things exist. This deity is omnipotent and rules over all spirits. The same deity is called by another name by a related people. Reverence for this deity dates back to the age of an ancient king, ruler of a kingdom on a great river. The first official recognition of this deity came from a kingdom, whose most notable ruler was that same king. This worship was incorporated into the religious life of a great stone city. The deity was frequently approached through spirit mediums at shrines located in a range of hills. The deity is regarded as kind and loving, controlling not only creation but also land fertility and the rains that bring blessing. The deity governs the forces of the Earth, including the fortune of journeys and social and political events. Though people sometimes prayed to the deity alone, it was common to use spirit mediums as intermediaries. It was believed that no one had the right to call upon the deity directly without first observing the proper protocol of expressing grievances or giving thanks through spirit mediums, who were possessed by ancestral and other spirits. In one region, the deity was contacted through spirit mediums or spirits; in other regions, the deity spoke to the people through an oracle. It was believed that anyone who defied this spiritual law and attempted to approach the deity directly would develop a skin disease, for the name of this holy, ineffable, and unknowable being was considered sacred and beyond all things.
Mwari.story: According to Shona and Venda tradition, Mwari is the supreme creator deity, the author of all things and all life, in whom all things exist. Mwari is omnipotent and rules over all spirits. The same deity is called Inkhosi by the Northern and Southern Ndebele people. Reverence for Mwari dates back to the age of the ancient king Monomotapa, ruler of the Mutapa Kingdom on the Zambezi River. The first official recognition of Mwari came from the Kingdom of Zimbabwe, whose most notable ruler was Monomotapa. This worship was incorporated into the religious life of Great Zimbabwe. Mwari was frequently approached through spirit mediums at shrines located at Matonjeni in the Matopo Hills. Mwari is regarded as kind and loving, controlling not only creation but also land fertility and the rains that bring blessing. Mwari governs the forces of the Earth, including the fortune of journeys and social and political events. Though people sometimes prayed to Mwari alone, it was common to use spirit mediums as intermediaries. It was believed that no one had the right to call upon Mwari directly without first observing the proper protocol of expressing grievances or giving thanks through spirit mediums, who were possessed by ancestral and other spirits. In northern regions, Mwari was contacted through spirit mediums or spirits; in other regions, Mwari spoke to the people through an oracle. It was believed that anyone who defied this spiritual law and attempted to approach Mwari directly would develop leprosy, for the name of this holy, ineffable, and unknowable God was considered sacred and beyond all things.

Mbombo.title: Mbombo
Mbombo.blind: In the beginning, the creator deity was alone, a giant white in form, while darkness and primordial water covered the whole earth. Feeling intense pain in his stomach, he vomited up the sun, moon, and stars. The sun's heat and light evaporated the covering waters, forming clouds, and in time dry hills emerged from the water. He vomited again, bringing forth nine animals: a leopard, an eagle, a crocodile, a fish, a tortoise, a black leopard-like creature, a white heron, a scarab, and a goat. He also vomited many men, one of whom was white like himself and was set to serve as a divine ruler upon the earth. The nine animals then created the world's other creatures: the heron made all flying birds except one, the crocodile made snakes and a lizard, the goat brought forth horned animals, the scarab made insects, and the fish-creature made all fish. Three of the creator's offspring then set out to finish creation. The first vomited white ants and died; the ants dug deep for dark soil to bury him, transforming the barren sands above. The second offspring created the first plant, from which came all trees, grasses, and flowers. The third made the last bird, a kite. The black leopard-like creature caused trouble, so the creator chased her into the sky, where she became the thunderbolt, leaving people without fire until he taught them to make it from trees. Once creation was complete and peaceful, the creator gave it to mankind and withdrew into the heavens. Meanwhile, a woman of the waters lived in the east, and her son became the first ruler of a people.

Unkulunkulu.title: Unkulunkulu
Unkulunkulu.blind: The ancestor figure is regarded among a group of related peoples as an "old-old one," or ancestor figure. In family and community contexts, such ancestor figures could be male or female, and were treated with great respect by their families. In a broader sense, the ancestor figure also existed as a single, ancient figure, understood to be male, who was regarded as the ancestor of humanity, though this role received little attention. With the spread of a foreign religion among these people, the ancestor figure came to be understood differently — no longer simply as an ancestor, but as a creator deity closely resembling the god of that foreign religion. In this newer form, the creator figure originated from reeds. From these same reeds he then created humans and a kind of livestock. Everything else in creation he made afterward, without drawing on any original source material. After completing all of his creation, the creator figure is said to have forgotten what he had made and abandoned his creations. No myths describe him beyond this point of creation.
Unkulunkulu.story: Unkulunkulu is regarded among the Zulu, Ndebele, and Swati people as an "old-old one," or ancestor figure. In family and tribal contexts, such ancestor figures (called Onkulunkulu in the plural) could be male or female, and were treated with great respect by their families. In a broader sense, Unkulunkulu also existed as a single, ancient figure, understood to be male, who was regarded as the ancestor of humanity, though this role received little attention. With the spread of Christianity among these people, Unkulunkulu came to be understood differently — no longer simply as an ancestor, but as a creator deity closely resembling the Christian God. In this newer form, Unkulunkulu originated from reeds. From these same reeds he then created humans and livestock. Everything else in creation he made afterward, without drawing on any original source material. After completing all of his creation, Unkulunkulu is said to have forgotten what he had made and abandoned his creations. No myths describe him beyond this point of creation.

Abassi.title: Abassi
Abassi.blind: A deity is worshipped by a group of peoples in a region of a country. The source provides no further narrative details about actions performed by this deity, other figures involved, or events that took place. It only identifies this figure as a spirit recognized by these peoples as a deity.
Abassi.story: Abassi is a deity worshipped by the Efik, Ibibio, and Annang peoples of Nigeria. The article provides no further narrative details about actions performed by Abassi, other figures involved, or events that took place. It only identifies Abassi as a spirit recognized by these three peoples as a deity.

Nyame.title: Nyankapon-Nyame-Odomankoma
Nyame.blind: The creator, made the universe—called simply "the Thing." He also created life, and he created death (a personified figure of Death). Mysteriously, the creator himself was later killed by Death, the very death he had created. After his death, life itself returned to awaken him. He revived as a spirit, and from then on lived on as the soul of a second, greater god, becoming that god's personality and successor. Now embodied as this soul, the creator struggled again with Death, managing to withstand Death's venom. The creator then forced Death to eat poison, achieving a total triumph over him. However, despite being defeated, Death remained alive and continued to cause the death of mortals. The creator communicates through a sacred drum, and has an appointed drummer, said to be the most knowledgeable person regarding traditional history. The creator is represented by two animals: the vulture and the spider. In some tellings, a trickster spider figure advised the creator in the creation of humans; in other tellings, the trickster spider figure is simply another name for the creator himself.
Nyame.story: Odomankoma, the creator, made the universe—called simply "the Thing." He also created life, and he created death (Owuo). Mysteriously, Odomankoma himself was later killed by Owuo, the very death he had created. After his death, life itself returned to awaken him. He revived as a spirit called Kra, and from then on lived on as the soul of Nyankopon, becoming Nyankopon's personality and successor. Now embodied as this soul, Odomankoma struggled again with Owuo, managing to withstand Owuo's venom. Odomankoma then forced Owuo to eat poison, achieving a total triumph over him. However, despite being defeated, Owuo remained alive and continued to cause the death of mortals. Odomankoma communicates through a sacred drum, and has an appointed drummer, said to be the most knowledgeable person regarding traditional history. Odomankoma is represented by two animals: the vulture and the spider. In some tellings, the trickster spider Ananse advised Odomankoma in the creation of humans; in other tellings, Ananse is simply another name for Odomankoma himself.

Heitsi-eibib.title: Heitsi-eibib
Heitsi-eibib.blind: The hero is a mythic hero and trickster figure in the mythology of a certain people, associated with the god of the underworld and another deity. He is a shapeshifter, sometimes appearing as an adult, sometimes as a child. In one story, the child hero became an adult and had sexual intercourse with his mother, then suddenly turned into a baby again. He is repeatedly resurrected and engages in deceptive and immoral acts, and these transgressions represent deeper cultural lessons. He has many real tombs in the form of cairns located across certain lands. He is also associated with celestial bodies, including the sun and moon. One of his notable deeds involves defeating a monster associated with the god of the underworld. This monster would sit at the edge of a deep hole and challenge people to throw a stone at his forehead; if anyone accepted, the stone would bounce back and kill the thrower. The hero discovered these deaths and decided to defeat the monster. He went to the monster's location, where the monster challenged him to throw a stone at his forehead. The hero refused the challenge, distracted the monster, and struck him behind the ear instead. The monster lost his balance and fell into the deep hole, dying. In another version, the monster chased the hero after he refused the challenge; they fought and both fell into the pit, but only the monster died, while the hero survived.
Heitsi-eibib.story: Heitsi-eibib is a mythic hero and trickster figure in Khoikhoi mythology, associated with Gaunab and Tsui'goab. He is a shapeshifter, sometimes appearing as an adult, sometimes as a child. In one story, the child Heitsi-eibib became an adult and had sexual intercourse with his mother, then suddenly turned into a baby again. He is repeatedly resurrected and engages in deceptive and immoral acts, and these transgressions represent deeper cultural lessons. He has many real tombs in the form of cairns located in South Africa and Namibia. He is also associated with celestial bodies, including the sun and moon. One of his notable deeds involves defeating Ga-Gorib, a monster associated with Gaunab, the god of the underworld. Ga-Gorib would sit at the edge of a deep hole and challenge people to throw a stone at his forehead; if anyone accepted, the stone would bounce back and kill the thrower. Heitsi-eibib discovered these deaths and decided to defeat Ga-Gorib. He went to Ga-Gorib's location, where Ga-Gorib challenged him to throw a stone at his forehead. Heitsi-eibib refused the challenge, distracted Ga-Gorib, and struck him behind the ear instead. Ga-Gorib lost his balance and fell into the deep hole, dying. In another version, Ga-Gorib chased Heitsi-eibib after he refused the challenge; they fought and both fell into the pit, but only Ga-Gorib died, while Heitsi-eibib survived.

Bumba.title: Bumba
Bumba.blind: A being, known by two names, was the supreme deity of a people.
Bumba.story: Bumba, also known as Mbombo, was the supreme deity of the Bushongo people.

Berossus.title: Berossus
Berossus.blind: In the beginning, a sea creature emerged from the sea and revealed all knowledge to humankind after Creation, teaching people writing, the arts, and sciences. Order was established when a chief god fought and defeated a primordial sea goddess, and from her body the world was formed. After this, a line of ten kings ruled before a great flood, beginning with the first king and ending with the tenth king, spanning a vast number of years. The tenth king was the one who survived the flood, his story closely resembling flood accounts known from other literature of the region. Separately, a queen who was in fact from a foreign land became the subject of mythologizing by outsiders: she was said to be the founder of a great city, daughter of a goddess, and wife of a king, the legendary founder of another city. These are the surviving mythic and legendary fragments preserved from a lost history, transmitted through later quoting authors, describing the creation of the world, the revelation of knowledge to humanity, the genealogy of kings before the flood, the flood itself, and the legendary founding of great cities by mythologized rulers.
Berossus.story: In the beginning, a sea monster named Oannes emerged from the sea and revealed all knowledge to humankind after Creation, teaching people writing, the arts, and sciences. Order was established when the god Bel (Marduk) fought and defeated Thalatte, the primordial sea goddess also known as Tiamat, and from her body the world was formed. After this, a line of ten kings ruled before a great flood, beginning with the first king, Aloros (Alulim), and ending with the tenth king, Xisouthros, spanning 432,000 years. Xisouthros was the king who survived the Babylonian Flood, his story closely resembling the flood account of Utnapishtim/Ziusudra known from other Mesopotamian literature. Separately, a queen named Semiramis, who was in fact Assyrian by origin, became the subject of Greek mythologizing: she was said to be the founder of the city of Babylon, daughter of the Syrian goddess Derketo, and wife of Ninus, the legendary founder of the city of Nineveh. These are the surviving mythic and legendary fragments preserved from the lost History of Babylonia, transmitted through later quoting authors, describing the creation of the world, the revelation of knowledge to humanity, the genealogy of kings before the flood, the flood itself, and the legendary founding of great cities by mythologized rulers.

Apkallu.title: Apkallu
Apkallu.blind: In ancient times, seven demigod sages, part man and part fish or bird, were sent to bring wisdom to humanity. Each was paired with a primeval king who ruled before a great flood. The first of these sages, emerging from the sea, taught humans the arts of civilization, including the story of how the world was created. After the flood, further sages and kings were named, though these later sages were considered human and were called by a different title than the seven demigods. The seven sages were entrusted with tablets recording destinies. One of them was said to have made a set of ritual remedies, which another sage carried up to the world above to gain favor. The sages were also credited with founding seven great cities, and with laying the foundations of a renowned city. In one tale, after the flood, the chief god banished the seven sages to the deep waters, declaring that they would not return. Later, a warrior god persuaded the chief god to leave his temple and fetch the sages back himself, promising to keep order in his absence. But while the chief god was away, chaos broke out, and instead of the sages, human experts were given the task of cleansing the god's shrine. One sage was recorded as the author of a myth about a legendary king. The last of the seven was said to have ascended into heaven. Another version of these stories, written later in a foreign language by a priest, described the first sage rising from the sea to give kings and humans knowledge, including the tale of the world's creation, before further kings ruled until the great flood came.

Yellow Emperor.title: Yellow Emperor
Yellow Emperor.blind:
The culture hero was a legendary sovereign, first among a group of legendary rulers. He is credited with originating a traditional calendar, a religious-philosophical tradition, wooden houses, boats, carts, a directional instrument, the earliest forms of writing, and a ball game. His animal form was a golden dragon.

He was also known by a second name, derived from a hill where he had lived, said to mean "a shaft of a cart." He was also called by a third name, meaning "possessor of a wild animal (bear)," linking him to bear-related legends. His family name was said to be one word, though another account says he took a different name after a river he lived near.

As a cosmological deity he was known by a title meaning "Great Ruler of the Central Peak," and in one text by a title meaning "the deity with four faces." He was identified as a deity of light and thunder, sometimes said to be one and the same with a storm deity; in other accounts that storm deity was instead distinguished as his foremost pupil.

In mythic conflict, the culture hero represented the power of rain and clouds, while his rival, also known by another name, stood for fire and drought.

The culture hero was claimed as ancestor by the royal house of a certain state. His descendants were also thought to have founded a later dynasty.

A later historian, seeking to verify these legends, traveled to sites associated with the culture hero and cross-checked oral traditions against ancient texts, selecting the most reliable accounts to compile a written history beginning with this figure.
Yellow Emperor.story:
The Yellow Emperor was a legendary sovereign and culture hero, first among the Five Emperors. He is credited with originating the traditional calendar, Taoism, wooden houses, boats, carts, the compass needle, the earliest forms of writing, and a ball game called cuju. His animal form was the Yellow Dragon.

He was also known as Xuanyuan, a name derived from a hill where he had lived, said to mean "Chariot Shaft." He was also called Youxiong, meaning "possessor of bears," linking him to bear legends. His family name was said to be Gongsun, though another account says he took the name Ji after a river he lived near.

As a cosmological deity he was known as the Great Emperor of the Central Peak, and in one text as the Yellow Emperor with Four Faces. He was identified as a deity of light and thunder, sometimes said to be one and the same with the Thunder God; in other accounts the Thunder God was instead distinguished as his foremost pupil.

In mythic conflict, the Yellow Emperor represented the power of rain and clouds, while his rival Chiyou, also called the Yan Emperor, stood for fire and drought.

The Yellow Emperor was claimed as ancestor by the royal house of the state of Qi. His descendants were also thought to have founded the Xia dynasty.

A later historian, seeking to verify these legends, traveled to sites associated with the Yellow Emperor and cross-checked oral traditions against ancient texts, selecting the most reliable accounts to compile a written history beginning with the Yellow Emperor.

Ayar Manco.title: Manco Cápac
Ayar Manco.blind:
The founder-hero was born at a cave of origin to a tribal chief, head of a nomadic kin-group. After his father's death, the hero led the group's wandering families toward a fertile valley, defeating three small tribes there and settling in a swampy area between two streams. He founded a great city, dividing it into four districts, though his people remained small compared to powerful neighboring tribes, a confederated group who often attacked the new city. The hero, and later his son, defended the city against these enemies. He married his sister, and together they had a son, his successor. The hero died naturally; his mummified body remained in the city until a later ruler moved it to a sacred temple on an island in a great lake.

In one legend, the hero was son of a creator god, traveling with three brothers and four sisters from the cave of origin, carrying a golden staff given by his father. He eliminated his brothers—turning them to stone or trapping them—to become sole leader, then married his sister and fathered his successor.

In another legend, the hero was son of the sun god and moon goddess, brother of another deity. Sent to earth from the cave of origin with the golden staff, he and his siblings traveled to the city to build a temple honoring the sun god.

A third legend says the hero was son of a sorceress, who enchanted the people of the city into naming her queen. She hid her infant son, declared a divine king would emerge from the cave of origin, and after two years revealed the hero as the new ruler. She then married her son, and they ruled together.
Ayar Manco.story:
Manco Cápac was born at Tamputoco to Apu Tambo, head of a nomadic ayllu. After his father's death, Manco Cápac led the group's wandering families toward the Cusco valley, defeating three small tribes—the Sahuares, Huallas, and Alcahuisas—and settling in a swampy area between two streams. He founded Cusco, dividing it into four districts, though his people remained small compared to powerful neighboring tribes like the confederated Ayarmacas and Pinaguas, who often attacked the new city. Manco Cápac, and later his son Sinchi Roca, defended Cusco against these enemies. He married his sister Mama Uqllu, and together they had Sinchi Roca, his successor. Manco Cápac died naturally; his mummified body remained in Cusco until ruler Pachacuti later moved it to the Temple of the Sun on Isla del Sol.

In one legend, Manco Cápac (called Ayar Manco) was son of Viracocha, traveling with three brothers and four sisters from Paqariq Tampu, carrying a golden staff given by his father. He eliminated his brothers—turning them to stone or trapping them—to become sole leader, then married his sister Mama Ocllo and fathered Sinchi Roca.

In another legend, Manco Cápac was son of the sun god Inti and moon goddess Mama Killa, brother of Pacha Kamaq. Sent to earth from the cave of Pacaritambo with the golden staff, he and his siblings traveled to Cusco to build a temple honoring Inti.

A third legend says Manco Cápac was son of sorceress Mama Waqu, who enchanted the people of Cusco into naming her queen. She hid her infant son, declared a divine king would emerge from Paqariq Tampu, and after two years revealed Manco Cápac as the new ruler. She then married her son, and they ruled together.

Wakan Tanka.title: Wakan Tanka
Wakan Tanka.blind: In the spirituality of a group of people, there is a term for the sacred or the divine, usually translated as "Great Spirit" and occasionally as "Great Mystery." This concept is understood as the power or sacredness that resides in everything, resembling animistic and pantheistic beliefs. Every creature and object is described as holy, or as having aspects that are holy. Part of the term corresponds to the meaning "Great" or "large." Before contact with foreign missionaries of another religion, the people used this term to refer to an organization or group of sacred entities whose ways were mysterious, thus giving rise to the translation "The Great Mystery." In more recent times, an activist from this group promoted the translation "Great Mystery" and argued that the spirituality of his people was not monotheistic, but rather centered on this broader, mysterious sacred power. Related terms for this same sacred concept, or a closely related one, exist in the languages of several neighboring peoples who speak related languages, showing that the idea of a great sacred power or mystery was shared, in some form, among a number of connected groups.
Wakan Tanka.story: In the spirituality of a Plains Native American people, there is a term for the sacred or the divine, usually translated as "Great Spirit" and occasionally as "Great Mystery." This concept is understood as the power or sacredness that resides in everything, resembling animistic and pantheistic beliefs. Every creature and object is described as holy, or as having aspects that are holy. Part of the term corresponds to the meaning "Great" or "large." Before contact with European Christian missionaries, the people used this term to refer to an organization or group of sacred entities whose ways were mysterious, thus giving rise to the translation "The Great Mystery." In more recent times, a Native American activist promoted the translation "Great Mystery" and argued that the spirituality of his people was not monotheistic, but rather centered on this broader, mysterious sacred power. Related terms for this same sacred concept, or a closely related one, exist in the languages of several neighboring peoples who speak languages related to that of the original people, showing that the idea of a great sacred power or mystery was shared, in some form, among a number of connected groups.

Waaq.title: Waaq
Waaq.blind: A word for the sky God appears among several related peoples in a region. In one language, the word still means 'God' today. The word appears in related forms among other groups, each with its own version of the term. Among one people, God is now primarily called by a name borrowed from a neighboring religious tradition, but the old name survives in personal and place names. A clan takes its name from the old word, meaning 'Path of God.' Several towns and villages in the region carry the old name within them. The word also appears in a neighboring language meaning 'protector,' and is found in that tradition's sacred text. Some traditions link the word to a particular region. A mystic wrote that the word was once a generic name for God, comparing it to another people's concept of a sky deity. Among these peoples, the old word was the name of God in a pre-monotheistic-religion faith believed to have been held by a broader ethnic-linguistic group. This belief was likely carried to the region by speakers of an ancestral language who migrated from a northern area during an early era. This faith may share roots with other major religious traditions, though it is not derived from them. This ethnic-linguistic group was also among the first peoples to practice a bodily rite central to those other traditions. In recent times, use of the old name has declined significantly following the arrival of a newer religion in the region.
Waaq.story: Waaq (also spelled Waaq or Waaqa) is the name given to the sky God among several related peoples, including the Oromo and Somali. In the Oromo language, Waaqa still means 'God' today. The word appears in related forms among other groups: the Konso call God Waaqa, the Rendille call God Wax, the Bayso call God Wah or Waa, the Daasanach call God Waag, the Hadiyya call God Waaʔa, and the Burji call God Waacʼi. Among the Somali, God is now primarily called by an Arabic-derived name, Allaah, but the old name Waaq survives in personal and place names. The Somali clan Jidwaaq take their name from Waaq, meaning 'Path of God.' Several towns and villages in Somalia carry the name Waaq within them. The word Waaq also appears in Arabic meaning 'protector,' and is found in the Quran. Some traditions link Waaq to the Harari region. A Sufi mystic named Ibn Arabi wrote that Waaq was once a generic name for God, comparing it to the Turkic peoples' concept of Tengri. Among the Oromo and Somali, Waaq, Waaqa, or Waaqo was the name of God in a pre-Islamic monotheistic faith believed to have been held by Cushitic peoples. This belief was likely carried to the Horn of Africa by speakers of a proto-Cushitic language who migrated from North Sudan during the Neolithic era. This faith may share roots with the Religions of the Book, though it is not derived from them. The Cushites were also among the first peoples to practice circumcision, a rite central to Abrahamic religions. In recent times, use of the name Waaq has declined significantly following the arrival of Islam in the Horn of Africa.

Oannes.title: Apkallu
Oannes.blind:
In an ancient myth, seven demigods—wise beings sometimes depicted as part man and part fish, or part man and part bird—were sent by the gods to bring wisdom and civilization to humanity. Each was paired with a primeval king who ruled before a great flood. After the flood, further sages and kings arose, though these later sages, called by a special term for 'human experts,' were considered fully human.

The first of the seven, a sage known by two names, emerged to teach humans the arts of civilization, including the recitation of a creation myth. The seven sages were also said to have laid the foundations of a great city and to have founded seven cities, listed by name in the original account. One temple hymn credits them with enlarging a temple.

The sages were entrusted with the tablets of destiny. One of them, a named sage, crafted twenty-one healing poultices, which were given to another god to carry up to the world above so that he might gain merit.

In another tale, the sages, described as fish-creatures, were banished by a great god into a body of primeval waters after the flood. Later, another god persuaded the great god to leave his temple and retrieve the banished sages. While the great god was away, chaos broke out, and instead of the sages returning, human craftsmen were given the task of cleansing the great god's shrine.

Figurines representing the sages, including fish-men and bird-headed hybrids, were placed in homes for protective rituals. One sage was credited as the author of a legendary tale.
Oannes.story:
In ancient Mesopotamian myth, seven demigods known as the Apkallu—wise beings sometimes depicted as part man and part fish, or part man and part bird—were sent by the gods to bring wisdom and civilization to humanity. Each was paired with a primeval king who ruled before a great flood. After the flood, further sages and kings arose, though these later sages, called Ummanu, were considered fully human.

The first of the seven, Oannes (also called Uanna), emerged to teach humans the arts of civilization, including the recitation of the creation myth, the Enūma Eliš. The seven sages were also said to have laid the foundations of the city of Uruk and to have founded seven cities: Eridu, Ur, Nippur, Kullab, Kesh, Lagash, and Shuruppak. One temple hymn credits them with enlarging a temple.

The sages were entrusted with the tablets of destiny. One of them, Anenlilda, crafted twenty-one healing poultices, which were given to the god Nudimmud to carry up to the world above so that he might gain merit.

In another tale, the sages, described as fish-creatures, were banished by the god Marduk into the primeval waters called Abzu after the flood. Later, the god Erra persuaded Marduk to leave his temple and retrieve the banished sages. While Marduk was away, chaos broke out, and instead of the sages returning, human craftsmen (Ummanu) were given the task of cleansing Marduk's shrine.

Figurines representing the sages, including fish-men and bird-headed hybrids, were placed in homes for protective rituals. One sage, Lu-Nanna, was credited as the author of the Myth of Etana.
